A01.title: Loan Review
A01.scenario: A lender uses application details to estimate whether a borrower will default during the next year. First, z = −3 + 0.04 × DTI + 1.2 × D − 0.03 × I combines the details into a log-odds score. Then p = 1 / (1 + exp(−z)) converts that score to an estimated probability. D is 1 if the applicant had the specified prior delinquency and 0 if not. The coefficients are supplied model settings; this exercise does not fit them from data.
A01.task: Use the values below to calculate the score, estimated probability, dollars lost if default occurs, and expected loss. Then compare the probability with the stated review cutoff. The cutoff is a policy choice, separate from the model's estimate.
A01.interpretation: Expected loss combines how often default is estimated to happen with how many dollars are expected to be lost if it happens. It is an average across comparable loans under the stated assumptions, not a certain loss on this applicant. The cutoff determines when this policy requests review; it does not make the probability more accurate. Calibration checks whether predicted chances match observed rates among similar cases over the same time period.

z.title: Combined score z (log-odds)
hints: Start at −3, add 0.04 × DTI and 1.2 × D, then subtract 0.03 × I.
z.explanation: This score combines the applicant details using the model's fitted weights. Debt and a past delinquency add to the score here; income subtracts from it. The score can be negative or positive and is not itself a probability. Zero corresponds to a 50% estimated chance; a negative score means below 50%.

p.title: Estimated default probability
hints: Calculate 1 / (1 + exp(−z)) using your score.
p.explanation: The score can be negative or positive, but a probability must stay between 0 and 1. The sigmoid formula converts the score into that range. A score of zero becomes 0.50, or a 50% estimated chance; a negative score becomes a probability below 50%. This estimate does not decide whether to lend.

lossOnDefault.title: Loss if default occurs
hints: Multiply the loan exposure by the loss fraction.
lossOnDefault.explanation: This estimates how many dollars would remain lost if the borrower defaults. Multiply the loan amount at risk by the fraction not recovered. It describes the size of a loss in the default scenario, not how likely default is.

EL.title: Expected credit loss
hints: Multiply the default probability by the loss if default occurs.
EL.explanation: This is a probability-weighted average across comparable loans: default chance times the dollars lost if default happens. The result is an average for planning under these assumptions, not a prediction that this applicant will lose that exact amount.

decision.title: Send to review?
hints: Compare the probability with the threshold. Equality triggers review.
decision.explanation: Compare the estimated probability with the chosen review cutoff. At or above the cutoff, the policy sends the application to a person for review. The cutoff is a policy setting; it is not learned by the probability formula, and review does not mean rejection.

workedExplanation: The calculation gives an estimated average loss of about $399 per comparable loan under these assumptions. That does not mean this applicant will cost exactly $399: the borrower either defaults or does not, and actual recovery can differ. The 9.975% estimate also needs calibration evidence before it should be trusted for real decisions. The 8% cutoff sends this example to review; review is not the same as rejection.

The two multiplications answer different questions. Multiplying $10,000 by 0.40 estimates the dollars still lost in the default scenario. Multiplying that $4,000 by the 9.975% default chance weights the loss by how often that scenario is expected across similar loans. Probability: p = 1 / (1 + exp(−(−2.2))) = 1 / (1 + exp(2.2)) ≈ 1 / (1 + 9.025) ≈ 0.09975, or 9.975%. The sigmoid keeps the estimate between 0% and 100%.
Loss if default occurs: $10,000 × 0.40 = $4,000. Expected loss: 0.09975 × $4,000 ≈ $399. The first number is conditional loss; the second includes the chance of default.

Compare 9.975% with the 8% review cutoff. Since 9.975% is greater than or equal to 8%, this policy sends the case to review. The comparison chooses an action; it does not change the estimated probability.

A02.title: A Fraud Split
A02.scenario: A card issuer separates payments into two groups: payments from a new device and payments from a trusted device. In this fictional training sample, each group contains both fraudulent and legitimate transactions.
A02.task: Calculate how mixed the full group is, then calculate how mixed each device group is. Weight each smaller group by how many transactions it contains before comparing the split with the original group. Finally, average three supplied tree scores and check whether the forest and first tree cross the same challenge cutoff.
A02.interpretation: Gini impurity describes how mixed a group is: zero means every transaction in that group has the same label. A positive reduction means the proposed split made these training groups more uniform; it does not prove the split will work on later transactions or that the forest scores are calibrated probabilities. The forest score is an average of the supplied scores, not a vote count.
A02.summary: The split reduces training-set impurity by {{result.gain}}. The average forest score is {{result.score}}; at the supplied cutoff, challenge: {{result.decision}}.

labels.counts: Transaction counts (new fraud, new legitimate, trusted fraud, trusted legitimate)

parent.title: Parent Gini impurity
hints: Combine both device groups to find the fraud and legitimate shares.
parent.explanation: Start with every transaction before asking the device question. Count fraud and legitimate outcomes within this full group, then square each group’s share and subtract both squares from 1. This gives the parent impurity: zero would mean the parent contains only one outcome, while a larger value means the two outcomes are more mixed.

newGini.title: New-device Gini impurity
hints: Divide each new-device count by the total in that group, square both shares, then subtract their sum from 1.
newGini.explanation: Now look only at payments from new devices. Divide each outcome count by the number of new-device payments to get the two shares. Squaring the shares gives more weight to the outcome that makes up most of the group; subtract their sum from 1 to measure how mixed this child is.

trustedGini.title: Trusted-device Gini impurity
hints: Use only trusted-device records when calculating the two class shares.
trustedGini.explanation: Repeat the same calculation using only trusted-device payments. Keeping this group separate matters because a split is useful when its resulting groups are each less mixed than the original group.

weighted.title: Weighted child impurity
hints: Multiply each child impurity by its share of all records, then add.
weighted.explanation: The new-device and trusted-device groups have different sizes. Multiply each child’s impurity by that child’s share of all transactions, then add them. This weighted average represents the mixedness across the full set; a larger child has more influence because it contains more cases.

gain.title: Reduction in impurity
hints: Subtract weighted child impurity from parent impurity.
gain.explanation: Subtract the weighted child impurity from the parent impurity. A positive difference means the groups are less mixed after the split in these training examples. It measures this split’s improvement on this sample, not its accuracy on future payments.

score.title: Average forest score
hints: Add the supplied tree scores and divide by the number of trees.
score.explanation: Add the three supplied tree scores and divide by three because the forest combines their numeric scores by an arithmetic average. The result is a model score for this example, not automatically a well-calibrated chance of fraud.

decision.title: Does the forest trigger a challenge?
hints: Challenge when the average score is at least the threshold.
decision.explanation: Compare the forest average with the stated cutoff. The policy says to challenge at or above the cutoff, so equality counts as a challenge. The cutoff changes the action; it does not change the score or prove that the payment is fraudulent.

firstDecision.title: Would the first tree trigger a challenge?
hints: Compare the first supplied tree score with the same threshold.
firstDecision.explanation: Check the first tree against the same cutoff to see what that tree alone would do. The forest can make a different choice because it combines all three scores; that comparison shows the effect of averaging, not which action is financially best.

readAloud: For one group, find the fraud share and the legitimate share, square each share, and subtract both squares from 1. Zero means the group is all one outcome; larger values mean more mixing. For the split result, calculate each child’s impurity and weight it by the fraction of all records in that child before adding.

The gain is the parent group’s impurity minus the size-weighted impurity after splitting. A positive gain means the split made the training groups more uniform; it does not by itself show how the split performs on new transactions.

Add the scores from all B trees and divide by B to get their arithmetic average. This combines numeric scores; it is not majority voting, and the average is not automatically a calibrated probability.
workedExplanation: The split makes the two training groups more uniform than their parent, so its weighted impurity is lower. This says how the split fits these supplied records; a separate later sample is needed to check whether the pattern holds beyond them.

The child groups must be weighted by size. A small group should not count as much toward the full result as a larger group. The forest score is a separate calculation: average the three numeric scores, then compare that average with the policy cutoff. Neither Gini gain nor the score average proves probability calibration.
workedArithmetic: Parent Gini uses all ten records: 4/10 are fraud and 6/10 are legitimate, so G = 1 − (4/10)² − (6/10)² = 0.48. This number summarizes the mixture before the device split.

For new devices, use only that group’s four records: 3/4 are fraud and 1/4 are legitimate, so its impurity is 1 − (3/4)² − (1/4)² = 0.375. For trusted devices, use six records: 1/6 are fraud and 5/6 are legitimate, giving about 0.2778.

The new-device group is 4/10 of all records and the trusted-device group is 6/10. Weighted child impurity = (4/10 × 0.375) + (6/10 × 0.2778) ≈ 0.3167. Gain = 0.48 − 0.3167 ≈ 0.1633, a reduction on these training records.

The forest average is (0.75 + 0.50 + 0.25) ÷ 3 = 0.50. Since 0.50 is below the 0.60 cutoff, this policy does not challenge. The first tree’s 0.75 is above the same cutoff, so that tree alone would challenge. The scores are supplied for arithmetic practice and are not confirmed probabilities.

A03.title: Update a Credit Score
A03.scenario: This teaching example starts with a supplied model score of −2, then adds two already-fitted tree corrections. Each correction is multiplied by a learning rate before it is added. The tree outputs are held fixed so you can compare the arithmetic for rates 0.50 and 0.25; in a real retraining, changing the rate can also change what later trees learn.
A03.task: For each learning rate, update the score after tree 1 and tree 2, then convert the final score to a default probability. Compare each probability with the same 0.18 (18%) review cutoff. Keep the score updates separate from the probability conversion and the later policy decision.
A03.interpretation: A tree adds an amount to the model's log-odds score. That amount is not a change in probability percentage points: the sigmoid's curve means the same score correction can move probabilities by different amounts depending on the starting score. This hand calculation holds the two fitted tree outputs fixed. During full training, a new learning rate can change which corrections later trees learn. The review cutoff is a policy assumption, not a setting learned by the sigmoid.

F1.title: Score after tree 1
hints: Add first learning rate × first tree output to the starting score.
F1.explanation: This first tree makes a correction to the starting score. Multiply its supplied output by the learning rate so the correction is deliberately smaller, then add it to the starting log-odds score. This is a score change, not a probability-point change.

F2.title: Score after tree 2
hints: Add first learning rate × second tree output to the preceding score.
F2.explanation: The second tree adds another scaled correction to the score after tree 1. Use that updated score as the starting point, multiply the second tree's output by the same learning rate, and add. The tree outputs are held fixed in this exercise.

p.title: Probability with the first learning rate
hints: Apply 1 / (1 + exp(−score)) to the score after both trees.
p.explanation: Only after both tree corrections are added do we convert the final score to a probability. The sigmoid keeps the answer between 0 and 1. Zero means 50%; a negative score means below 50%. A score change does not translate into the same number of percentage points everywhere.

smallF1.title: Comparison score after tree 1
hints: Restart from the original score and use the comparison learning rate.
smallF1.explanation: For a fair comparison, restart from the same original score and the same tree output. The only changed input is the learning rate, which scales how much of this tree's correction is added.

smallF2.title: Comparison score after tree 2
hints: Add comparison learning rate × second tree output.
smallF2.explanation: Continue from the comparison score after tree 1. Scale the second supplied tree output by the comparison learning rate and add it. The fixed trees isolate the arithmetic effect; retraining can produce different trees too.

smallP.title: Probability with the comparison rate
hints: Apply the logistic function to the comparison score after both trees.
smallP.explanation: Convert the completed comparison score into a probability using the same sigmoid as before. Keeping the conversion the same lets us compare the two learning rates on equal terms. This is still an estimated chance, not a decision by itself.

decision.title: Review with the first learning rate?
hints: Compare the first probability with the review threshold.
decision.explanation: Apply the stated review policy to the first probability: review when it is at least the cutoff. The calculation shows what this policy would do; it does not show that the cutoff is optimal or fair.

smallDecision.title: Review with the comparison rate?
hints: Compare the comparison probability with the same threshold.
smallDecision.explanation: Use the same review cutoff for the comparison probability. Holding the policy fixed shows whether the changed score crosses the boundary; equality also triggers review.

readAloud: Start with the score from the previous trees. Scale the new tree's correction by the learning rate, then add it. Once the updated score is ready, the sigmoid converts it to a probability. The supplied tree corrections stay fixed in this exercise, so the comparison isolates the learning-rate arithmetic.

Once the updated score is ready, the sigmoid converts it to a probability. The supplied tree corrections stay fixed in this exercise, so the comparison isolates the learning-rate arithmetic.

workedExplanation: At learning rate 0.50, the model adds half of each supplied correction. The final probability is about 19.78%, just above the 18% review cutoff, so this example's policy requests review. At 0.25, it adds one quarter of each correction and estimates about 15.45%, below the same cutoff. This result is specific to the fixed starting score and two fixed tree outputs; a newly trained model could learn different trees.

The score corrections live on the log-odds scale. Adding 0.4 to a score does not add 40 percentage points to default risk. The sigmoid bends that scale into probabilities, so the same score-sized correction can have a different probability effect at different starting points. Ranking, calibration, and a policy decision answer different questions and still need their own checks.
workedArithmetic: Rate 0.50, tree 1: scale the supplied correction before adding it: F₁ = −2 + (0.50 × 0.8) = −1.6. The model adds half of this tree's proposed 0.8 score correction.
Rate 0.50, tree 2: start from the updated score: F₂ = −1.6 + (0.50 × 0.4) = −1.4. The trees contribute in sequence, so tree 2 does not restart from −2.
Convert only the finished score: p = 1 / (1 + exp(1.4)) ≈ 0.1978 = 19.78%. Compare this estimated chance with 18%; because it is at least 18%, the policy sends the case to review.
Rate 0.25, tree 1: return to the same starting score and scale the same supplied correction: F₁ = −2 + (0.25 × 0.8) = −1.8.
Rate 0.25, tree 2: continue from −1.8: F₂ = −1.8 + (0.25 × 0.4) = −1.7. This isolates the arithmetic effect of the smaller rate while the two tree outputs stay fixed.

Convert −1.7 with the same sigmoid: p = 1 / (1 + exp(1.7)) ≈ 0.1545 = 15.45%. This is below the same 18% cutoff, so this policy does not send the case to review. The lower cutoff outcome does not prove that 0.25 is the best training choice.

A04.title: Group Savings Behavior
A04.scenario: A bank looks at four fictional customers’ savings rates. K-means starts with two centers, 10% and 60%, and puts each customer in the nearer group. The group labels describe similar rates; they are not grades or credit decisions.
A04.task: Compare each customer’s rate with both starting centers and assign the closer one. Move each center to the average rate of its assigned customers. Then compare a new customer’s rate with the updated centers. If two distances tie, this exercise assigns the customer to group 1.
A04.interpretation: A center is the average behavior of the customers currently in its group, not a savings target. The groups summarize this sample and do not establish creditworthiness. Rates and distances are measured in percentage points here; because there is only one measurement, absolute and squared distances select the same nearest center.

groups.title: Group for each customer
hints: Compare each rate with both starting centers. Enter 1 or 2 in customer order.
groups.explanation: Compare every customer’s savings rate with both starting centers. Assign the customer to the closer center because K-means forms groups from feature similarity. Keep the original centers fixed during this pass; the exercise specifies group 1 for an exact tie.

c1.title: Updated center 1
hints: Average the rates assigned to group 1.
c1.explanation: Take the arithmetic mean of the savings rates assigned to group 1. The average moves center 1 toward the customers it now represents; it summarizes this sample and is not a recommended savings level.

c2.title: Updated center 2
hints: Average the rates assigned to group 2.
c2.explanation: Average the rates assigned to group 2 for the same reason. Recomputing the center makes it represent the current members before the next assignment step.

d1.title: New customer distance to center 1
hints: Take the absolute difference between the new rate and updated center 1.
d1.explanation: Measure how far the new customer’s rate is from updated center 1 by taking the absolute difference. Absolute value makes distance nonnegative, so a customer below the center is just as far away as one equally far above it.

d2.title: New customer distance to center 2
hints: Take the absolute difference between the new rate and updated center 2.
d2.explanation: Use the same absolute-difference calculation for updated center 2. Keeping the distance definition identical makes the two centers comparable; here the result is measured in percentage points.

group.title: Group for the new customer
hints: Choose the updated center with the smaller distance. Enter 1 or 2.
group.explanation: Choose the center with the smaller distance because it is the closer group under the selected feature. The number 1 or 2 is only a group label; it does not describe a customer’s quality or ability to repay.

readAloud: Move center j to the arithmetic average of the examples assigned to group C_j. Add their feature values and divide by how many examples are in that group. This makes the center describe its current members; it does not create a target customers should reach.

Distance d_ij is the absolute difference between example i’s value and center j. Compare distances using the same feature units; the smaller value identifies the nearer center. A distance describes similarity on the selected input only, not a person’s creditworthiness.

These are two distinct steps: first membership changes, then the group averages change. Repeating them may settle into stable groups, but the result depends on the starting centers and chosen feature.

The new customer is assigned using the updated centers and the same distance rule. A group describes which savings-rate pattern is nearest in this example; it does not establish what the customer should save or whether they qualify for credit.

Average the rates in each group: center 1 becomes (10 + 20) ÷ 2 = 15 percentage points; center 2 becomes (60 + 70) ÷ 2 = 65 percentage points.

For the new customer at 35, compare distances to the updated centers: |35 − 15| = 20 and |35 − 65| = 30 percentage points. Since 20 is smaller, assign this customer to group 1. This is a similarity assignment, not a judgment about the customer.

A05.title: Rank Unusual Payments
A05.scenario: Three transactions were each sent through three randomly built isolation trees. A path length counts how many random cuts a tree made before a transaction stood alone. The first three lengths belong to A, the next three to B, and the final three to C.
A05.task: First average the three path lengths for each transaction so one unusually short or long tree does not decide the result by itself. Then calculate s = 2^(−average path / c), using the supplied normalization value c = 4. Rank the scores for the one investigation slot available. This ranks unusualness; it does not decide whether a transaction is fraud.
A05.interpretation: A transaction isolated in fewer cuts receives a higher anomaly score under this exercise’s convention. The score describes how unusual it looks compared with the reference data; it is neither a fraud probability nor proof of wrongdoing. Investigators need other evidence to reach that conclusion.
A05.summary: Average paths for A, B and C: {means}. Their anomaly scores: {scores}. The highest-scoring transaction number is {top} (1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C).

labels.paths: Path lengths (three for A, then B, then C)

means.title: Average path lengths for A, B and C
hints: Average each consecutive group of three path lengths.
means.explanation: Each transaction has three path lengths because three trees examined it. Average those lengths to give every tree equal weight and summarize how many cuts were usually needed. A smaller mean means the transaction was separated sooner in this set of trees.

scores.title: Anomaly scores for A, B and C
hints: For each mean h, calculate 2^(−h / c).
scores.explanation: Convert each average path into the score defined above. This puts the path lengths on a scale where a larger value means the transaction was isolated more easily. Keep the direction of this exact formula in mind when ranking; other libraries may return scores with the opposite direction.

top.title: Highest-scoring transaction (A=1, B=2, C=3)
hints: The shortest average path gives the largest score.
top.explanation: Compare the three scores and select the largest because this exercise defines larger values as more unusual. The answer chooses the first case to investigate under a one-case review limit; it does not declare that case fraudulent.

readAloud: For each transaction, add its path lengths and divide by the number of trees to get the average path. Then divide that average by c, the supplied path-length normalization value, make the result negative, and raise 2 to that power. With c = 4, an average path of 2 gives 2 to the negative one-half power, about 0.7071. Shorter paths produce larger scores under this exercise’s convention.
workedExplanation: A’s average path is 2 cuts, compared with 4 for B and 6 for C. Because a shorter path makes the exponent less negative, A gets the largest score: about 0.7071. This says A was easiest to separate from the reference transactions; it does not mean there is a 70.71% chance of fraud. A normal seasonal or high-value payment can also be unusual.

The normalization turns path length into a score that can be ranked consistently. It does not add labels about fraud, intent, or customer harm. With only one investigation slot, A is the first case to review, and the investigator’s findings provide evidence the score does not contain.
workedArithmetic: 0.7071 > 0.5 > 0.3536, so the one available investigation slot goes to A.

A06.title: Forecast Settlement Outflows
A06.scenario: Treasury has two known daily outflows: $110 million on the previous day and $116 million on the latest day. A fitted ARIMA(1,1,0) example uses the latest change to forecast the next change: multiply it by 0.5. The example sets drift to zero and assumes future forecast errors are zero. Outflows and forecasts are in millions of dollars.
A06.task: Forecast the next two outflow levels without using the later actual. Add the stated $10 million planning buffer to the first forecast. Only after making that forecast, use the later actual to compare its absolute error with a simple forecast that repeats the latest observed level.
A06.interpretation: The first forecast is a level in dollars; the step between levels is a change, also measured in dollars. The later actual is reserved for evaluation because treasury could not know it when making the forecast. A one-day comparison does not show that the model or a fixed cash buffer will work reliably in the future.

change.title: Latest observed change
hints: Subtract the previous outflow from the latest outflow.
change.explanation: Find how much the outflow changed between the two observations. Subtract the earlier level from the latest level; this separates the movement from the starting amount. Here 116 − 110 = 6, so outflow rose by $6 million.

nextChange.title: First predicted change
hints: Multiply the latest change by the autoregressive coefficient.
nextChange.explanation: Use the fitted coefficient to carry part of the latest movement into the next day. Multiplying 6 by 0.5 gives a predicted increase of $3 million. The coefficient is a learned relationship in this example, not a guarantee that half the change will repeat.

next.title: First forecast outflow
hints: Add the predicted change to the latest observed level.
next.explanation: A predicted change is not yet the amount treasury needs to fund. Add the $3 million forecast increase to the latest observed level of $116 million to estimate the next level: $119 million.

secondChange.title: Second predicted change
hints: Multiply the first predicted change by the same coefficient.
secondChange.explanation: For a second day ahead, the first predicted change is the newest available change because the real next-day observation has not happened yet. Apply the same coefficient: 0.5 × 3 = $1.5 million.

second.title: Second forecast outflow
hints: Add the second predicted change to the first forecast level.
second.explanation: Add the second predicted change to the first predicted level. This produces a two-day-ahead level of $120.5 million while using only information available when the forecast was made.

liquidity.title: Liquidity to hold
hints: Add the buffer to the first forecast.
liquidity.explanation: The exercise asks treasury to keep a fixed $10 million cushion above the first-day forecast. Add 10 to 119 to get $129 million. This is a planning choice supplied by the example, not a promise that it covers every possible outflow.

modelError.title: Model absolute error
hints: Take the absolute difference between the later actual and first forecast.
modelError.explanation: Once the forecast is recorded, compare it with the later actual. Absolute error is the distance between them without regard to whether the forecast was too high or too low: |125 − 119| = $6 million. The actual is allowed here because this is evaluation after the event.

baselineError.title: Last-value forecast absolute error
hints: Take the absolute difference between the later actual and latest observed level.
baselineError.explanation: Compare the same actual outflow with a simple alternative that predicts no change and repeats the latest observed $116 million level. Its absolute error is |125 − 116| = $9 million. Using the same date and actual makes the comparison meaningful, though one date is not enough to choose a forecasting method.

readAloud: First subtract the previous outflow from the latest one to find the observed change. Multiply that change by 0.5 to forecast the next change, then add it to the latest outflow to return to a dollar level. For example, 116 minus 110 is a $6 million increase; half is a predicted increase of $3 million; 116 plus 3 gives a $119 million forecast. The hatted y values are predictions, not later observations.
workedExplanation: The latest change is a $6 million increase. The fitted coefficient carries half of that change forward, so the predicted increase is $3 million and the first forecast is $119 million. Adding the $10 million planning buffer gives $129 million to hold. The actual later outflow of $125 million is used only after forecasting: the model missed by $6 million, while repeating the latest $116 million level missed by $9 million.

The model has lower absolute error on this one date, but one day does not establish which method will work better across future conditions. The $10 million buffer is a chosen planning cushion, not a prediction interval or a statistically verified safety margin. Treasury should compare many later dates and account for the cost of having too much or too little cash.
workedArithmetic: Latest change = 116 − 110 = 6 million. Next predicted change = 0.5 × 6 = 3 million; next level = 116 + 3 = 119 million.
Second predicted change = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 million; second level = 119 + 1.5 = 120.5 million.
Liquidity holding = 119 + 10 = $129 million.
Model absolute error = |125 − 119| = $6 million; last-value error = |125 − 116| = $9 million.

Multiply that change by 0.5 to forecast the next change, then add it to the latest outflow to return to a dollar level. For example, 116 minus 110 is a $6 million increase; half is a predicted increase of $3 million; 116 plus 3 gives a $119 million forecast. The hatted y values are predictions, not later observations.

A07.title: Trace Shared Connections
A07.scenario: This small undirected teaching graph has five links: A—Device 7, B—Device 7, B—Merchant 9, C—Merchant 9, and D—Device 8. Accounts are letters; squares or names identify shared devices and merchants. “Undirected” means each listed relationship can be followed either way.
A07.task: Find the separate connected groups and count every account, device, and merchant in each group. Then count each account’s direct neighbors, trace the fewest links from A to C, and decide whether these relationships alone prove fraud. A path counts links, not nodes or money transfers.
A07.interpretation: A component groups nodes that can reach one another by following links. Degree counts only an account’s direct neighbors; shortest-path length counts the links along the least-link route. These are descriptions of the recorded network. Sharing a device or merchant can be legitimate and does not prove misconduct.
A07.summary: Component sizes: {sizes}. Account degrees: {degrees}. The shortest A-to-C path uses {edges} edges. Do the links prove fraud? {proof}.

components.title: Number of connected components
hints: Group nodes that can reach one another by following links.
components.explanation: A connected component is a set of nodes that can reach one another by following one or more listed links. Count the disconnected groups, not just the account letters; devices and merchants are also nodes.

sizes.title: Nodes in each component
hints: Count devices and merchants as well as accounts; enter the larger component first.
sizes.explanation: For each component, count all its nodes, including shared devices and merchants as well as accounts. The connected group A–B–C has five nodes; D and Device 8 have two. Listing the larger first follows the requested answer format.

degrees.title: Account degrees (A, B, C, D)
hints: Count direct neighbors of each account.
degrees.explanation: Degree counts the direct neighbors of each account, not every account reachable through a longer route. A touches Device 7 once, B touches Device 7 and Merchant 9 twice, C touches Merchant 9 once, and D touches Device 8 once: [1, 2, 1, 1].

edges.title: Edges on the shortest A-to-C path
hints: Trace A → Device 7 → B → Merchant 9 → C.
edges.explanation: Trace the shortest route and count each link crossed: A to Device 7, Device 7 to B, B to Merchant 9, and Merchant 9 to C. That is four edges. The route visits five nodes, so counting nodes would give a different quantity.

proof.title: Do these links prove fraud?
hints: A shared relationship alone does not establish an account’s intent.
proof.explanation: No. The graph shows recorded relationships, not the reason they exist or whether anyone intended harm. Shared devices and merchants can be ordinary. Treat the path as a lead for investigation, then check the edge definitions, timing, match quality, and other evidence.

readAloud: A connected component is a group of nodes where each node can reach every other by following links. Degree counts the direct neighbors of one account. For the route from A to C, follow A to Device 7, then B, Merchant 9, and C: that is four links. Count links when measuring the path, and count accounts, devices, and merchants when measuring component size. A connection records a relationship, not proof of fraud.
workedExplanation: A, B, and C belong to one five-node component because links connect them through Device 7 and Merchant 9. D and Device 8 form a second two-node component. In the account order A, B, C, D, their direct-neighbor counts are 1, 2, 1, and 1. The shortest A-to-C route uses four links.

These numbers tell us how the supplied records connect. They do not say that money moved along every link: the graph includes shared devices and merchants, not just transfers. A shared device can belong to a household, and many customers can pay the same merchant. Investigators need reliable link definitions and other evidence before drawing conclusions about intent.
workedArithmetic: The first component is {A, B, C, Device 7, Merchant 9}: 5 nodes. The second is {D, Device 8}: 2 nodes.
Account degrees in A, B, C, D order are [1, 2, 1, 1].
A → Device 7 → B → Merchant 9 → C uses 4 edges. These shared relationships do not prove fraud.

formulas.readAloud: A connected component is a group of nodes where each node can reach every other by following links. Degree counts the direct neighbors of one account. For the route from A to C, follow A to Device 7, then B, Merchant 9, and C: that is four links. Count links when measuring the path, and count accounts, devices, and merchants when measuring component size. A connection records a relationship, not proof of fraud.

A08.title: A Small Attention Calculation
A08.scenario: This toy exercise uses two tokens: “loss” and “narrowed.” It supplies already-scaled attention scores and a numeric value for each token. These made-up values let us follow the arithmetic; they are not FinBERT weights or predictions.
A08.task: First apply softmax to the two attention scores so the token weights add to 1. Use those weights to combine the token values into h. Then a separate teaching classifier turns [2h, 0, −2h] into positive, neutral, and negative probabilities. Assign a label automatically only if the largest class probability reaches the supplied 70% threshold.
A08.interpretation: The attention weights say how the toy calculation combines token values; the later class probabilities describe the three sentiment labels. Both sets add to 1, but they answer different questions. The representation h is not a probability, and the toy arithmetic is not an explanation of a real FinBERT decision.
A08.summary: Attention weights: {weights}. Class probabilities (positive, neutral, negative): {probabilities}. Automatic label assignment: {decision}.

weights.title: Attention weights (loss, narrowed)
hints: Exponentiate both logits, then divide each exponential by their sum.
weights.explanation: Softmax turns the two supplied scores into shares that add to one. Exponentiate each score, then divide each by the total. Here exp(ln 1)=1 and exp(ln 3)=3, giving weights 0.25 and 0.75. This says how the toy calculation mixes token values, not which sentiment label is most likely.

h.title: Combined token representation h
hints: Multiply each token value by its attention weight and add.
h.explanation: Multiply each supplied token value by its attention share and add: 0.25 × (−1) + 0.75 × 1 = 0.50. This combined representation h carries token information forward to the next calculation. It is a number used by the teaching classifier, not a 50% sentiment probability.

classLogits.title: Class logits (positive, neutral, negative)
classLogits.explanation: Use the toy rule [2h, 0, −2h] to create one score for each of the three labels. With h = 0.50, the scores are [1, 0, −1]. They are unnormalized scores, so do not read them as probabilities yet.

probabilities.title: Class probabilities (positive, neutral, negative)
hints: Exponentiate all three class logits and divide each by their sum.
probabilities.explanation: Apply softmax to the three class scores so the resulting positive, neutral, and negative probabilities add to one. The class probabilities are distinct from the earlier token attention weights: one set mixes words, the other compares labels.

decision.title: Assign a label automatically?
hints: Compare the largest class probability with the automatic-label threshold.
decision.explanation: Find the largest of the three class probabilities and compare it with the supplied 70% cutoff. The largest is about 66.52%, below the cutoff, so the rule sends the sentence to human review. Passing this cutoff would still not guarantee a correct label.

readAloud: For each token, raise e to its supplied score. Divide each result by the sum of both exponentials. This softmax step makes the attention weights add to 1: with scores ln(1) and ln(3), the weights are 1/4 and 3/4. These are shares used to combine token values, not chances that either word is positive.

Multiply each token value vᵢ by its attention weight aᵢ and add the contributions to get h. With values −1 and 1 and weights 0.25 and 0.75, h is 0.25 times −1 plus 0.75 times 1, which equals 0.50. h is a combined representation, not a sentiment probability. The separate class scores are converted to probabilities afterward.

The teaching classifier assigns scores 2h, zero, and negative 2h to positive, neutral, and negative. Here h is 0.50, so those scores are 1, 0, and −1. Softmax across these three scores creates class probabilities. This is an invented classroom rule, not the output layer used by FinBERT.
workedExplanation: The second token receives three quarters of the attention weight, so its value contributes more to h. That makes the toy classifier lean positive, but its largest estimated class probability is only about 66.52%. This does not mean the text is an investment recommendation, and a token weight alone does not explain a real transformer.

The attention softmax allocates weight across tokens. The class softmax allocates probability across positive, neutral, and negative labels. Since 66.52% is below the 70% auto-label cutoff, this example sends the result to a person. The cutoff is a routing rule, not proof that the model is correct when it passes.
workedArithmetic: Exponentiated attention logits are exp(ln 1) = 1 and exp(ln 3) = 3. Weights are 1/4 = 0.25 and 3/4 = 0.75.
Softmax denominator ≈ 2.718 + 1 + 0.368 = 4.086. Class probabilities are approximately [66.52%, 24.47%, 9.01%].
66.52% < 70%, so the largest class score does not meet the automatic-label threshold; use human review.

formulas.readAloud: For each token, raise e to its supplied score. Divide each result by the sum of both exponentials. This softmax step makes the attention weights add to 1: with scores ln(1) and ln(3), the weights are 1/4 and 3/4. These are shares used to combine token values, not chances that either word is positive.

A09.title: Retrieve, Then Calculate
A09.scenario: A question and three passages are represented by toy two-dimensional number vectors. A contains the old-period revenue, B contains the new-period revenue, and C is about branch locations. The two revenue amounts use the same units and accounting basis.
A09.task: Compare the question vector with each passage using cosine similarity and retrieve the two highest-ranked passages. Then calculate growth as (new revenue − old revenue) ÷ old revenue. Search ranks candidate evidence; the calculation must use both revenue values.
A09.interpretation: Cosine similarity ranks passages by vector direction; it is not a probability that the passage is true or answers the question. A supported growth answer needs both periods, the same revenue definition, and checked arithmetic. A citation should point to the passages that support the stated figures.
A09.summary: Chunk similarities (A, B, C): {similarities}. Revenue growth: {growth}.

labels.docs: Document coordinates (A then B then C)

similarities.title: Cosine similarities for A, B and C
hints: Divide the dot product of the query and each document by the product of their lengths.
similarities.explanation: Compare the query vector with all three passage vectors using the stated cosine formula. This measures direction after accounting for each vector’s length, so it ranks candidates of different sizes more fairly. The highest score here belongs to B (0.80), but that score is not a probability of correctness.

growth.title: Revenue growth
hints: Subtract old revenue from new revenue, then divide by old revenue.
growth.explanation: Use the two retrieved revenue figures. Subtract the old $100 million from the new $120 million to find a $20 million increase, then divide by the starting $100 million: 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20, or 20%. Dividing by the old value expresses growth relative to where revenue began.

readAloud: For each passage, calculate the dot product with the question vector and divide by the question length times the passage length. The result compares direction after accounting for vector size. In this example the query length is 1 and each passage length is 5, so the similarities are 0.60 for A, 0.80 for B, and 0 for C. The score ranks possible matches; it is not a chance the passage is correct.

In two dimensions, multiply the first coordinates and add the product of the second coordinates. To find a vector’s length, square each coordinate, add the squares, then take the square root. For example, a document vector with coordinates 3 and 4 has length √(9 + 16) = 5. The dot product and lengths supply the parts used to calculate cosine similarity.

Subtract old-period revenue from new-period revenue to find the increase. Divide by the old amount so the change is measured relative to where it started. Here (120 − 100) ÷ 100 = 0.20, or 20%. Both figures need the same units and revenue definition. The retrieved passages provide inputs; arithmetic calculates the growth.
workedExplanation: Passage B ranks first at 0.80 and A second at 0.60, so the two retrieved passages contain the new and old revenue figures. A score of 0.80 is a similarity score, not an 80% chance that an answer is correct. The unrelated branch passage ranks last.

With both source figures available and on the same basis, growth is (120 − 100) ÷ 100 = 0.20, or 20%. Retrieval found the inputs; the arithmetic and source checks support the conclusion. If either figure or its definition were missing, the system could not justify this comparison.
workedArithmetic: The query has length 1. Each document vector has length 5: √(3² + 4²) = √(4² + 3²) = √(0² + 5²) = 5.
Cosine similarities are A = 3/5 = 0.60, B = 4/5 = 0.80, C = 0/5 = 0. Retrieve B, then A.
Revenue growth = (120 − 100) / 100 = 0.20 = 20%. Both revenue chunks are needed to support this comparison.

The result compares direction after accounting for vector size. In this example the query length is 1 and each passage length is 5, so the similarities are 0.60 for A, 0.80 for B, and 0 for C. The score ranks possible matches; it is not a chance the passage is correct.

S01.title: Check the Evidence Before Retrieval
S01.scenario: A filing parser is checked before retrieval is evaluated. Table integrity counts tables retaining all required headers, rows and units. Section coverage counts required sections present. Numeric error counts wrong numbers or units in audited cells.
S01.task: Calculate table integrity, section coverage, numeric error rate and numeric correctness using the audit counts.
S01.interpretation: Tables, sections and cells are separate units of evaluation. High section coverage cannot compensate for an incorrectly extracted debt figure.
S01.summary: Table integrity: {integrity}; section coverage: {coverage}; numeric error: {error}; numeric correctness: {correct}.

labels.intact: Tables with every required element intact
labels.wrong: Cells with a wrong number or unit

integrity.title: Table integrity rate
hints: Divide intact tables by audited tables.
integrity.explanation: Divide the number of tables with all required headers, rows, and units intact by the number of tables audited. Here 7 of 8 are intact, or 87.5%. This counts whole tables, so it does not say whether the separate numeric cells were correct.

coverage.title: Section coverage
hints: Divide required sections present by required sections audited.
coverage.explanation: Divide the required sections found by the number of required sections checked. Here 9 of 10 appear, or 90%. Section presence does not guarantee that its table or figures were extracted accurately.

error.title: Numeric extraction error rate
hints: Divide wrong numeric cells by audited numeric cells.
error.explanation: Divide the cells with a wrong value or unit by all numeric cells audited. Six of 200 is a 3% extraction error rate. This counts cells, not tables or sections.

correct.title: Numeric correctness rate
hints: Subtract the numeric error rate from 1.
correct.explanation: Subtract the error rate from 1 because each audited cell is either correct or counted as an extraction error under this exercise’s definition. One minus 3% is 97% numeric correctness. A high overall rate can still hide an error in a critical debt figure.

readAloud: For table integrity, divide fully intact tables by all audited tables. For section coverage, divide the required sections found by all required sections checked. Each proportion has a different unit: whole tables versus document sections. Neither tells whether every number in a table is correct.

Count audited numeric cells that contain a wrong number or unit, then divide by all audited numeric cells to get the error rate. Subtract that rate from 1 to get correctness under this exercise’s definition. Here 6 of 200 cells are wrong, so error is 3% and correctness is 97%. A critical error can still matter even when the overall rate is small.
workedExplanation: The retriever cannot reliably recover information that parsing omitted or corrupted. A filing can have most sections present and still support a materially wrong answer. These are separate audit measures with explicit classroom definitions, not an invitation to average table, section, and cell percentages into one score.

An intact table is a whole-table success, whereas a numeric error is counted cell by cell. A single table can therefore contain multiple erroneous cells, and the three scores need not move together. Their averages cannot establish whether a critical debt or covenant value is usable.
workedArithmetic: Table integrity = 7/8 = 87.5%. Section coverage = 9/10 = 90%.
Numeric extraction error = 6/200 = 3%. Numeric correctness = (200 − 6) / 200 = 97%.
The counts do not reveal whether the six incorrect cells contain financially material figures.

formulas.readAloud: For table integrity, divide fully intact tables by all audited tables. For section coverage, divide the required sections found by all required sections checked. Each proportion has a different unit: whole tables versus document sections. Neither tells whether every number in a table is correct.

the number of tables audited
required sections found in the document
the number of sections the audit expected

Subtract that rate from 1 to get correctness under this exercise’s definition. Here 6 of 200 cells are wrong, so error is 3% and correctness is 97%. A critical error can still matter even when the overall rate is small.

S02.title: Did It Answer the Whole Question?
S02.scenario: An answer rubric lists required components for each question. All supplied components are correct; no extra unsupported claims are present.
S02.task: Count questions with every required component, then calculate question-level exactness and pooled component completeness.
S02.interpretation: Exactness gives each question equal weight. Pooled completeness gives each required component equal weight. Missing a critical fact may matter more than the aggregate score suggests.
S02.summary: Fully answered questions: {complete}. Exactness: {exactness}. Component completeness: {completeness}.

labels.correct: Correct supplied components for each question

complete.title: Fully answered questions
hints: Count positions where supplied and required component counts are equal.
complete.explanation: A question counts as fully answered only when every required component is supplied correctly. Q1 and Q4 meet that rule; Q2 and Q3 do not, even though Q2 has some correct pieces. The result is two complete questions.

exactness.title: Answer exactness
hints: Divide fully answered questions by the number of questions.
exactness.explanation: Divide fully answered questions by all questions. Two out of four gives 50%. Each question gets one equal vote, whether its rubric has one required fact or several.

required.title: Total required components
hints: Add the required component counts.
required.explanation: Add the required component counts for all four questions: 2 + 3 + 1 + 4 = 10. This is the denominator for the pooled completeness rate.

correct.title: Total correct components supplied
hints: Add the correct supplied component counts.
correct.explanation: Add the supplied correct components: 2 + 2 + 0 + 4 = 8. Because the example assumes supplied components are correct and no unsupported extras appear, this count captures the completed parts.

completeness.title: Component completeness
hints: Divide total correct supplied components by total required components.
completeness.explanation: Divide the eight correct components by the ten required components: 8/10 = 80%. This weights each component equally, unlike exactness, which weights each question equally. Neither score tells us whether the missing facts were financially important.

readAloud: Exactness counts questions whose every required component is correct and divides by all questions. Completeness pools the correct components and divides by all required components. Here exactness is 2 of 4, or 50%; completeness is 8 of 10, or 80%. These measures weight the units differently and do not say whether a missing fact is critical.
workedExplanation: The system supplied most required facts but fully answered only half the questions. Reporting 80% alone would hide the incomplete answers. Components are equally weighted in this exercise; missing a critical covenant or denominator may matter more than missing a minor descriptive detail.

Exactness gives every question one vote. Pooled completeness gives every required component one vote. A partly answered three-component question can contribute two correct components but zero fully correct questions. Neither measure alone establishes whether a missing component is financially critical.
workedArithmetic: Q1 supplies 2/2 components and Q4 supplies 4/4; both are complete. Q2 supplies 2/3 and Q3 supplies 0/1, so both are incomplete.
Exactness = 2 fully answered questions / 4 questions = 50%.
Required components = 2 + 3 + 1 + 4 = 10. Correct supplied components = 2 + 2 + 0 + 4 = 8. Completeness = 8/10 = 80%.

formulas.readAloud: Exactness counts questions whose every required component is correct and divides by all questions. Completeness pools the correct components and divides by all required components. Here exactness is 2 of 4, or 50%; completeness is 8 of 10, or 80%. These measures weight the units differently and do not say whether a missing fact is critical.

all questions evaluated
required components correctly supplied across all questions

A10.title: Choose a Feasible Portfolio
A10.scenario: A portfolio can use only the listed stock shares; the rest goes into bonds. The example treats stock and bond returns as uncorrelated, meaning neither tends to move up or down with the other. Their future returns are estimates, and the portfolio must reach the stated minimum expected annual return.
A10.task: For each allowed stock share, combine the two estimated returns to find portfolio return. Estimate variance and take its square root to get volatility. Remove choices that miss the return requirement, then choose the remaining allowed choice with the smallest variance. Finally convert the selected shares into dollars.
A10.interpretation: This exercise chooses among three listed allocations using estimated returns and a zero-correlation assumption. It does not search every possible allocation or guarantee realized return or risk. Check the return rule before comparing risk: an allocation with lower volatility is unusable here if it fails the required return.
A10.summary: Chosen stock weight: {weight}. Stock allocation: {stockDollars}; bond allocation: {bondDollars}.

returns.title: Expected return of each candidate
returns.explanation: This weighted average estimates the portfolio return if each asset earns its supplied estimate. Multiply each asset’s estimated return by the fraction invested in it, then add the contributions. The result is an expected annual return, not the return the portfolio is certain to earn.
hints: For each allowed stock share, multiply the stock share by the stock return and the remaining bond share by the bond return, then add.

variances.title: Variance of each candidate
variances.explanation: Variance measures the portfolio’s modeled spread of returns around its expected return. Each asset’s variance is weighted by the square of its portfolio share. Because this exercise assumes stock and bond returns have zero correlation, their co-movement term is zero and drops out. Variance is in squared-return units, so it is less intuitive than volatility.
hints: Square each asset’s volatility to get its variance, multiply by the square of its portfolio share, and add. The co-movement term is zero under the stated assumption.

volatilities.title: Volatility of each candidate
volatilities.explanation: Take the square root of variance to return to the same percentage scale as returns. Volatility summarizes how widely returns may vary in this model; it does not say whether a particular year will be a loss or how large that loss will be.
hints: Take the square root of each portfolio variance; enter the result as a proportion.

weight.title: Stock weight of the chosen candidate
weight.explanation: The return minimum is a rule each eligible allocation must pass. Cross out any candidate below it before comparing risk. Of the candidates that remain, choose the one with the smallest variance. This is the lowest-variance choice among the listed feasible candidates, not necessarily among every possible allocation.
hints: First check each candidate against the minimum expected return. Among those that pass, select the one with the smallest variance.

stockDollars.title: Dollar allocation to stocks
stockDollars.explanation: A portfolio share is a fraction of the total investment. Multiply the total portfolio value by the selected stock share to find how many dollars go to stocks. This converts a percentage choice into a dollar amount.
hints: Multiply the total portfolio value by the selected stock share.

bondDollars.title: Dollar allocation to bonds
bondDollars.explanation: Stocks and bonds together make up the whole portfolio, so the bond share is one minus the selected stock share. Multiply that remaining share by the total portfolio value. The two dollar allocations should add back to the original portfolio value.

readAloud: The first expression multiplies each asset’s estimated return by its share of the portfolio and adds the two contributions. A11.title: Update an Execution Decision
A11.scenario: A training simulator records costs as negative rewards. At each moment the policy can buy now or wait. We update the estimated long-run value (Q-value) of buying now and compare it with the supplied estimate for waiting. These numbers describe the simulator example, not live market prices.
A11.task: Choose the highest next-state action value, add its discounted value to the immediate reward to form a target, and move the old estimate toward that target using the learning rate. Compare buy-now with waiting, then calculate the target when the sequence ends.
A11.interpretation: A Q-value estimates accumulated reward in the simulator’s units; it is not a probability or promised trading result. Here costs are negative, so the larger (less negative) value is preferred. A terminal state has no future-value term, and a single update does not prove that a policy is robust.

best.title: Best next-state action value
hints: Choose the largest next-state value; less negative is larger.
best.explanation: The next situation has several allowed actions, each with a supplied Q-value. Choose the largest because Q estimates the reward from acting and continuing afterward. Values can all be negative: when costs are written as negative rewards, the value closer to zero is preferred. This is only an estimate under the supplied simulator.

target.title: Q-learning update target
hints: Add immediate reward to discount factor × best next-state value.
target.explanation: The target combines the immediate reward with the best estimated future reward, reduced by the discount factor. This is the value the current estimate will move toward, not a guaranteed total or probability.

error.title: Target minus old Q-value
hints: Subtract the old Q-value from the target. Subtracting a negative adds its magnitude.
error.explanation: Subtract the old Q-value from the target to find their gap, called the temporal-difference error. A positive gap means the old estimate was lower than the target; a negative gap means it was higher. Subtracting a negative adds its magnitude.

updated.title: Updated buy-now Q-value
hints: Add learning rate × update error to the old Q-value.
updated.explanation: The learning rate sets what fraction of the gap to use now. Multiply the error by that rate and add it to the old estimate. A rate of 0.5 moves halfway toward the target. One update does not establish that the full policy is safe or effective.

decision.title: Does the greedy policy choose buy now?
hints: Choose buy now when its updated Q-value is at least the wait value.
decision.explanation: Compare the updated buy-now estimate with the supplied wait value and choose the larger. A less negative value is preferred when both represent costs. This single comparison omits model error and any costs not included in the exercise.

terminal.title: Target if the episode ends
hints: With no next state to act in, the target is the immediate reward.
terminal.explanation: When this is the final action, there is no next situation or future action value. The target is only the immediate reward; adding a future value would invent a step that did not occur.

readAloud: Select the largest next-state Q-value. The target is the immediate reward plus the best future value multiplied by γ, which discounts later outcomes. The target T is immediate reward plus the discounted best next action value. The error δ is target minus the old Q-value. At the end of an episode no next action exists, so use only the immediate reward.

S03.title: Include the Shares You Did Not Buy
S03.scenario: A buy order requests a number of shares but only some are filled. This example’s implementation-shortfall rule compares filled and unfilled shares with the arrival price. It adds execution slippage, benchmark opportunity cost on unfilled shares, and fees.
S03.task: Calculate completion, extra cost on filled shares, benchmark cost on unfilled shares, total shortfall, and the full intended-order value at arrival. Express shortfall in basis points of that full value.
S03.interpretation: Unfilled-share opportunity cost is a benchmark estimate, not a cash fee. Report completion with shortfall so a strategy cannot look cheap simply by leaving work unfinished. Results depend on the stated benchmark and sign convention.

completion.title: Order completion rate
hints: Divide total filled shares by intended shares.
completion.explanation: Completion asks what fraction of the requested order was actually filled. Add the executed share amounts and divide by the intended share count. A result of 0.80 means 80% of the requested shares were bought; it does not measure cost.

slippage.title: Executed-price slippage
hints: For each fill, multiply shares by execution price minus arrival price, then add.
slippage.explanation: Slippage measures the extra amount paid on filled shares compared with the arrival price. For each fill, multiply shares by execution price minus arrival price, then add. A positive value means the buy fills cost more than the benchmark under this convention.

opportunity.title: Opportunity cost on unfilled shares
hints: Multiply unfilled shares by closing price minus arrival price.
opportunity.explanation: Some requested shares were never bought. If the closing price rose above arrival price, those shares could have been bought more cheaply earlier. Multiply unfilled shares by closing price minus arrival price to estimate this missed-opportunity cost. It is a benchmark estimate, not a broker fee.

total.title: Total implementation shortfall
hints: Add slippage, opportunity cost and fees.
total.explanation: The stated shortfall convention adds extra price paid on filled shares, benchmark opportunity cost on unfilled shares, and fees. Counting all three keeps a policy from appearing cheap simply because it left part of the order unfinished.

notional.title: Intended arrival-price notional
hints: Multiply intended shares by arrival price.
notional.explanation: Notional is the dollar value of the full intended order at the arrival price. Multiply requested shares by arrival price. This is the reference amount even when the order was only partly filled.

bps.title: Shortfall in basis points
hints: Divide shortfall by intended notional, then multiply by 10,000.
bps.explanation: Basis points express cost as a small fraction of order value; one basis point is 0.01%. Divide total shortfall by the intended-order notional and multiply by 10,000. Keep the full order in the denominator.

readAloud: For each fill, compare execution price with arrival price and add the extra dollar cost. For unfilled shares, compare closing price with arrival to estimate missed opportunity. Add fees for total shortfall. Divide by the full intended order’s arrival-price value and multiply by 10,000 for basis points.

Unfilled shares equal requested minus executed shares. Completion is executed shares divided by requested shares. Intended notional V₀ is requested shares times arrival price. Keep these measures tied to the full order.
workedExplanation: Looking only at executed prices would omit the cost of missing 200 shares while the market rose. The opportunity cost is a benchmark-based estimate, not a cash fee. The stated shortfall convention and completion rate should accompany the result.

The intended order is the economic reference. Ignoring unfilled shares could make a policy look cheap simply by avoiding trades while the market moves against the unfinished order. Reporting completion alongside full-order shortfall exposes that failure.
workedArithmetic: Unfilled opportunity cost = 200 × (50.30 − 50.00) = $60. Total shortfall = 120 + 60 + 20 = $200.

S04.title: A Better Average Can Hide Worse Executions
S04.scenario: Each completed order has a cost in basis points and counts equally in the averages. The baseline assigns the same supplied cost to every order. Ten examples make the arithmetic clear but are too few to estimate rare future costs reliably.
S04.task: Calculate the equal-weight mean, nearest-rank 90th and 95th percentiles, and average cost among the worst 20% of orders. Compare the policy’s mean and tail mean with the constant-cost baseline.
S04.interpretation: A lower average can occur alongside worse high-cost orders. Percentiles are cutoffs; the tail mean averages selected high-cost orders. With ten observations, p95 is the largest observation. These sample results do not reliably forecast rare future execution costs.
S04.summary: Mean cost: {mean}. Tail mean: {tailMean}. Mean saving versus baseline: {meanSaving}; extra tail cost: {tailExtra}.

mean.title: Mean execution cost
hints: Add all order costs and divide by the number of orders.
mean.explanation: The mean is the average cost when each completed order counts equally. Add the costs and divide by the number of orders. A lower mean can hide a few very expensive executions, so compare it with tail measures.

p90.title: 90th-percentile cost
hints: Sort costs and select rank ceiling(0.90 × count), starting ranks at 1.
p90.explanation: The 90th percentile is a high-cost cutoff. Sort costs from smallest to largest, calculate rank ceiling(0.90 × number of orders), and take that 1-based position. It is a threshold, not the average of the worst 10%.

p95.title: 95th-percentile cost
hints: Sort costs and select rank ceiling(0.95 × count).
p95.explanation: The 95th percentile uses the same nearest-rank rule at 95%. With only ten observations it is the largest observed cost, not a reliable estimate of a rare future event.

tailMean.title: Mean cost in the worst tail
hints: Average the largest tail-fraction of order costs; round the count upward if needed.
tailMean.explanation: The tail mean averages the highest-cost selected share of orders. Count the tail orders, rounding up when needed, and average their costs. Unlike a percentile threshold, it describes the average cost within that selected tail. A small sample makes it uncertain.

meanSaving.title: Mean cost saving versus baseline
hints: Subtract the policy mean from baseline cost.
meanSaving.explanation: Subtract the policy mean from the baseline mean. A positive result means the policy cost less on average in these observations; it does not show whether unusually costly orders were acceptable.

tailExtra.title: Extra tail cost versus baseline
hints: Subtract baseline cost from the policy tail mean.
tailExtra.explanation: Subtract baseline tail cost from policy tail cost. A positive difference means the policy’s selected worst cases cost more. Read this with average savings because average and tail performance can move in opposite directions.

readAloud: The mean adds N order costs and divides by N. For percentile p, sort costs and select position ceiling(p times N), counting the first as rank 1. TailMean averages the worst 20 percent; if the number is not whole, this exercise rounds the count up.
workedExplanation: The learned policy improves average cost by 2.6 bps, but its worst fifth costs 13 bps more than the baseline’s worst fifth. Choosing between them requires an explicit tolerance for execution tail risk. Ten orders are enough for arithmetic, not for a reliable estimate of future tail performance.

The mean can improve when many orders get slightly cheaper even as a few become much more expensive. Percentiles describe thresholds and the tail mean describes the average beyond the selected worst-fraction boundary. Neither the small sample nor a lower overall mean establishes acceptable future tail behavior.
workedArithmetic: p90 uses rank ceiling(0.90 × 10) = 9, giving 20 bps. p95 uses rank 10, giving 30 bps.
The worst 20% contains two orders: (20 + 30) / 2 = 25 bps.
Mean saving = 12 − 9.4 = 2.6 bps. Extra tail cost = 25 − 12 = 13 bps.

A12.title: Simulate Loan Losses
A12.scenario: Two loans each have a stated probability of default, balance, and fraction lost if default occurs. The ten supplied random numbers are paired by trial, one for each loan. A draw below that loan’s probability means it defaults; a draw exactly equal to the probability does not. The example assumes the two loans default independently.
A12.task: For each trial, identify defaults and add the resulting dollar losses. Find the average loss and fraction of trials with loss greater than the reserve. Compare the simulation average with expected loss calculated directly, then calculate the chance both loans default under independence.
A12.interpretation: A simulation summarizes outcomes implied by its inputs; more trials reduce random sampling noise but do not confirm the default probabilities or independence assumption. Expected losses add using each loan’s chance, balance, and loss fraction. Multiplying the two chances to find joint default requires independence. Reserve breach is a separate question about the distribution of combined losses.

labels.draws: Uniform draws (loan A then B for each run)

lossOnDefault.title: Loss from one default
hints: Multiply exposure per loan by loss fraction.
lossOnDefault.explanation: This estimates the dollars lost if one loan defaults. Multiply the balance owed by the fraction the lender expects not to recover. For example, a 50% loss fraction means half the balance is lost and half is recovered. It is a modeled loss, not automatically the final realized amount.

losses.title: Loss in each simulation
hints: For each pair, count draws below PD and multiply by loss from one default.
losses.explanation: Each trial represents one possible set of outcomes for both loans. Compare each supplied random draw with its loan’s default probability; a draw strictly below the probability means default. Count defaults and multiply by the loss per default. A draw equal to the cutoff does not count under the stated rule.

mean.title: Mean simulated portfolio loss
hints: Add scenario losses and divide by the number of simulations.
mean.explanation: The simulation mean estimates average loss across the trials shown. Add the dollar losses from every trial and divide by the number of trials. A small set may differ from the model’s expected average simply because it contains few random outcomes.

breach.title: Fraction of runs exceeding the reserve
hints: Count losses strictly greater than the reserve and divide by run count.
breach.explanation: A reserve breach occurs only when trial loss is greater than the reserve; a loss exactly equal to the reserve is not above it. Count such trials and divide by all trials. This fraction estimates how often the modeled loss crosses the reserve under the supplied assumptions.

analytical.title: Analytical expected portfolio loss
hints: Multiply 2 × PD × exposure per loan × loss fraction.
analytical.explanation: This provides a direct expected-loss calculation to compare with the simulation average. For each loan, multiply default chance by balance and loss fraction, then add the two expected losses. Average losses add even if defaults move together; this is not the chance that the reserve is exceeded.

exact.title: Probability both loans default
hints: Under independence, multiply PD by PD.
exact.explanation: Under the exercise’s independence assumption, the chance both loans default is the product of their individual chances. Multiply the two default probabilities. This is the exact joint-default chance under that assumption, not the reserve-breach chance in general; here the reserve is exceeded only when both loans default.

readAloud: In each trial j, mark a loan as defaulted if its random draw U is below its default probability PD. Multiply that 0-or-1 indicator by the amount owed EAD and loss fraction LGD, then add across loans to get trial loss L_j. Expected loss is calculated separately: add each loan’s PD × EAD × LGD.

The simulation mean L-bar is the total of N trial losses divided by N. To estimate reserve-breach chance, count trials where loss is strictly greater than reserve B and divide by N. Equal-to-reserve trials are not counted as breaches.
workedExplanation: Five runs produce noisy estimates: $4,000 versus a true model mean of $2,000, and 20% versus a true model breach probability of 4%. More independent runs reduce simulation noise; they do not validate the assumed 20% default probability or independence.

The default indicators are 0/1, the portfolio losses are dollars, and the breach estimate is a proportion. Analytical expected loss does not require independent defaults when the individual expected losses are given; independence is required for the simple product used to calculate the probability that both loans default.
workedArithmetic: Loss per default = $10,000 × 0.50 = $5,000. The five default patterns are A only, neither, both, neither, B only, giving losses [$5,000, $0, $10,000, $0, $5,000].
Simulated mean = (5,000 + 0 + 10,000 + 0 + 5,000) / 5 = $4,000. Only the third loss exceeds $5,000, so estimated breach probability = 1/5 = 20%.
Analytical expected loss = 2 × 0.20 × $10,000 × 0.50 = $2,000.
Under independence, both-default probability = 0.20 × 0.20 = 4%. Here both defaults are needed to exceed the reserve.

Multiply that 0-or-1 indicator by the amount owed EAD and loss fraction LGD, then add across loans to get trial loss L_j. Expected loss is calculated separately: add each loan’s PD × EAD × LGD.

M01.title: Count the Four Outcomes
M01.scenario: A fraud detector flags transactions. Later investigators confirm which transactions were fraud. Here, fraud is called the positive outcome, and a flag is the detector’s positive prediction. “Positive” names the outcome being counted; it does not mean good.
M01.task: For each transaction, compare what actually happened with whether it was flagged. Count caught frauds (TP), false alerts (FP), missed frauds (FN), and legitimate transactions correctly passed (TN). Then check that every transaction appears once in the total.
M01.interpretation: The number of flags includes caught fraud and false alerts. The number of actual fraud cases includes caught and missed fraud. Those totals are different groups, so precision divides by all flags while recall divides by all actual fraud. The counts describe outcomes at this cutoff; they are not probabilities.

cells.title: Outcome counts (TP, FP, FN, TN)
hints: TP is caught fraud; FP = alerts − caught; FN = fraud − caught; TN is the remainder.
cells.explanation: Fill the four boxes by asking two questions for each transaction: was it actually fraud, and did the detector flag it? TP means both yes; FP means flagged but legitimate; FN means missed fraud; TN means legitimate and not flagged. Use the known totals so no transaction is counted twice or left out.

total.title: Total transactions accounted for
hints: Add all four outcome counts.
total.explanation: Add TP, FP, FN, and TN to check the accounting. These four groups should cover every transaction exactly once, so their total should match the population N. A mismatch means at least one outcome count was calculated incorrectly.

readAloud: Use the supplied alert count and caught-fraud count to find false positives, and the actual-fraud count and caught count to find missed fraud. Then subtract all three known groups from the population to find true negatives.

The total number of flags includes false alarms. The total number of actual frauds includes missed fraud. Those two totals are usually different, which is why precision and recall require different denominators.

M02.title: Compare Against Doing Nothing
M02.scenario: Compare a fraud detector with a simple baseline—a reference rule that marks every transaction legitimate and never flags one. Both are checked against the same actual outcomes, with fraud as the positive class.
M02.task: Calculate the share of all transactions the detector labels correctly and count its mistakes. Then do the same for the always-legitimate baseline, including how many frauds it catches.
M02.interpretation: Accuracy gives each transaction equal weight. Because legitimate transactions are usually more common, a rule that passes everyone can have high accuracy while catching no fraud. Accuracy also treats a missed fraud and a false alert as equal mistakes; deciding between policies requires the dollar cost of errors and the workload from reviewing alerts.

accuracy.title: Detector accuracy
hints: Divide TP + TN by TP + FP + FN + TN.
accuracy.explanation: Accuracy answers what share of all transactions received the correct label. Add the caught frauds (TP) to the correctly passed legitimate transactions (TN), then divide by the full population. A high result can still hide missed fraud when legitimate transactions are much more common.

mistakes.title: Detector mistakes
hints: Add false positives and false negatives.
mistakes.explanation: Count the two ways the detector can be wrong: legitimate transactions it flags (FP) and fraud it misses (FN). Add them to get total mistakes. This count shows the number of errors, while accuracy expresses correct classifications as a share of all transactions.

baseline.title: Always-legitimate baseline accuracy
hints: Divide all actual legitimate transactions by all transactions.
baseline.explanation: The baseline predicts “legitimate” for every transaction. It is correct for every actually legitimate transaction, so divide the legitimate count (TN + FP) by all transactions. This shows how accuracy can look strong even when the baseline catches no fraud.

caught.title: Frauds caught by the baseline
hints: A detector that never flags a transaction catches no fraud.
caught.explanation: Because this baseline never flags a transaction, it catches zero of the actual fraud cases. That is a count, not a rate; its recall is zero whenever the evaluation set contains fraud.

baselineMistakes.title: Baseline mistakes
