baselineMistakes.explanation: Every actual fraud is labeled legitimate by this rule, so every fraud is a mistake. Legitimate transactions are all correct. This makes the baseline’s main failure visible even if its overall accuracy is high.

readAloud: Add the correctly flagged frauds and correctly passed legitimate transactions, then divide by all transactions to find the share classified correctly.
Every mistake is either a false alarm or a missed fraud, so add FP and FN to count all incorrect classifications.

More information is needed to decide whether the detector’s additional interruptions are worthwhile.

The 96% result refers to all transactions, including the many legitimate cases. The loss of two percentage points versus the baseline does not tell you whether catching 15 frauds compensates for the 35 false alerts. That requires a cost model.
workedArithmetic: Detector accuracy = (15 + 945) / 1,000 = 96%. Detector mistakes = 35 + 5 = 40.
The always-legitimate baseline correctly passes 980 transactions: 980 / 1,000 = 98% accuracy.
It catches 0 frauds and misses all 20. Its higher accuracy does not mean better fraud detection.

M03.title: Give Both Classes a Voice
M03.scenario: Compare a fraud detector with a baseline that always predicts legitimate. A class is one actual outcome group: fraud or legitimate. Balanced accuracy gives those two groups equal influence, even when one group is much larger.
M03.task: Calculate recall (the share of actual fraud caught) and specificity (the share of actual legitimate transactions correctly passed). Average the two rates, then calculate the same score for the always-legitimate baseline.
M03.interpretation: Balanced accuracy first calculates a success rate within each actual outcome group, then gives fraud and legitimate cases equal weight. It differs from ordinary accuracy, which counts every transaction equally, and it does not price either kind of error in dollars.
M03.summary: Detector balanced accuracy: {balanced}; baseline balanced accuracy: {baseline}.

recall.title: Fraud recall
hints: Divide TP by TP + FN.
recall.explanation: Recall asks what share of all actual frauds the detector catches. Divide caught fraud (TP) by all fraud (TP + FN). A missed fraud stays in the denominator, so missing more fraud lowers recall.

specificity.title: Legitimate-transaction specificity
hints: Divide TN by TN + FP.
specificity.explanation: Specificity asks what share of all legitimate transactions the detector correctly leaves unflagged. Divide correctly passed legitimate transactions (TN) by all legitimate transactions (TN + FP). False alarms stay in the denominator and lower this rate.

balanced.title: Balanced accuracy
hints: Average recall and specificity with equal weights.
balanced.explanation: Balanced accuracy gives fraud and legitimate cases equal weight: add recall and specificity, then divide by two. This prevents the much larger legitimate group from dominating the score. It does not include the financial cost of either kind of mistake.

baseline.title: Always-legitimate balanced accuracy
hints: The baseline has zero recall and perfect specificity. Average those rates.
baseline.explanation: The always-legitimate rule catches no fraud, so its recall is 0; it correctly passes every legitimate transaction, so specificity is 1. Giving the two classes equal weight produces (0 + 1) / 2 = 0.5, or 50% balanced accuracy.

readAloud: Calculate the fraud-catch rate and the legitimate-pass rate separately, then average them so each actual class contributes half of the balanced-accuracy score.
Recall is the share of actual fraud caught. Specificity is the share of actual legitimate transactions correctly passed. Their denominators use the actual class, not the number flagged.
workedExplanation: The detector performs substantially better when fraud and legitimate transactions receive equal class-level weight: 85.71% versus 50%. This still does not price errors in dollars. Balanced accuracy is not a claim that 85.71% of all individual transactions were classified correctly.

Balanced accuracy first normalizes within each class. The rare fraud class therefore contributes as much as the much larger legitimate class. It is still a statistical weighting convention, not a financial cost weighting.
workedArithmetic: The always-legitimate baseline has 0% recall and 100% specificity, so balanced accuracy = (0 + 1) / 2 = 50%.

M04.title: How Productive Is the Review Queue?
M04.scenario: An issuer sends alerts to two fraud-investigation queues drawn from the same transaction population. Queue A reviews 50 alerts and confirms 15 frauds; queue B reviews 10 alerts and confirms 8. Every review costs $4, whether the alert is fraud or a legitimate purchase.
M04.task: For each queue, calculate precision (the share of reviewed alerts confirmed as fraud), total review dollars, and review dollars per confirmed fraud. Then explain why a cheaper cost per discovery does not by itself prove that a queue is the better policy.
M04.interpretation: Queue B finds more fraud per alert and costs less per confirmed fraud, but queue A finds seven more fraud cases overall. Precision only describes the alerts that were reviewed; it does not count fraud left outside either queue. Decide between policies only after considering missed-loss amounts and available review capacity.
M04.summary: Queue A precision: {precisionA}; queue B: {precisionB}. Cost per confirmed fraud: A {perA}, B {perB}.

precisionA.title: Queue A precision
hints: Divide confirmed frauds in A by all alerts reviewed in A.
precisionA.explanation: Queue A precision uses confirmed frauds as the numerator and every alert in queue A as the denominator. This tells an investigator how often an A alert is useful; it does not count fraud the queue missed.

precisionB.title: Queue B precision
hints: Divide confirmed frauds in B by all alerts reviewed in B.
precisionB.explanation: Queue B precision uses the same definition as queue A: confirmed frauds in B divided by all B alerts. The matching denominator makes the two queues comparable, while recall is still needed to see what each queue left behind.

costA.title: Queue A review cost
hints: Multiply alerts reviewed in A by cost per review.
costA.explanation: Each reviewed alert uses analyst time. Multiply the number of queue A alerts by the stated dollars per review to estimate this queue’s review cost.

costB.title: Queue B review cost
hints: Multiply alerts reviewed in B by cost per review.
costB.explanation: Multiply queue B’s review count by the same per-review cost. Holding that cost assumption fixed makes the workload comparison fair.

perA.title: Review cost per fraud found in A
hints: Divide queue A review cost by frauds found in A.
perA.explanation: Divide queue A’s review cost by the frauds it found. This estimates the review dollars spent per confirmed fraud found; if the queue finds none, the ratio is undefined rather than zero.

perB.title: Review cost per fraud found in B
hints: Divide queue B review cost by frauds found in B.
perB.explanation: Divide queue B’s review cost by the frauds it found. Compare this with queue A only alongside how many frauds each queue found and how much fraud each may have missed.

readAloud: Precision divides the fraud found in queue A by all alerts sent to review. Cost per fraud found divides the review dollars for that queue by its confirmed frauds. These answer alert usefulness and resource cost per result, which are different questions.
Multiply the number of alerts by the cost to review each one. This is the direct review workload cost before counting losses or missed fraud.
workedExplanation: Queue B has higher precision: 8 of 10 alerts are fraud (80%), compared with 15 of 50 (30%) for A. B also spends less per confirmed fraud, but it finds seven fewer fraud cases in this example. The numbers do not say what those extra cases cost or whether the remaining alerts fit the team’s capacity, so they do not settle the policy choice.

Precision is a fraction of alerts and has no dollar unit. Review cost per fraud found has dollars in its numerator. An 80% precision score therefore does not mean fraud losses fell by 80%; it means 80 out of every 100 reviewed alerts were confirmed in this sample.
workedArithmetic: Precision uses all reviewed alerts as the denominator: A = 15 confirmed frauds ÷ 50 alerts = 30%; B = 8 ÷ 10 = 80%.
Review spending is number of alerts times $4 each: A = 50 × $4 = $200; B = 10 × $4 = $40.

Dollars per discovery divides each queue’s review spending by its confirmed frauds: A = $200 ÷ 15 ≈ $13.33; B = $40 ÷ 8 = $5. A nevertheless finds 15 − 8 = 7 more frauds, whose loss amounts are not supplied.

formulas.readAloud: Precision divides the fraud found in queue A by all alerts sent to review. Cost per fraud found divides the review dollars for that queue by its confirmed frauds. These answer alert usefulness and resource cost per result, which are different questions.

M05.title: Put a Price on Missed Fraud
M05.scenario: Two fraud detectors are evaluated on the same batch of 20 confirmed fraud cases. Detector A catches 15 and detector B catches 8. For this teaching calculation, each missed fraud is assumed to cause the same $2,000 unrecovered loss.
M05.task: For each detector, calculate recall (the share of actual fraud cases caught), the number missed, and the modeled dollar loss from those misses. Compare the missed-fraud losses while keeping the equal-$2,000 assumption visible.
M05.interpretation: The same denominator—20 actual frauds—makes recall comparable between detectors. Because this exercise assigns the same loss to every case, event recall also tracks the share of fraud dollars caught here. Real fraud amounts vary; recall alone does not measure dollar capture, false-alert workload, review costs, or whether an intervention prevents the loss.
M05.summary: Residual fraud loss: A {lossA}, B {lossB}. A’s reduction in missed-fraud loss: {saving}.

recallA.title: Detector A recall
hints: Divide frauds caught by A by all actual frauds.
recallA.explanation: Queue A recall divides its caught frauds by all actual frauds in the evaluated group. The denominator includes both caught and missed fraud, so the rate answers how much of the known fraud A found.

recallB.title: Detector B recall
hints: Divide frauds caught by B by all actual frauds.
recallB.explanation: Queue B recall uses all actual frauds as the denominator too. This shared group lets us compare detection coverage, though recall alone says nothing about alert workload.

missedA.title: Frauds missed by A
hints: Subtract A’s caught frauds from actual frauds.
missedA.explanation: Subtract queue A’s caught frauds from all actual frauds. The remainder is fraud that was present but not detected by A.

missedB.title: Frauds missed by B
hints: Subtract B’s caught frauds from actual frauds.
missedB.explanation: Subtract queue B’s caught frauds from all actual frauds. Keep the total fraud count fixed so the difference reflects the detector, not a different sample.

lossA.title: Residual loss with A
hints: Multiply frauds missed by A by loss per missed fraud.
lossA.explanation: Multiply queue A’s missed-fraud count by the stated loss for one missed case. This gives a scenario-based dollar estimate that depends on the assumed loss per case.

lossB.title: Residual loss with B
hints: Multiply frauds missed by B by loss per missed fraud.
lossB.explanation: Multiply queue B’s missed cases by the same per-case loss assumption. If real fraud amounts vary, this equal-loss shortcut will not match actual dollar loss.

saving.title: Reduction in residual loss using A
hints: Subtract A’s residual loss from B’s.
saving.explanation: Subtract A’s remaining loss estimate from B’s. A positive result means A has lower estimated missed-fraud loss under this scenario; it does not include extra review or intervention costs.

readAloud: Recall divides fraud caught by all fraud present. Residual loss multiplies missed fraud cases by the assumed loss for each miss. One describes detection coverage; the other adds a dollar assumption.
All actual fraud F equals the cases caught TP plus the cases missed FN. Rearranging gives missed cases as total fraud minus caught fraud.
workedExplanation: A catches 15 of 20 frauds (75%) and misses 5. B catches 8 of 20 (40%) and misses 12. At the assumed $2,000 loss for each miss, A’s missed-fraud loss is $14,000 lower. This is only the missed-loss part of the comparison; the exercise does not include the extra alerts, review expense, or whether the intervention actually stops a fraud.

Recall counts events, giving every fraud one equal count. Multiplying misses by a single assumed loss turns that count into modeled dollars only because this example assigns the same $2,000 to every case. If losses differ, a detector can have higher event recall but capture a smaller share of fraud dollars.
workedArithmetic: Recall divides caught cases by all 20 actual frauds: A = 15 ÷ 20 = 75%; B = 8 ÷ 20 = 40%.
Misses are actual frauds minus caught frauds: A = 20 − 15 = 5; B = 20 − 8 = 12.
Multiply misses by the assumed loss per miss: A = 5 × $2,000 = $10,000; B = 12 × $2,000 = $24,000. The difference is $24,000 − $10,000 = $14,000 under this equal-loss assumption.

formulas.readAloud: Recall divides fraud caught by all fraud present. Residual loss multiplies missed fraud cases by the assumed loss for each miss. One describes detection coverage; the other adds a dollar assumption.

symbols.meaning: Frauds the detector caught.
Frauds the detector missed.
Assumed dollar loss for one missed fraud.

M06.title: Count Customer Interruptions
M06.scenario: Among 980 legitimate transactions, the detector correctly passes 945 and incorrectly flags 35. Project those observed rates to a future period with 1,000,000 legitimate transactions, assuming the mix of customers and detector behavior stay similar.
M06.task: Calculate specificity (the share of legitimate activity passed) and false-positive rate (the share incorrectly flagged). Confirm that they add to 100%, then estimate future false alerts using the stated one-million legitimate transactions.
M06.interpretation: Both rates use all legitimate transactions as the denominator, so they are complementary: a legitimate transaction is either passed or incorrectly flagged. This is different from one minus precision, which divides false alerts by all alerts. The future count is a projection, not a promise; it assumes the 35-of-980 rate carries over to the later population.
M06.summary: Specificity: {specificity}; false-positive rate: {FPR}. Expected false alerts at the larger volume: {falseAlerts}.

specificity.title: Specificity
hints: Divide correctly passed legitimate transactions by TN + FP.
specificity.explanation: Divide correctly passed legitimate transactions by all legitimate transactions, which are TN plus FP. This asks what share of genuine activity avoids an incorrect alert.

FPR.title: False-positive rate
hints: Divide incorrectly flagged legitimate transactions by TN + FP.
FPR.explanation: Divide legitimate transactions incorrectly flagged by all legitimate transactions. The result is the share of genuine activity that gets interrupted; it is not the share of all alerts that are false.

total.title: Specificity plus false-positive rate
hints: Both rates partition the same legitimate-transaction population.
total.explanation: Specificity and false-positive rate divide the legitimate transactions into two outcomes: passed or incorrectly flagged. Because these are complementary shares of the same group, they add to 1 (100%).

falseAlerts.title: Expected future false alerts
hints: Multiply future legitimate volume by the false-positive rate.
falseAlerts.explanation: Multiply the expected future volume of legitimate transactions by the false-positive rate to estimate false alerts. This projection assumes the rate remains similar in that future population.

readAloud: Both rates use all legitimate activity, TN plus FP, as the denominator. Specificity counts the legitimate transactions passed; the false-positive rate counts those incorrectly flagged.

Specificity and the false-positive rate are the two possible outcomes for a legitimate transaction, so they sum to 1. Multiply future legitimate volume by the false-positive rate to estimate alert count, assuming the rate carries over.
workedExplanation: The observed false-positive rate is about 3.57%. If that rate stayed the same across one million legitimate transactions, about 35,714 would be interrupted. A percentage that looks small can still create a large workload at high volume; actual counts depend on the future population and whether the rate remains stable.

Both specificity and the false-positive rate count legitimate transactions, but they count opposite outcomes. One minus precision has the same false-alert numerator but divides by all alerts instead, so it answers a different question. Always name the group underneath a percentage.
workedArithmetic: Specificity = correctly passed legitimate transactions ÷ all legitimate transactions = 945 ÷ 980 ≈ 96.43%. False-positive rate = incorrectly flagged legitimate transactions ÷ all legitimate transactions = 35 ÷ 980 ≈ 3.57%. Their unrounded fractions add to 1 (100%).
Project the same false-positive fraction to a future million legitimate transactions: 1,000,000 × (35 ÷ 980) ≈ 35,714 expected false alerts, if the rate carries over.

formulas.readAloud: Both rates use all legitimate activity, TN plus FP, as the denominator. Specificity counts the legitimate transactions passed; the false-positive rate counts those incorrectly flagged.

symbols.meaning: Legitimate transactions correctly passed.
Legitimate transactions incorrectly flagged.

formulas.readAloud: Specificity and the false-positive rate are the two possible outcomes for a legitimate transaction, so they sum to 1. Multiply future legitimate volume by the false-positive rate to estimate alert count, assuming the rate carries over.

symbols.meaning: All legitimate transactions, or 100% of that population. Specificity and false-positive rate divide this whole into passed and incorrectly flagged transactions.

M07.title: Balance Capture and Queue Quality
M07.scenario: At one chosen review cutoff, a detector has precision P = 0.30 (30% of alerts are fraud) and recall R = 0.75 (it catches 75% of actual fraud). Compare F1, F-beta with beta set to 2, and their ordinary arithmetic average. None of these calculations changes the alerts.
M07.task: Calculate F1, F2, and the arithmetic mean of precision and recall. Explain why F2 is larger in this example and what changing beta does—and does not—mean for the lending or fraud policy.
M07.interpretation: F1 combines precision and recall and is pulled toward the weaker rate; this combination is called the harmonic mean. F-beta changes the score’s emphasis, and beta above 1 gives recall more weight. Beta is a preference in a summary formula, not a ratio of dollar costs. These scores describe one operating point and omit true dollar loss, probability calibration, and investigator capacity.

F1.title: F1 score
hints: Calculate 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall).
F1.explanation: Use precision for P and recall for R. The harmonic-mean formula gives one score and falls when either rate is low, so a strong value on one side cannot completely hide a weak value on the other.

F2.title: F-beta score
hints: Use (1 + beta²) × precision × recall / (beta² × precision + recall).
F2.explanation: Use the F-beta formula with beta set to 2. Because beta is above 1, this score emphasizes recall more than precision; that is a chosen scoring preference, not a dollar-cost ratio.

arithmetic.title: Arithmetic mean of precision and recall
hints: Add precision and recall, then divide by 2.
arithmetic.explanation: Add precision and recall, then divide by two to calculate their ordinary arithmetic average. This gives both rates equal weight, but it can stay high when one rate is strong and the other weak.

readAloud: P is precision and R is recall. F1 gives each equal emphasis using a harmonic mean; F-beta changes the emphasis using beta. When beta is above 1, recall receives more weight. These are summary scores, not cost calculations.
Add precision and recall and divide by two. This is their ordinary average, shown as a comparison; unlike F1 it is not pulled down as strongly by a low value on one side.
workedExplanation: The scores are F1 ≈ 0.429, F2 ≈ 0.577, and arithmetic mean = 0.525. F2 is larger because this example has higher recall than precision and beta = 2 gives recall more influence. The detector and its alerts are unchanged; only the summary rule changes. A higher F2 is not proof of a better model or a lower-cost policy.

F1, F2, and the ordinary average are three ways to summarize the same 30% precision and 75% recall. F1’s harmonic mean falls more when one input is low; F-beta deliberately changes the weighting. Neither score includes dollars, review workload, or whether probabilities match real event rates.
workedArithmetic: Arithmetic mean = (0.30 + 0.75) / 2 = 0.525.

formulas.readAloud: P is precision and R is recall. F1 gives each equal emphasis using a harmonic mean; F-beta changes the emphasis using beta. When beta is above 1, recall receives more weight. These are summary scores, not cost calculations.

symbols.meaning: Precision: share of alerts that are confirmed fraud.
Recall: share of actual fraud the detector catches.
Preference parameter: values above 1 put more weight on recall.

formulas.readAloud: Add precision and recall and divide by two. This is their ordinary average, shown as a comparison; unlike F1 it is not pulled down as strongly by a low value on one side.

symbols.meaning: Precision: share of alerts that are confirmed fraud.
Recall: share of actual fraud the detector catches.

M08.title: Move the Threshold
M08.scenario: Each transaction has a model score and an actual outcome in the same order. A score is a ranking signal, not automatically a probability. The label is 1 for fraud and 0 for legitimate. At a cutoff, flag every transaction whose score is equal to or above it.
M08.task: For each score cutoff, count caught frauds (true positives, TP) and legitimate transactions flagged by mistake (false positives, FP). Divide TP by all actual frauds for the true-positive rate (TPR, also called recall), and FP by all actually legitimate transactions for the false-positive rate (FPR). Plot FPR on the horizontal axis and TPR on the vertical axis.
M08.interpretation: Lowering the cutoff usually flags more transactions, which can catch more fraud and interrupt more legitimate activity. The actual fraud and legitimate totals stay fixed, so the denominators for both rates stay fixed too. The ROC curve displays these tradeoffs; it does not choose a cutoff or account for investigation costs by itself.
M08.summary: At the listed cutoffs, the share of all actual fraud caught is {TPR}; the share of all actually legitimate transactions flagged is {FPR}.

labels.scores: Model scores (higher scores are ranked as more fraud-like)
labels.thresholds: Score cutoffs (a score equal to the cutoff is flagged)

TP.title: True positives at each threshold
hints: For each threshold, count flagged transactions whose label is 1.
TP.explanation: At each threshold, count only transactions whose score reaches the cutoff and whose actual label is fraud. The cutoff changes which scores count as flagged; it does not change the labels. This gives the true-positive count for each operating point.

FP.title: False positives at each threshold
hints: For each threshold, count flagged transactions whose label is 0.
FP.explanation: For the same threshold, count flagged transactions whose actual label is legitimate. These are false alarms. Counting them at each cutoff shows the extra review burden as the rule becomes more or less permissive.

FPR.title: False-positive rates at each threshold
hints: Divide each FP count by the total number of label-0 transactions.
FPR.explanation: Divide false alarms by all actually legitimate transactions (FP + TN). This is the false-positive rate: the share of legitimate transactions flagged. The denominator stays the total number of legitimate examples at every threshold.

TPR.title: True-positive rates at each threshold
hints: Divide each TP count by the total number of label-1 transactions.
TPR.explanation: Divide caught fraud (TP) by all actual fraud (TP + FN). This is the true-positive rate, also called recall: the share of fraud caught at that threshold. Plot it against the false-positive rate to compare how many frauds are caught for a given false-alarm rate.

readAloud: For each threshold, divide flagged frauds by all actual frauds to get the true-positive rate; divide flagged legitimate transactions by all actual legitimate transactions to get the false-positive rate.
For transaction i, predict fraud (one) when its score sᵢ is at least the selected threshold t; otherwise predict legitimate (zero). Equality is included in the flagged group.
workedExplanation: Each ROC point represents a different capture-versus-interruption tradeoff. These are selected points, not the full curve. The ROC curve itself does not choose the economically appropriate threshold.

The curve shows possible operating choices, not one mandatory threshold. Moving toward higher capture may also interrupt more legitimate activity. In this small set, the denominators stay fixed, so changes in rates come entirely from changes in the flagged cases.
workedArithmetic: There are three actual frauds and three legitimate transactions.
At 0.85, only A is flagged: TP = 1, FP = 0, so (FPR, TPR) = (0/3, 1/3).
At 0.65, A, B and C are flagged: TP = 2, FP = 1, so (FPR, TPR) = (1/3, 2/3).
At 0.25, A through E are flagged: TP = 3, FP = 2, so (FPR, TPR) = (2/3, 1).

formulas.readAloud: For each threshold, divide flagged frauds by all actual frauds to get the true-positive rate; divide flagged legitimate transactions by all actual legitimate transactions to get the false-positive rate.

Frauds missed at this threshold.
Legitimate transactions flagged at this threshold.

The chosen score cutoff for flagging.

An indicator: one when the condition inside is true, and zero otherwise.

M09.title: Count Correct Rankings
M09.scenario: Compare every fraud score with every legitimate-transaction score. Award 1 ranking point if fraud scores higher, 0 if lower and half a point for a tie.
M09.task: For every fraud–legitimate pair, award ranking points as described, then divide the total by the number of pairs to get ROC-AUC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). Also calculate ranking Gini as 2 × AUC − 1; this is distinct from decision-tree Gini impurity.
M09.interpretation: AUC summarizes fraud–legitimate pair rankings without choosing a threshold. It is not classification accuracy, a fraud probability or profit. Ranking Gini is different from tree-node Gini impurity.

wins.title: Pair-ranking points
hints: Compare each fraud score with every legitimate score; count ties as 0.5.
wins.explanation: Each fraud is compared with each legitimate transaction because ranking quality is about whether fraud tends to receive the higher score. Award one point for a fraud ranked above a legitimate transaction and half a point for a tie. These points summarize all positive–negative comparisons; they do not measure probability accuracy.

pairs.title: Number of fraud–legitimate pairs
hints: Multiply the number of frauds by the number of legitimate transactions.
pairs.explanation: The total number of comparisons is the number of fraud cases multiplied by the number of legitimate cases. Every cross-class pair contributes one comparison, so this is the denominator needed to turn ranking points into a share.

AUC.title: ROC-AUC
hints: Divide ranking points by total pair count.
AUC.explanation: Divide the ranking points by all fraud–legitimate pairs. The result is ROC-AUC: the share of cross-class pairs ordered correctly, with ties counting halfway. A value near 0.5 is about random ordering; it does not say whether the scores are calibrated chances.

gini.title: AUC-derived Gini coefficient
hints: Double AUC and subtract 1.
gini.explanation: Convert AUC to the Gini scale by doubling it and subtracting 1. This maps random ordering at AUC 0.5 to Gini 0 and perfect ordering at AUC 1 to Gini 1. It is a rescaling of the same ranking information, not a separate test.

readAloud: For every fraud–legitimate pair, award one point when the fraud score is higher and half a point when the two scores tie. Divide the total points by all such pairs to get ROC-AUC. Gini is the same ranking result rescaled as twice AUC minus one.
workedExplanation: The model ranks a fraud above a legitimate transaction in two-thirds of these pairs. AUC is not threshold-specific accuracy, a fraud probability, or a profit estimate. This Gini is a rescaling of ranking AUC, not tree-node impurity.

AUC uses all nine fraud–legitimate comparisons. Accuracy at a particular cutoff would use six yes/no decisions instead. The two fractions summarize different questions even when calculated from the same records.
workedArithmetic: The fraud at 0.90 outranks all three legitimate scores; 0.70 outranks two; 0.30 outranks one. There are no ties.
Pair-ranking points = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Total pairs = 3 × 3 = 9.

formulas.readAloud: For every fraud–legitimate pair, award one point when the fraud score is higher and half a point when the two scores tie. Divide the total points by all such pairs to get ROC-AUC. Gini is the same ranking result rescaled as twice AUC minus one.

symbols.meaning: Area under the ROC curve; here, the fraction of fraud–legitimate pairs ordered correctly, with ties counting halfway.
Pair points earned by fraud scores above legitimate scores.
Fraud–legitimate pairs with equal scores; each contributes one-half point.
Number of fraud cases in the evaluated sample.
Number of legitimate cases in the evaluated sample.
AUC rescaled so random ranking is 0 and perfect ranking is 1.

M10.title: Find the Largest Separation
M10.scenario: A validation sample is a set of past applications with outcomes already known, reserved to check how a model ranks them. At each candidate score cutoff, the exercise gives the counts of defaults and non-defaults flagged. The cutoffs are numbered in the order shown.
M10.task: For each cutoff, divide flagged defaults by all defaults and flagged non-defaults by all non-defaults. Find the absolute gap between those two rates, then report the largest gap and its cutoff number. This maximum gap is the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic (KS).
M10.interpretation: Each rate has its own outcome-group denominator. A KS gap of 0.45 is a 45 percentage-point difference between the two rates at the best-separating tested cutoff. KS describes separation in this sample; it does not account for lending margins, loss severity, review capacity, or which action a policy should take.
M10.summary: KS: {KS}. The largest gap occurs at cutoff number {cutoff}.

TPR.title: Default capture rates
hints: Divide defaults flagged at each cutoff by all actual defaults.
TPR.explanation: At each listed cutoff, count the actual defaults whose scores meet the flagging rule, then divide by all actual defaults. This true-positive rate answers what fraction of defaults the policy catches at that cutoff; it is also called recall.

FPR.title: Non-default flag rates
hints: Divide non-defaults flagged at each cutoff by all actual non-defaults.
FPR.explanation: For each cutoff, count flagged non-defaults and divide by all actual non-defaults. This false-positive rate measures the share of people who would not default but are still sent for review. Its denominator is the non-default group, not everyone.

gaps.title: Absolute capture-rate gaps
hints: Take the absolute difference between the two rates at each cutoff.
gaps.explanation: Subtract the non-default flag rate from the default capture rate at each cutoff and take the absolute value. The gap measures how far apart the two rates are at that point on the ROC curve; larger separation means stronger ranking separation there, not lower financial cost.

KS.title: KS statistic
hints: Select the largest absolute gap.
KS.explanation: Choose the largest of the cutoff-by-cutoff absolute gaps. This maximum vertical separation is the KS statistic. It summarizes the best separation found across these cutoffs, but does not identify a financially optimal policy by itself.

cutoff.title: Cutoff number with the largest gap
hints: Enter its position in the listed cutoff order, starting at 1.
cutoff.explanation: Report the position of the cutoff that produced the maximum gap, counting the listed cutoffs from 1. This tells you where the greatest separation occurred; ties follow the exercise’s stated ordering rule and the selected cutoff still needs a cost and capacity review.

readAloud: At each cutoff, compare the fraction of actual defaults flagged with the fraction of actual non-defaults flagged. The KS statistic is the largest absolute difference between those rates across the tested cutoffs.

For a given cutoff, divide flagged defaults by all defaults to get the default capture rate. Divide flagged non-defaults by all non-defaults to get the false-positive rate. The denominator changes with the outcome group being measured.
workedExplanation: At B, the model has captured 60% of defaults but only 15% of non-defaults. That separation is a ranking diagnostic. Choosing a lending action still requires loss severity, approval value, capacity, and policy constraints.

Dividing both counts by all 100 applicants would answer a different question. KS compares within-class capture rates, so each class needs its own denominator. The biggest statistical gap does not include lending margins or loss severity.
workedArithmetic: Absolute gaps are [22.5, 45, 40, 0] percentage points. KS = 0.45 at cutoff B, the second listed cutoff.

formulas.readAloud: At each cutoff, compare the fraction of actual defaults flagged with the fraction of actual non-defaults flagged. The KS statistic is the largest absolute difference between those rates across the tested cutoffs.

M11a.title: Build It From a Ranked List
M11a.scenario: The transactions are ordered from the highest model score to the lowest; that order is called a ranking. Each known outcome is 1 for fraud or 0 for legitimate. The scores organize the queue but are not stated as probabilities.
M11a.task: For each queue size K, count how many frauds appear in the first K reviews. Precision is the share of those K reviews that find fraud; recall is the share of all fraud cases found so far. Plot recall horizontally and precision vertically to see how queue usefulness changes as you review more cases.
M11a.interpretation: Adding a legitimate case increases the queue size without adding fraud. Adding a fraud can raise precision. Recall cannot decrease when a queue only expands.
M11a.summary: Captured frauds by queue size: {captured}. Precision: {precision}. Recall: {recall}.

labels.labels: Outcomes in score order (1 = fraud; 0 = legitimate)
labels.fraud: Total fraud cases in the evaluated group (the denominator for recall)

captured.title: Frauds captured as the queue grows
hints: Calculate the cumulative sum of the ranked labels.
captured.explanation: Read the ranked transactions from highest score downward and keep a running count of fraud labels. At each queue size, this cumulative total answers how many frauds a reviewer would have reached by that point; it does not assume every flagged case is fraud.

precision.title: Precision at each queue size
hints: Divide captured frauds by the current queue size.
precision.explanation: Divide the frauds found so far by the number of transactions reviewed so far. This is precision at that queue size: the fraction of review work that finds fraud. A larger queue can catch more cases while lowering this fraction.

recall.title: Recall at each queue size
hints: Divide captured frauds by all actual frauds.
recall.explanation: Divide the frauds found in the queue by all frauds in the evaluated sample. This is recall: the fraction of known fraud captured. It rises as the queue expands, but says nothing about the review hours or cost unless those are included separately.

readAloud: As the ranked queue grows, add each transaction’s 1-for-fraud or 0-for-legitimate label to get cumulative frauds found. Divide that count by queue size for precision, or by all fraud cases for recall. These answer different operational questions.
workedExplanation: Reviewing six cases captures every fraud in this sample, but half the queue is legitimate. An empirical precision–recall curve can rise locally; precision does not necessarily fall at every additional rank.

Recall cannot decrease when the queue only expands, because caught frauds are not removed. Precision can rise or fall: its numerator and denominator change differently depending on whether the next case is fraud.
workedArithmetic: Cumulative frauds at K = 1 through 6 are [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3].
Recalls are [1/3, 1/3, 2/3, 2/3, 2/3, 3/3]. Adding rank 2 lowers precision only; adding rank 3 raises both precision and recall.

formulas.readAloud: As the ranked queue grows, add each transaction’s 1-for-fraud or 0-for-legitimate label to get cumulative frauds found. Divide that count by queue size for precision, or by all fraud cases for recall. These answer different operational questions.

symbols.meaning: Cumulative fraud cases among the first K ranked transactions.
Outcome label for ranked transaction i: 1 for fraud, 0 for legitimate.
Precision in the first K reviews: frauds found divided by K.
Recall among the first K reviews: frauds found divided by all frauds F.

M11b.title: State the Convention
M11b.scenario: A ranked list is summarized in two different ways. Average precision (AP) weights precision at each newly found fraud by the recall gained there. Trapezoidal precision–recall (PR) area joins neighboring points with straight lines. The exercise supplies the recall increase and precision values needed for both calculations.
M11b.task: Calculate average precision (AP) by multiplying each precision at a newly found fraud by the recall increase at that step, then adding. Separately calculate each trapezoid as its recall width times the average of its two endpoint precision values, then add those areas. Name which convention you report as PR-AUC.
M11b.interpretation: AP and trapezoidal PR area can differ for the same ranking because one uses stepwise weighting and the other connects points with straight lines. Neither number is “the percent of transactions correct.” When comparing models, state which convention you report as PR-AUC.

labels.precisions: Precision when each new fraud is found
labels.delta: Recall gained in each interval (its horizontal width)
labels.starts: Precision at the beginning of each interval
labels.ends: Precision at the end of each interval

AP.title: Average precision
hints: Multiply each discovery precision by the recall increment and add.
AP.explanation: Average precision adds the precision observed at each newly found fraud, weighted by how much recall increased at that discovery. Each increase is 1 divided by the total fraud count. The result rewards ranking fraud earlier; it is not the same area convention as trapezoidal PR area.

areas.title: Areas of the supplied trapezoids
hints: For each interval, multiply its width by the average of its two endpoint precisions.
areas.explanation: For each adjacent pair of points on the supplied precision–recall curve, find the recall width and multiply it by the average of the two endpoint precisions. This is the trapezoid area for that interval. It uses linear interpolation between the supplied points.

trapezoid.title: Total trapezoidal PR area
hints: Add all trapezoid areas.
trapezoid.explanation: Add the interval areas to obtain the total trapezoidal precision–recall area. This summarizes the plotted curve under the trapezoid convention. Average precision uses a different stepwise convention, so the two results can differ without either calculation being wrong.

readAloud: Average precision adds precision at each newly found positive, multiplied by the recall increase at that discovery. Trapezoidal area instead treats neighboring plotted points as linearly connected and adds the areas of the resulting trapezoids; the conventions can produce different values.
The recall width of an interval is its ending recall minus its starting recall. A negative width would mean the points are out of the expected order and should be checked.
workedExplanation: AP = 0.7222 and trapezoidal PR-area = 0.6778 describe the same ranking using different interpolation conventions. AP is a recall-weighted summary of precision, not “72.22% of transactions are correct.” Report the convention explicitly when comparing models.

The difference between 0.7222 and 0.6778 is not a change in the model or its ranking. It comes from the way the curve’s area is summarized. Comparing these two numbers as if they were the same statistic would manufacture a performance difference.
workedArithmetic: Trapezoid 3 = (1/3) × (2/5 + 1/2) / 2 = 0.15. Total area ≈ 0.3333 + 0.1944 + 0.15 = 0.6778. Vertical movements add zero area.

formulas.readAloud: Average precision adds precision at each newly found positive, multiplied by the recall increase at that discovery. Trapezoidal area instead treats neighboring plotted points as linearly connected and adds the areas of the resulting trapezoids; the conventions can produce different values.

symbols.meaning: Average precision under the stepwise convention, weighted by recall gained at each positive discovery.
Recall increase over interval j.
Precision at the positive discovery associated with interval j.

Precision at the end of interval j.

symbols.meaning: Recall at the end of interval j minus recall at its start.
Recall at the end of interval j.
Recall at the start of interval j.

M12.title: Match Review Capacity
M12.scenario: The transactions are ranked from highest to lowest score. Compare reviewing the first 5 with reviewing the first 10. In this past sample, later investigation results are known, so the exercise can count detected fraud; real future reviews may not be perfect. Each review costs the supplied dollar amount.
M12.task: For each queue, divide detected fraud by reviews to get precision and by all fraud to get recall. Then find the extra reviews and extra fraud found when expanding from 5 to 10. Multiply added reviews by cost per review, then divide that added cost by only the additional frauds found.
M12.interpretation: Discovering a fraud does not guarantee that its loss can be prevented or recovered. Use incremental discoveries, not all discoveries in the larger queue, when pricing the expansion.
M12.summary: Five reviews: precision {P5}, recall {R5}. Ten reviews: precision {P10}, recall {R10}. Added review cost per additional fraud found: {perExtra}.

P5.title: Precision in the smaller queue
hints: Divide its caught frauds by its queue size.
P5.explanation: Divide the frauds found in the first five reviews by five. This gives the share of those five reviews that found fraud, which helps estimate how productive the smaller queue is.

R5.title: Recall in the smaller queue
hints: Divide its caught frauds by all actual frauds.
R5.explanation: Divide frauds found in the first five reviews by all frauds in the sample. This measures how much of the known fraud the smaller queue catches; it is not the fraction of five reviews that are fraud.

P10.title: Precision in the larger queue
hints: Divide its caught frauds by its queue size.
P10.explanation: Divide frauds found in the first ten reviews by ten. Compare this precision with the five-review precision to see whether extending the queue adds useful cases or mostly lower-ranked cases.

R10.title: Recall in the larger queue
hints: Divide its caught frauds by all actual frauds.
R10.explanation: Divide frauds found in the first ten reviews by all frauds in the sample. This shows the additional reach of the larger queue against the same full set of frauds.

extraReviews.title: Additional reviews
hints: Subtract smaller queue size from larger queue size.
extraReviews.explanation: Subtract five from ten to find the extra review slots required by the larger queue. This is added workload, not a fraud count.

extraFrauds.title: Additional frauds found
hints: Subtract smaller-queue frauds from larger-queue frauds.
extraFrauds.explanation: Subtract the frauds found in the first five positions from the frauds found in the first ten. This isolates how many additional frauds the extra reviews found.

extraCost.title: Additional review cost
hints: Multiply additional reviews by cost per review.
extraCost.explanation: Multiply the additional review slots by the cost of one review. The result is the added review spending needed to move from the smaller queue to the larger one.

perExtra.title: Cost per additional fraud found
hints: Divide additional review cost by additional frauds.
perExtra.explanation: Divide the added review cost by the added frauds found. This marginal cost answers how many dollars the extra reviews spend per additional fraud detected. If the extra fraud count is zero, this ratio is undefined.

readAloud: At queue size K, precision is the share of reviewed transactions that are fraud; recall is the share of all fraud cases found. Both use the same fraud count in the numerator but answer different questions.

The extra cost per extra fraud divides added review spending by the added fraud cases found. It measures the marginal price of expanding review from K1 to K2, and is undefined if the larger queue finds no additional fraud.
workedExplanation: Expanding the queue lowers precision from 60% to 50% but increases fraud coverage from 37.5% to 62.5%. The extra cases may be worth reviewing, but the institution must have capacity and a useful intervention. Higher precision alone is not the objective.

Use the difference in fraud discoveries to assess the added five reviews. Dividing incremental spending by all five frauds in the expanded queue would over-credit discoveries already made by the smaller queue.
workedArithmetic: At K = 5: precision = 3/5 = 60%; recall = 3/8 = 37.5%.
At K = 10: precision = 5/10 = 50%; recall = 5/8 = 62.5%.
Additional reviews = 10 − 5 = 5; additional frauds = 5 − 3 = 2.
Additional cost = 5 × $2 = $10; cost per additional fraud = $10/2 = $5.

formulas.readAloud: At queue size K, precision is the share of reviewed transactions that are fraud; recall is the share of all fraud cases found. Both use the same fraud count in the numerator but answer different questions.

symbols.meaning: Fraud cases in the first K reviews divided by K.
Fraud cases in the first K reviews divided by all fraud cases F.
Fraud cases found among the first K ranked transactions.
Number of transactions reviewed.
Total fraud cases in the population.

symbols.meaning: Cost of reviewing one transaction.

M13.title: Compare With Random Review
M13.scenario: A team ranks transactions from highest to lowest model score and reviews the first K. Compare those K cases with a same-size uniformly random sample, meaning each transaction has the same chance of selection. Fraud prevalence means the share of all transactions that are fraud.
M13.task: Calculate the fraud share in the whole population and in the ranked queue. Divide queue share by population share for lift. Separately divide caught frauds by all frauds for cumulative gain. Also find the average fraud count expected under random review and the share of the population the team reviews.
M13.interpretation: Lift compares fraud concentration with random review. It is not a profit multiplier. A random sample need not contain exactly its expected fraud count.
M13.summary: Lift versus random review: {lift}. Share of all fraud found in the queue (cumulative gain): {gain}. Average frauds expected in an equally sized random queue: {random}.

prevalence.title: Population fraud prevalence
hints: Divide actual frauds by population transactions.
prevalence.explanation: Divide all fraud cases by all transactions to get population prevalence. This is the random-review benchmark: if cases were selected without using scores, this fraction would be the expected fraud share, assuming the sample represents the population.

precision.title: Queue precision
hints: Divide frauds in the queue by queue size.
precision.explanation: Divide fraud cases in the selected queue by the queue size. This gives the queue’s fraud share and can be compared with population prevalence to see whether ranking concentrates fraud near the top.

lift.title: Lift over random review
hints: Divide queue precision by population fraud prevalence.
lift.explanation: Divide queue precision by population prevalence. A lift of 1 means the queue has the same fraud share as random selection; a lift above 1 means it is more concentrated in this sample. Lift does not report the total number caught.

gain.title: Cumulative gain
hints: Divide frauds found in the queue by all actual frauds.
gain.explanation: Divide frauds found in the queue by all frauds in the population. Cumulative gain answers what share of all known fraud is captured at this queue size.

random.title: Expected frauds in a random queue
hints: Multiply queue size by population fraud prevalence.
random.explanation: Multiply queue size by population prevalence to estimate how many frauds a random queue of that size would contain on average. This is a benchmark expectation, not a promise about any particular random draw.

reviewShare.title: Share of the population reviewed
hints: Divide queue size by population transactions.
reviewShare.explanation: Divide the queue size by the full population size. This tells what fraction of transactions receive review, so it can be compared with cumulative gain to assess how much fraud is captured for that workload.

readAloud: Lift compares the fraud share in the top K reviewed cases with the population fraud share. Cumulative gain compares frauds found in those K cases with all frauds. One is concentration relative to random selection; the other is coverage of all fraud.

Population prevalence is total fraud divided by total transactions. The reviewed share is K divided by N. Under random selection, expected fraud count is the reviewed count multiplied by prevalence; it is an average benchmark.
workedExplanation: Reviewing the top 5% captures 75% of frauds, with 15 times the fraud concentration of random review. This is not a 15-fold profit increase; fraud value, review cost, and the ability to prevent or recover losses remain separate questions.
A random sample will not necessarily contain exactly the expected fraud count. The lift comparison uses its expected concentration, not a claim that every random sample produces the same result.
workedArithmetic: Prevalence = 20/1,000 = 2%; precision@50 = 15/50 = 30%.
Lift = 0.30/0.02 = 15. Cumulative gain = 15/20 = 75%.
Expected frauds in a random queue = 50 × 0.02 = 1. Population reviewed = 50/1,000 = 5%.

formulas.readAloud: Lift compares the fraud share in the top K reviewed cases with the population fraud share. Cumulative gain compares frauds found in those K cases with all frauds. One is concentration relative to random selection; the other is coverage of all fraud.

symbols.meaning: Precision in the top K divided by overall fraud prevalence.
Fraud share among the first K ranked cases.
Overall fraud prevalence: all F frauds divided by all N transactions.
Share of all fraud cases found in the first K reviews.
Fraud cases found in the first K ranked transactions.

formulas.readAloud: Population prevalence is total fraud divided by total transactions. The reviewed share is K divided by N. Under random selection, expected fraud count is the reviewed count multiplied by prevalence; it is an average benchmark.

symbols.meaning: Overall fraction of transactions that are fraud.
Number of fraud cases in the population.
Total number of transactions.
Number of cases selected for review.
Expected fraud count in a random queue of size K.

M14.title: Do the Probabilities Match Outcomes?
M14.scenario: A risk band groups loans with similar predicted default probabilities. Each band has a loan count, average predicted chance of default, and observed number of defaults. All loans use the supplied dollars-lost-per-default assumption.
M14.task: Calculate expected defaults and observed rates by band, observed-minus-predicted gaps, totals and expected versus realized loss. Plot predicted probability against observed rate.
M14.interpretation: Mean probability × group size equals the sum of its individual probabilities. A single loan’s binary outcome cannot establish calibration; assess frequencies, uncertainty and stability across cases.
M14.summary: Expected loss: {EL}; realized loss: {realized}. Realized minus expected loss: {difference}.

expected.title: Expected defaults in each band
hints: Multiply each band’s count by its mean predicted probability.
expected.explanation: For each risk band, multiply the band’s loan count by its average predicted default probability. This estimates the number of defaults the model expects across that group; fractional expected counts are valid averages.

observed.title: Observed default rates
hints: Divide observed defaults by loan count within each band.
observed.explanation: Divide actual defaults in a band by the number of loans in that same band. This is the observed default rate. Matching the band and denominator matters because the comparison checks whether predictions agree with outcomes for similar predicted risks.

gaps.title: Observed minus predicted default rates
hints: Subtract the predicted probability from each observed rate.
gaps.explanation: Subtract the band’s mean predicted probability from its observed default rate. A positive gap means defaults occurred more often than predicted in that band; a negative gap means less often. Differences are in probability points, not relative percent change.

expectedTotal.title: Total expected defaults
hints: Add expected counts across bands.
expectedTotal.explanation: Add expected default counts across all bands to get the portfolio-wide expected count. Adding group estimates works because the bands partition the same loan population.

actualTotal.title: Total actual defaults
hints: Add observed default counts.
actualTotal.explanation: Add the actual default counts across bands. This is the realized total in the sample, which can differ from the expected count because an expected value is an average, not a guaranteed outcome.

EL.title: Probability-based expected loss
hints: Multiply total expected defaults by loss per default.
EL.explanation: Multiply the expected default count by the loss per default. This gives probability-based expected loss in dollars under the supplied fixed-loss assumption; it is an estimate for planning, not the realized bill.

realized.title: Realized default loss
hints: Multiply actual defaults by loss per default.
realized.explanation: Multiply actual defaults by loss per default to calculate the loss that occurred in this sample under the exercise assumption. It describes realized outcomes, not what the model expected beforehand.

difference.title: Realized minus expected loss
hints: Subtract expected loss from realized loss.
difference.explanation: Subtract expected loss from realized loss. A positive result means the sample lost more than the probability-based estimate; a negative result means less. One sample’s difference does not by itself prove the model is biased.

readAloud: Within each predicted-risk band, multiply the number of loans by the average predicted probability to get expected defaults. Separately divide actual defaults by loan count to get the observed rate. Comparing these checks calibration at the group level.

Expected loss multiplies expected defaults by loss per default; realized loss uses actual defaults instead. The difference separates a probability-weighted forecast from the outcome that happened in this sample.
workedExplanation: The highest band understates observed risk in this sample, affecting the expected-loss calculation. The sample does not establish a permanent calibration error; uncertainty, time stability, and larger validation samples still matter.

Mean probability times group size equals the sum of individual probabilities, so it is appropriate for the expected count. Individual loans still default or do not default; a probability is evaluated by frequencies across cases, not by demanding that every single outcome match it exactly.
workedArithmetic: Observed-minus-predicted gaps are [−2, 0, 10] percentage points. Calibration points are (5%, 3%), (10%, 10%), (20%, 30%).
Expected loss = 35 × $4,000 = $140,000; realized loss = 43 × $4,000 = $172,000; difference = $32,000.

formulas.readAloud: Within each predicted-risk band, multiply the number of loans by the average predicted probability to get expected defaults. Separately divide actual defaults by loan count to get the observed rate. Comparing these checks calibration at the group level.

symbols.meaning: Expected default count in band b, found from count times average predicted probability.
Number of loans in band b.
Average predicted default probability for loans in band b.
Actual default share in band b.
Number of observed defaults in band b.

formulas.readAloud: Expected loss multiplies expected defaults by loss per default; realized loss uses actual defaults instead. The difference separates a probability-weighted forecast from the outcome that happened in this sample.

symbols.meaning: Probability-based expected loss across the supplied bands.
Assumed dollars lost for each default.
Expected defaults in band b.
Loss calculated from defaults that actually occurred.
