M15.title: Check Probability Error
M15.scenario: A model predicts default probabilities for loans whose outcomes are now known. A historical baseline assigns the same supplied probability to every loan.
M15.task: Calculate each squared probability error and the mean Brier score. Compare with the baseline and identify the largest contribution.
M15.interpretation: A lower Brier score means better probability accuracy on this evaluated sample. One non-default with a high predicted probability does not by itself establish miscalibration.
M15.summary: Model Brier score: {brier}; constant baseline: {baseline}. Largest individual squared error: {largest}.

terms.title: Squared probability errors
hints: For each loan, square predicted probability minus its 0/1 outcome.
terms.explanation: For each loan, subtract its actual outcome (1 for default, 0 for no default) from its predicted probability, then square the difference. Squaring makes every penalty nonnegative and penalizes larger misses more. A confident wrong probability is therefore costly.

brier.title: Model Brier score
hints: Average the individual squared probability errors.
brier.explanation: Add the squared errors for all loans and divide by the number of loans. This mean Brier score summarizes probability error on a scale where lower is better, but comparing models fairly also requires the same cases and outcome definition.

baseline.title: Constant-baseline Brier score
hints: Use the baseline probability for every outcome, square each error and average.
baseline.explanation: Give every loan the supplied constant baseline probability, calculate a squared error against each actual 0/1 outcome, then average. This comparison asks whether the model improves on a simple fixed-probability forecast for these same outcomes.

largest.title: Largest individual squared error
hints: Select the largest of the model’s squared-error terms.
largest.explanation: Choose the largest individual squared error from the model. This identifies its worst single probability miss in the sample; the average score can hide such a case.

readAloud: For each case, subtract the actual outcome from the predicted probability and square the difference. Average those squared errors across N cases. A lower Brier score means smaller average squared probability errors on this dataset; it does not by itself isolate calibration from other sources of error.
workedExplanation: The model has better average probability accuracy on these four loans than the constant baseline. 0.1125 is not an 11.25% default rate or dollar loss. One non-default on a 60% prediction does not, by itself, establish miscalibration; probability quality is assessed across cases.

For a non-default, the error is the probability assigned to default. For a default, it is one minus that probability in magnitude. Squaring and averaging produces a unitless scoring penalty, not money lost on the loans.
workedArithmetic: The constant 0.25 baseline gives squared errors [0.0625, 0.5625, 0.0625, 0.0625], so Brier = 0.75/4 = 0.1875. Loan C contributes the largest model error, 0.36.

formulas.readAloud: For each case, subtract the actual outcome from the predicted probability and square the difference. Average those squared errors across N cases. A lower Brier score means smaller average squared probability errors on this dataset; it does not by itself isolate calibration from other sources of error.

symbols.meaning: Mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual 0/1 outcomes.
Number of evaluated cases.
Predicted probability for case i.
Actual outcome for case i: 1 if the event happened, 0 otherwise.

M16.title: Penalize a Confident Mistake
M16.scenario: Two models estimate the chance that each transaction is fraud. Label 1 means fraud and 0 means legitimate. A positive prediction here means the model flags fraud because its probability is at or above the supplied cutoff.
M16.task: For each transaction, select the probability assigned to what actually happened (p for fraud, 1 − p for legitimate). Apply the negative natural logarithm to make a penalty: a lower assigned probability creates a much larger penalty. Average these penalties for each model. Separately apply the cutoff to Model A and count its wrong yes/no predictions.
M16.interpretation: Log loss evaluates the full probability assigned to the actual outcome, so confident mistakes hurt more even when the yes/no prediction is unchanged. The mathematical loss is infinite if the true outcome is assigned probability zero; this exercise floors that probability at 10⁻¹⁵ to keep the calculation finite. It is not a dollar loss.
M16.summary: Mean log loss: A {LLA}, B {LLB}. Model A classification errors: {errors}.

LLA.title: Model A mean log loss
hints: For each transaction, use p when fraud occurred and 1 − p when it was legitimate; then apply −ln to that probability.
LLA.explanation: For each case, assign a penalty based on the probability Model A gave to what actually happened: if fraud occurred use negative log of its fraud probability; if legitimate use negative log of its legitimate probability. Average the penalties across cases. A confident correct prediction gets a small penalty; a confident wrong one gets a large penalty.

LLB.title: Model B mean log loss
hints: Apply the same log-loss calculation to B’s probabilities and the same outcomes.
LLB.explanation: Repeat the same log-loss calculation using Model B’s probabilities and the identical outcomes. Keeping the cases and labels fixed makes the comparison about the models’ probability forecasts rather than a change in sample.

errors.title: Classification errors made by A
hints: Threshold A’s probabilities and count predictions different from the actual labels.
errors.explanation: Apply the stated classification cutoff to Model A’s probabilities, turn each into a fraud/not-fraud prediction, and count disagreements with the actual labels. This count measures thresholded classification mistakes; unlike log loss, it ignores how confident each probability was.

readAloud: Choose the probability of the outcome that happened, then take its negative natural logarithm. This creates a small penalty when the model gave the outcome a large chance and a large penalty when it gave it almost no chance; average the case penalties. This exercise floors a zero probability at 10⁻¹⁵ so the result stays finite.
workedExplanation: Model A’s 99% fraud probability on a legitimate transaction receives a much larger penalty than B’s 60%. Identical classification accuracy can conceal very different probability quality. Log loss is not a dollar-cost calculation.

Both models make the same yes/no decisions at 0.50, but the more confident mistake puts much less probability on the true outcome. Log loss detects that difference because it evaluates the full probabilities rather than only the thresholded labels.
workedArithmetic: At threshold 0.50 both predict [1, 0, 1], making the same one classification error.

formulas.readAloud: Choose the probability of the outcome that happened, then take its negative natural logarithm. This creates a small penalty when the model gave the outcome a large chance and a large penalty when it gave it almost no chance; average the case penalties. This exercise floors a zero probability at 10⁻¹⁵ so the result stays finite.

symbols.meaning: Average penalty for the probability assigned to the outcome that actually occurred; lower is better on the evaluated sample.
Number of evaluated cases.
Actual binary outcome for case i: 1 for fraud, 0 for legitimate.
Model’s predicted probability that case i is fraud.
Natural logarithm, which makes very small assigned probabilities produce large penalties.

M17a.title: Check Economics and Capacity
M17a.scenario: Two fraud cutoffs are tested on the same transactions. A false negative (FN) is a fraud that passes; a false positive (FP) is a legitimate transaction sent for review. The example assigns a dollar cost to each error and treats correct decisions as having no extra cost. Every flagged transaction needs a reviewer.
M17a.task: For each cutoff, multiply missed frauds and false alerts by their stated costs, then add those amounts. Separately count all flagged transactions as reviews. Compare both the modeled dollars and the workload with the daily review limit.
M17a.interpretation: The dollar total prices the two kinds of prediction error; it does not include every possible review expense. A policy can have lower modeled error cost and still be unusable if its queue is larger than the team can review. Do not count an unreviewed alert as a prevented fraud.
M17a.summary: Modeled costs: A {costA}, B {costB}. Review volumes: A {volumeA}, B {volumeB}. B’s excess over capacity: {excess}.

labels.TPA: Frauds correctly flagged by cutoff A
labels.FPA: Legitimate transactions mistakenly flagged by A
labels.TPB: Frauds correctly flagged by cutoff B
labels.FPB: Legitimate transactions mistakenly flagged by B
labels.cFN: Assumed dollar cost for each missed fraud
labels.cFP: Assumed dollar cost for each false alert
labels.capacity: Maximum alerts reviewers can handle per day

costA.title: Threshold A error cost
hints: Multiply A’s missed frauds by their cost and false alerts by their cost; add.
costA.explanation: Apply policy A’s confusion counts to the stated cost per false positive and false negative, then add the two cost totals. This turns different error types into a common dollar measure under the supplied assumptions.

costB.title: Threshold B error cost
hints: Apply the same loss table to B’s FN and FP counts.
costB.explanation: Use the same cost rates for policy B. Keeping the cost assumptions fixed makes the comparison reflect the policies’ different predictions rather than a different price for errors.

savings.title: Modeled saving from A to B
hints: Subtract B’s error cost from A’s.
savings.explanation: Subtract policy B’s modeled cost from policy A’s. A positive saving means B is cheaper under these assumed costs; it does not establish that B is feasible or that the error costs are complete.

volumeA.title: Reviews required by A
hints: Add A’s true and false positives.
volumeA.explanation: Count the cases policy A sends for review. This is the human workload the policy creates over the stated period, regardless of whether each review finds a problem.

volumeB.title: Reviews required by B
hints: Add B’s true and false positives.
volumeB.explanation: Count reviews required by policy B using the same population and period. The result can be compared directly with A and with the available review capacity.

excess.title: B’s reviews beyond capacity
hints: Subtract capacity from B’s review count; use zero if the difference is negative.
excess.explanation: Subtract available review capacity from B’s required reviews, keeping only a positive excess. A positive value means the policy would create more work than reviewers can handle in the stated period.

readAloud: For each policy, multiply false positives and false negatives by their assumed costs and add the amounts. Compare total modeled costs, then check review volume against capacity separately: a lower-cost policy can still exceed operational capacity.
workedExplanation: B has lower modeled error cost but is not feasible under the stated review policy. A is the feasible choice among these two today. B requires additional capacity or a separately tested workflow—not an assumption that unreviewed alerts still prevent fraud.

A lower computed cost assumes the required interventions can be delivered. Once the review queue exceeds capacity, the loss calculation is no longer enough to justify that operating point. Unreviewed alerts must not be credited as prevented fraud.
workedArithmetic: Modeled saving from B = $2,640 − $1,328 = $1,312.
A requires 15 + 35 = 50 reviews; B requires 18 + 82 = 100. With capacity 75, A fits and B exceeds capacity by 100 − 75 = 25.

formulas.readAloud: For each policy, multiply false positives and false negatives by their assumed costs and add the amounts. Compare total modeled costs, then check review volume against capacity separately: a lower-cost policy can still exceed operational capacity.

symbols.meaning: Modeled total cost under the supplied error-cost assumptions.
False-positive cases, such as non-defaulting applicants incorrectly flagged.
False-negative cases, such as defaults the policy did not flag.
Assumed cost per false positive.
Assumed cost per false negative.

M17b.title: Why the Cutoff Need Not Be 50%
M17b.scenario: Choose whether to pass or flag a transaction whose estimated fraud probability is p. A probability is calibrated when, among many comparable cases assigned a chance like p, about that share are fraud. Passing fraud has a loss; flagging a legitimate transaction has a cost. For this exercise, flagging always prevents the fraud loss and correct actions add no cost.
M17b.task: Find the probability where the average cost of passing equals the average cost of flagging. Then calculate both costs for each listed probability. “Expected” means a probability-weighted average across comparable decisions, not a bill guaranteed for one transaction. Ignore capacity and other costs here.
M17b.interpretation: The break-even point depends on the stated costs and the assumption that flagging prevents every fraud. Real review costs, imperfect intervention, customer impact, or limited capacity can move the cutoff. The calculation alone does not set a real policy.
M17b.summary: Break-even probability: {threshold}. Pass costs: {pass}. Flag costs: {review}.

labels.cFN: Assumed loss when a fraudulent transaction passes ($)
labels.cFP: Assumed cost when a legitimate transaction is flagged ($)
labels.probs: Estimated fraud chances to compare (percent or proportion)

threshold.title: Break-even fraud probability
hints: Set cFN × p = cFP × (1 − p), giving p = cFP / (cFN + cFP).
threshold.explanation: Set passing cost equal to flagging cost and solve for the probability where the two choices break even. Below this value, passing has lower expected cost under the stated costs; above it, flagging does. The calculation depends on the assumptions and is not a universal cutoff.

pass.title: Expected passing costs
hints: Multiply each fraud probability by the missed-fraud loss.
pass.explanation: Multiply the estimated fraud probability by the loss if fraud occurs to find the expected cost of passing the transaction. This averages the fraud-loss possibility across similar decisions; it is not the loss certain to occur here.

review.title: Expected flagging costs
hints: Multiply each probability of legitimacy, 1 − p, by the false-alert cost.
review.explanation: Multiply the chance the transaction is legitimate by the cost of reviewing or rejecting it to find expected flagging cost. Compare this with passing cost to choose the lower-cost action under the supplied model; nonfinancial constraints may still matter.

readAloud: At the break-even probability, the expected cost of passing equals the expected cost of flagging. Solve that equality using the stated fraud loss and review cost. The chosen action changes at this point only under these particular cost assumptions.
workedExplanation: Under this loss table, flagging becomes preferable above about 0.79%, not 50%. This is a classroom optimum for the stated assumptions; adding review costs, imperfect intervention, customer harm, or capacity constraints changes the decision.

A cost-based threshold can be far below 50% because the penalties are unequal. The calculation depends on calibrated probabilities and the assumed effectiveness of flagging. It does not establish a universal threshold for fraud detection.
workedArithmetic: At p = 0.005: pass cost = 500 × 0.005 = $2.50; flag cost = 4 × 0.995 = $3.98. Passing is cheaper.
At p = 0.01: pass cost = $5; flag cost = $3.96. At p = 0.10: pass cost = $50; flag cost = $3.60. Flagging is cheaper in both cases.

formulas.readAloud: At the break-even probability, the expected cost of passing equals the expected cost of flagging. Solve that equality using the stated fraud loss and review cost. The chosen action changes at this point only under these particular cost assumptions.

symbols.meaning: Break-even event probability where the two modeled actions have equal expected cost.
Expected cost of allowing the transaction to pass.
Expected cost of flagging or reviewing it.

M18.title: Expose the Weak Class
M18.scenario: A sentiment classifier labels each sentence neutral, positive, or negative. In the matrix, each row is what a person actually wrote and each column is what the model predicted. Every sentence has one actual label and one prediction.
M18.task: First calculate F1 for each sentiment class. Then combine the class scores three ways: macro gives all classes equal weight, weighted gives common classes more weight, and micro pools all correct and incorrect counts before scoring. Compare these summaries with the individual class scores.
M18.interpretation: The three averages answer different questions. Macro-F1 gives rare and common classes equal influence; weighted-F1 follows how often each class appears; micro-F1 pools all decisions and equals accuracy here. A high overall score can still hide a class the model never recognizes.
M18.summary: Class F1 scores: {perClass}. Macro: {macro}; weighted: {weighted}; micro: {micro}.

labels.matrix: Confusion matrix by row (neutral, positive, negative)

perClass.title: F1 by class (neutral, positive, negative)
hints: For each class use 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN), taking TP from its diagonal cell.
perClass.explanation: Calculate precision and recall separately for each class, then combine each pair into that class’s F1 score. This reveals which type of prediction is weak; a single overall score could hide poor performance on a less common class.

macro.title: Macro-F1
hints: Average the three class F1 scores with equal weights.
macro.explanation: Add the per-class F1 scores and divide by the number of classes. Macro-F1 gives each class equal influence, so a rare class matters as much as a common one. It can be sensitive to small samples for rare classes.

weighted.title: Support-weighted F1
hints: Weight each class F1 by its actual row total, then divide by all records.
weighted.explanation: Multiply each class F1 by that class’s number of actual examples, add those weighted scores, and divide by the total examples. Common classes influence the result more, so a high weighted score can hide weak results on a rare class.

micro.title: Micro-F1
hints: Pool TP, FP and FN across classes, then apply the F1 formula.
micro.explanation: Add true positives, false positives, and false negatives across classes before calculating precision, recall, and F1. In single-label classification this emphasizes total case-level performance and can be dominated by common classes.

TP.title: Pooled true positives
hints: Add the three diagonal counts.
TP.explanation: Add correct positive predictions across the classes. These pooled true positives form the numerator for micro-precision and micro-recall.

FP.title: Pooled false positives
hints: For each class, count predictions of that class from other actual classes; add.
FP.explanation: Add predictions assigned to a class that were actually another class. These pooled false positives lower micro-precision.

FN.title: Pooled false negatives
hints: For each class, count actual records predicted as another class; add.
FN.explanation: Add actual cases of a class that the model assigned elsewhere. These pooled false negatives lower micro-recall.

readAloud: For each class, calculate its F1 from that class’s precision and recall. Macro averaging gives every class equal weight; support weighting gives more weight to classes with more actual examples. Those choices answer different questions about performance.

Micro-averaging pools the class counts first, then calculates precision, recall, and F1. In a single-label task, each mistaken case contributes a false positive for one class and a false negative for another.

Precision is correct positive predictions divided by all positive predictions. Recall is correct positive predictions divided by all actual positives. These denominators differ, so one rate can be high while the other is low.
workedExplanation: The classifier catches none of the negative statements. Micro-F1 and weighted-F1 conceal more of that weakness because neutral examples dominate. Here micro-F1 equals accuracy, 11/16, because every record has exactly one label.

A wrong neutral-to-negative prediction adds a false negative to neutral and a false positive to negative. The same record therefore appears in two pooled error counts. Micro-F1 accounts for that convention; it must not be calculated by simply averaging the class F1 scores.
workedArithmetic: Neutral counts (TP, FP, FN) = (8, 3, 2), so F1 = 16/21 ≈ 0.7619. Positive counts (3, 1, 1) give F1 = 6/8 = 0.75. Negative counts (0, 1, 2) give F1 = 0.
Pooled counts are TP = 11, FP = 5, FN = 5. Micro-F1 = 22 / (22 + 5 + 5) = 0.6875.

formulas.readAloud: For each class, calculate its F1 from that class’s precision and recall. Macro averaging gives every class equal weight; support weighting gives more weight to classes with more actual examples. Those choices answer different questions about performance.

symbols.meaning: F1 score for class c, combining that class’s precision and recall.
Correct class-c predictions divided by all predictions labeled c.
Correct class-c predictions divided by all actual class-c cases.
Number of classes.
Number of actual examples belonging to class c.

formulas.readAloud: Micro-averaging pools the class counts first, then calculates precision, recall, and F1. In a single-label task, each mistaken case contributes a false positive for one class and a false negative for another.

symbols.meaning: Total correct positive assignments pooled over classes.
Total incorrect positive assignments pooled over classes.
Total missed positive assignments pooled over classes.
F1 calculated after pooling the class-level counts.

formulas.readAloud: Precision is correct positive predictions divided by all positive predictions. Recall is correct positive predictions divided by all actual positives. These denominators differ, so one rate can be high while the other is low.

symbols.meaning: Cases correctly assigned to the positive class.
Cases assigned to the positive class that belong elsewhere.
Actual positive cases assigned to another class.

M19.title: Compare Rates, Not Just Counts
M19.scenario: This teaching example supplies repayment outcomes for every applicant, including people the simulated policy would reject, so we can compare rates. A real lender usually cannot observe repayment by applicants it declined. Here, approval is the predicted positive decision and repayment is the positive outcome.
M19.task: For each group, divide approvals by all applicants to get the approval rate. Compare B with A as a ratio, then calculate the approval rate among actual repayers and among actual non-repayers. Report the gap between two rates in percentage points: subtract the proportions and multiply by 100.
M19.interpretation: A ratio compares rates relatively; a gap in percentage points compares their direct difference. Different approval rates can coexist with equal false-positive rates when repayment prevalence differs. These are warning signals to investigate, not proof of a cause or a complete fairness or legal judgment.
M19.summary: Approval-rate ratio B/A: {ratio}. Repayer TPR gap: {gap}. FPRs: A {FPRA}, B {FPRB}.

selectionA.title: Group A approval rate
hints: Divide A’s approvals by A’s applicants.
selectionA.explanation: Divide approved applicants in group A by all applicants in group A. This gives the approval or selection rate for that group; counts alone cannot compare groups of different sizes.

selectionB.title: Group B approval rate
hints: Divide B’s approvals by B’s applicants.
selectionB.explanation: Use group B’s approved count divided by all group B applicants. Both groups must use the same definition of approval and evaluation window for the rates to be comparable.

ratio.title: Selection-rate ratio B/A
hints: Divide B’s approval rate by A’s approval rate.
ratio.explanation: Divide group B’s selection rate by group A’s. A ratio of 1 means equal rates; a ratio below 1 means B’s rate is lower. This summary does not explain why rates differ or establish fairness by itself.

TPRA.title: Group A repayer true-positive rate
hints: Divide approved repayers in A by all repayers in A.
TPRA.explanation: Among group A applicants who repaid, divide those approved by all who repaid. This measures how often the policy correctly approves repayers, using actual repayers as the denominator.

TPRB.title: Group B repayer true-positive rate
hints: Divide approved repayers in B by all repayers in B.
TPRB.explanation: Calculate the same approval rate among actual repayers in group B. Comparing it with group A asks whether repayers have similar chances of approval across the groups.

gap.title: Absolute repayer TPR gap
hints: Take the absolute difference between the two TPRs.
gap.explanation: Subtract the two repayer true-positive rates and take the absolute value. Report the result as a percentage-point gap: for example, 0.08 is an 8 percentage-point difference. It is not an 8 percent relative change.

FPRA.title: Group A non-repayer false-positive rate
hints: Subtract approved repayers from approvals; divide by applicants minus repayers in A.
FPRA.explanation: Among group A applicants who did not repay, divide those approved by all non-repayers. This is the false-positive rate for repayment, so the denominator is actual non-repayers.

FPRB.title: Group B non-repayer false-positive rate
hints: Use the corresponding non-repayer counts for B.
FPRB.explanation: Calculate the corresponding approval rate among group B non-repayers. Compare these rates to see whether non-repayers are incorrectly approved at different rates; the result alone does not identify the cause.

readAloud: Selection rate is approvals divided by all applicants in a group. The ratio compares group B’s rate with group A’s. For error-rate comparisons, calculate rates within the relevant actual outcome group, then report their difference in percentage points.

Compare each group’s rates using matching outcome denominators. The rate gap is the absolute difference in percentage points, while the selection-rate ratio is a relative comparison; equal values on one measure do not guarantee equality on the other.
workedExplanation: Approval rates and repayer capture differ even though both groups have the same FPR. These diagnostics identify differences that need investigation; they do not independently establish fairness, unfairness, or a legal conclusion. Outcome definitions, population differences, and uncertainty remain important.

The two groups have different repayment prevalences in the supplied benchmark. Equal FPR alone therefore does not imply equal approval rates or equal TPR. The arithmetic describes the pattern, not its cause or whether any decision is legally justified.
workedArithmetic: Approval rates: A = 600/1,000 = 60%; B = 400/1,000 = 40%. B/A selection-rate ratio = 0.40/0.60 ≈ 0.667.
Repayer TPRs: A = 560/800 = 70%; B = 300/500 = 60%; gap = 10 percentage points.
A has 1,000 − 800 = 200 non-repayers and 600 − 560 = 40 approved non-repayers, so FPR = 40/200 = 20%.
B has 1,000 − 500 = 500 non-repayers and 400 − 300 = 100 approved non-repayers, so FPR = 100/500 = 20%.

formulas.readAloud: Selection rate is approvals divided by all applicants in a group. The ratio compares group B’s rate with group A’s. For error-rate comparisons, calculate rates within the relevant actual outcome group, then report their difference in percentage points.

symbols.meaning: Approved applicants in group A divided by all applicants in group A.
Approved applicants in group B divided by all applicants in group B.
Approval rate among actual repayers in group A.
Approval rate among actual repayers in group B.
Approval rate among actual non-repayers in group A.
Approval rate among actual non-repayers in group B.

formulas.readAloud: Compare each group’s rates using matching outcome denominators. The rate gap is the absolute difference in percentage points, while the selection-rate ratio is a relative comparison; equal values on one measure do not guarantee equality on the other.

symbols.meaning: Rate for group A within the stated actual-outcome denominator.
Corresponding rate for group B using the same outcome definition.
Absolute difference between two proportions; multiply by 100 to state percentage points.
One group’s rate divided by the comparison group’s rate.

M20.title: How Many Dollars Was the Forecast Off?
M20.scenario: Treasury compares a model’s daily settlement forecasts with actual cash outflows on the same four days. The model is compared with a simpler reference forecast, called the baseline. All amounts are in thousands of dollars and listed in matching day order.
M20.task: Find the average size of the model’s forecast miss (mean absolute error, or MAE) and the baseline’s average miss. Then calculate how much smaller the model’s miss is in dollars and as a share of the baseline miss.
M20.interpretation: MAE measures the size of forecast errors, not funding cost or savings. Absolute values stop overforecasts and underforecasts from canceling, but do not distinguish their financial consequences.
M20.summary: Model MAE: {MAE}; baseline MAE: {baseline}. Reduction: {reduction}, equivalent to {dollars} less average absolute forecast error.

MAE.title: Model mean absolute error
hints: Average the absolute differences between model forecasts and actuals.
MAE.explanation: Find the absolute difference between each forecast and actual dollar outflow, then average those differences. MAE reports the typical miss size in dollars; taking absolute values prevents positive and negative errors from canceling.

baseline.title: Baseline mean absolute error
hints: Repeat the calculation with the baseline forecasts.
baseline.explanation: Calculate the same average absolute error for the supplied simple comparison forecast. Both models must be measured on the same dates and dollar units for the comparison to be meaningful.

reduction.title: Proportional reduction in MAE
hints: Divide baseline MAE minus model MAE by baseline MAE.
reduction.explanation: Subtract model MAE from baseline MAE, then divide by baseline MAE. This expresses the improvement as a fraction of the baseline error; if baseline MAE is zero, the reduction is undefined.

dollars.title: Reduction in absolute error, in dollars
hints: Multiply the MAE difference in thousands by 1,000.
dollars.explanation: Subtract model MAE from baseline MAE to find the average dollar reduction in forecast error per period. A positive number means the model’s average miss is smaller on these observations.

readAloud: For each period, take the absolute forecast error so overestimates and underestimates do not cancel, then average. Compare this dollar MAE with the baseline using the same observations; the reduction can be stated as dollars or as a fraction of baseline error.
A percentage reduction divides the decrease in error by the baseline error. The dollar reduction is just baseline MAE minus model MAE. These are relative and absolute descriptions of the same change.
workedExplanation: The model misses actual settlement outflow by $12,500 per day on average, versus $22,500 for the baseline in this sample. The smaller miss is not automatically an equal dollar saving: MAE measures forecast error, not funding cost. It also does not show whether the forecast was too high or too low.

Using absolute differences stops overforecasts and underforecasts from cancelling each other. The mean remains in the financial target’s units, which makes it interpretable. It does not distinguish the funding consequences of a shortage from those of excess cash.
workedArithmetic: Baseline absolute errors are [0, 20, 20, 50]. MAE = 90/4 = $22.5 thousand.
MAE reduction = 22.5 − 12.5 = $10 thousand = $10,000; proportional reduction = 10/22.5 ≈ 44.44%.

formulas.readAloud: For each period, take the absolute forecast error so overestimates and underestimates do not cancel, then average. Compare this dollar MAE with the baseline using the same observations; the reduction can be stated as dollars or as a fraction of baseline error.

symbols.meaning: Mean absolute forecast error in the same units as the target, here dollars.
Forecast for period t.
Actual outflow for period t.
Number of evaluated periods.
Mean absolute error from the supplied comparison forecast.

formulas.readAloud: A percentage reduction divides the decrease in error by the baseline error. The dollar reduction is just baseline MAE minus model MAE. These are relative and absolute descriptions of the same change.

symbols.meaning: Fraction of baseline MAE removed by the model.
Baseline mean absolute error.
Model mean absolute error.

M21.title: Which Forecast Has the More Dangerous Miss?
M21.scenario: Forecast A and B have errors for the same four days, measured as forecast minus actual in thousands of dollars. A negative error means the forecast was too low (an underforecast); a positive error means it was too high.
M21.task: For each forecast, calculate MAE, the average size of a miss, and RMSE. RMSE squares each miss, averages those squared values, and takes the square root so the answer returns to thousands of dollars. Squaring makes one unusually large miss count more heavily.
M21.interpretation: RMSE gives larger misses more weight, but does not distinguish shortage from excess. Keep the error signs and funding consequences when making a treasury decision.
M21.summary: MAE: A {MAEA}, B {MAEB}. RMSE: A {RMSEA}, B {RMSEB}.

MAEA.title: Forecast A MAE
hints: Average the absolute values of A’s errors.
MAEA.explanation: For forecast A, average the absolute differences between its forecast and each actual outflow. This measures typical miss size in dollars while treating over- and under-forecasts symmetrically.

MAEB.title: Forecast B MAE
hints: Average the absolute values of B’s errors.
MAEB.explanation: Calculate B’s absolute errors on the same periods. Matching the dates lets the comparison reflect forecast quality rather than an easier test sample.

RMSEA.title: Forecast A RMSE
hints: Square A’s errors, average them, then take the square root.
RMSEA.explanation: Square each forecast A error, average the squared errors, then take the square root to return to dollars. Because squaring magnifies large misses, RMSE reacts more strongly to a few dangerous errors than MAE.

RMSEB.title: Forecast B RMSE
hints: Square B’s errors, average them, then take the square root.
RMSEB.explanation: Repeat the squared-error calculation for B on the same observations. Compare RMSE with MAE: a model’s RMSE being much larger relative to its MAE signals some large misses, but neither measure identifies their cause.

readAloud: MAE averages absolute errors, giving a typical miss in dollars. RMSE squares errors before averaging and takes a square root afterward, also returning dollars; the squaring gives unusually large errors extra influence.
Compare the two forecasts using the same actual values. MAE treats each dollar of error proportionally, while RMSE penalizes larger errors more sharply because it squares them.
workedExplanation: B has the smaller average absolute miss—$7,500 versus $10,000—but a $30,000 underforecast on one day. RMSE ranks A better because it gives large misses more weight. RMSE itself does not distinguish shortages from excess cash; the sign and funding consequences require separate attention.

The root does not undo the greater weight given to large errors; averaging occurs after squaring and before taking the root. A US$30,000 underforecast contributes nine times the squared penalty of a US$10,000 miss.

formulas.readAloud: MAE averages absolute errors, giving a typical miss in dollars. RMSE squares errors before averaging and takes a square root afterward, also returning dollars; the squaring gives unusually large errors extra influence.

symbols.meaning: Average absolute difference between forecast and actual.
Square root of mean squared forecast error.
Forecast for period t.
Actual value for period t.
Number of evaluated periods.

formulas.readAloud: Compare the two forecasts using the same actual values. MAE treats each dollar of error proportionally, while RMSE penalizes larger errors more sharply because it squares them.

symbols.meaning: Forecast error for period t.
Mean absolute error.
Root mean squared error.

M22.title: Percentage of What?
M22.scenario: Use the later test days to measure forecast errors; keep the separate earlier training history for the comparison scale. Amounts are in thousands of dollars. The simple nonseasonal naive forecast assumes the next value will equal the previous observation.
M22.task: Calculate test MAE, then compare errors as percentages in two ways: MAPE averages each day’s error relative to that day’s actual value; WAPE compares all absolute errors with total actual volume. Finally divide test MAE by the average training error of the previous-value forecast to get MASE. Enter MAPE and WAPE as proportions or with a percent sign.
M22.interpretation: MAPE averages daily proportional errors; WAPE divides total absolute error by total actual volume. MASE compares test error with the training naive-error scale, not necessarily a naive forecast’s test error. MAPE is undefined if an actual is zero.

MAE.title: Test mean absolute error
hints: Average absolute test actual-minus-forecast differences.
MAE.explanation: Average the absolute differences between the test forecasts and actual values. This establishes the typical error in the target’s units before converting it to relative or scaled measures.

MAPE.title: Mean absolute percentage error
hints: Divide each absolute error by its absolute actual, then average.
MAPE.explanation: For each observation, divide absolute error by its actual value, convert to a percentage, and average. If an actual value is zero, that term is undefined; very small actuals can also dominate the score.

WAPE.title: Weighted absolute percentage error
hints: Divide the sum of absolute errors by the sum of absolute actuals.
WAPE.explanation: Add all absolute errors, then divide by the sum of actual values. Unlike MAPE, this weights periods by their actual size, so high-volume days contribute more. The denominator must be positive.

naiveScale.title: Training naive-error scale
hints: Average absolute changes between consecutive training observations.
naiveScale.explanation: On the training data only, calculate the average absolute error from the stated naive forecast, such as using the previous period. This creates a reference scale without using the test outcomes to tune the denominator.

MASE.title: Mean absolute scaled error
hints: Divide test MAE by the training naive-error scale.
MASE.explanation: Divide test MAE by the training naive-error scale. A value below 1 means the test MAE is smaller than that training reference scale; it does not guarantee performance will stay better in future periods.

readAloud: MAE is the average absolute error in the target’s own units. MAPE averages each absolute error divided by its actual value, which is undefined at zero and unstable near zero. WAPE divides total absolute error by total actual volume.

A naive forecast uses a simple rule such as carrying the last observation forward. Its average training error becomes a scale. MASE compares test MAE with that scale; below one means the test error is smaller than the reference.
This percentage form divides the sum of absolute errors by the sum of actual values, then converts to percent. It is undefined if total actual volume is zero.
workedExplanation: MAPE averages each day’s percentage miss. WAPE compares total absolute error with total volume. MASE says the test error is 62.5% of the training naive-error scale; it does not, by itself, establish superiority to a naive forecast on the test period. MAPE is undefined at zero actuals.

The denominators intentionally differ. MAPE gives each day’s proportional miss equal weight; WAPE evaluates error relative to total volume; MASE compares against a historical forecasting scale. A name containing “percentage” is not permission to ignore zeros, signs, or the evaluation window.
workedArithmetic: Absolute errors are [10, 10, 20, 10]; test MAE = 50/4 = 12.5.

formulas.readAloud: MAE is the average absolute error in the target’s own units. MAPE averages each absolute error divided by its actual value, which is undefined at zero and unstable near zero. WAPE divides total absolute error by total actual volume.

symbols.meaning: Mean absolute error in the target units.
Mean of absolute errors relative to each actual value; zero actuals require a stated convention.
Total absolute error divided by total actual volume.
Actual value at time t.
Forecast at time t.

formulas.readAloud: A naive forecast uses a simple rule such as carrying the last observation forward. Its average training error becomes a scale. MASE compares test MAE with that scale; below one means the test error is smaller than the reference.

symbols.meaning: Test mean absolute error divided by training-set naive forecast MAE.
Mean absolute error on held-out test periods.
Mean absolute error of the specified naive forecast on training periods.

formulas.readAloud: This percentage form divides the sum of absolute errors by the sum of actual values, then converts to percent. It is undefined if total actual volume is zero.

symbols.meaning: Total absolute error divided by total actual amount.
Sum of absolute forecast errors.
Sum of actual values over the evaluated periods.

M23.title: Improvement Over Predicting the Mean
M23.scenario: A settlement forecast is compared with actual outflows in thousands of dollars. R-squared (R²) compares the model’s squared misses with the squared variation around the average actual value for these same days.
M23.task: Find the sample’s average actual outflow. Then total the model’s squared misses (SSE) and the squared distances from that average (SST). Calculate R² = 1 − SSE/SST. The sample average is an evaluation yardstick, not a future forecast known to treasury.
M23.interpretation: The evaluated sample’s mean is a scoring reference, not a forecast available in advance. R² measures relative squared-error reduction, not the fraction of exactly correct forecasts.
M23.summary: R²: {R2}. Model SSE: {SSE}; sample-mean reference SST: {SST}.

actualMean.title: Mean actual outflow
hints: Add actuals and divide by observation count.
actualMean.explanation: Add the observed outflows and divide by the number of periods. This mean-only forecast is the reference that R-squared compares against; it uses the test-set mean here as a descriptive benchmark.

SSE.title: Model sum of squared errors
hints: Square every actual-minus-forecast error and add.
SSE.explanation: Subtract each model forecast from the actual, square each error, and add the squares. Squaring prevents cancellation and emphasizes large misses; SSE is in squared dollars.

SST.title: Sample-mean sum of squared deviations
hints: Square each actual’s deviation from the actual mean and add.
SST.explanation: Subtract the sample mean from each actual value, square those differences, and add them. SST measures how much actual outflows vary around the mean-only reference.

R2.title: R²
hints: Calculate 1 − model SSE / reference SST.
R2.explanation: Calculate one minus SSE divided by SST. A value of 1 is a perfect fit; 0 matches the mean-only reference in squared-error terms; a negative value is worse than that reference. If SST is zero, R-squared is undefined.

readAloud: SSE adds squared gaps between model forecasts and actual values. SST adds squared gaps between actual values and their mean. R-squared is one minus SSE divided by SST, so zero matches the mean reference and a negative result performs worse on this sample.

The mean actual value is the reference prediction for every case. Compare the model’s squared error with that reference’s squared variation; a negative R-squared means the model’s error sum is larger.
workedExplanation: The model removes 73.83% of squared error relative to the sample-mean reference. It does not mean 73.83% of forecasts are correct. The test-set mean is an evaluation reference—not a forecast treasury could know before those outcomes occurred.

The 73.83% interpretation refers to a reduction in squared-error total, not a share of exactly correct forecasts. A forecast can receive a positive R-squared without matching any daily actual exactly.

formulas.readAloud: SSE adds squared gaps between model forecasts and actual values. SST adds squared gaps between actual values and their mean. R-squared is one minus SSE divided by SST, so zero matches the mean reference and a negative result performs worse on this sample.

M24.title: Covered, but Useful?
M24.scenario: Treasury receives intervals meant to contain 90% of similar future outflows over many dates. Each interval has a lower and upper amount, in millions of dollars. In this small five-day example, a value exactly on either boundary counts as covered; one sample can land above or below 90% by chance.
M24.task: Count the days when actual outflow falls inside its interval and divide by five to get observed coverage. Separately subtract each lower bound from its upper bound and average to get interval width. Widen each interval by the supplied amount on both sides and calculate coverage and width again.
M24.interpretation: Wider intervals may cover more outcomes but give less precise guidance. Coverage and width should be read together, and a small sample cannot establish long-run calibration.

labels.widen: Amount added to each side ($ millions)

coverage.title: Observed interval coverage
hints: Count actuals between their bounds, including endpoints, and divide by observation count.
coverage.explanation: Count the observed values that fall between their lower and upper forecast bounds, then divide by all observations. This empirical coverage can be compared with the interval’s stated target, but matching coverage alone does not make an interval useful.

width.title: Mean interval width
hints: Subtract lower from upper for each interval, then average.
width.explanation: For each observation, subtract the lower bound from the upper bound and average the widths. Width is measured in the target’s units; narrower intervals are more informative only when coverage remains adequate.

wideCoverage.title: Coverage after widening
hints: Check each actual against lower − widen and upper + widen.
wideCoverage.explanation: Recount how many actual values fall inside the widened intervals and divide by the same number of observations. This shows whether the adjustment improves coverage on these data.

wideWidth.title: Mean width after widening
hints: Each interval gains twice the widening amount.
wideWidth.explanation: Average the widened upper-minus-lower bounds. Compare with the original width to see the price paid for additional coverage; wider is not automatically better if intervals become unusable.

readAloud: Coverage is the share of observed outcomes inside their predicted intervals. Mean width is the average distance between upper and lower bounds. Evaluate them together: high coverage can be achieved by making intervals so wide that they provide little guidance.
workedExplanation: Wider ranges cover more outcomes but give less precise funding guidance. Neither result alone determines the better system: treasury needs sufficiently reliable coverage and useful width. Five observations are too few to conclude that the original 90% intervals are systematically miscalibrated.

Making every interval very wide can raise coverage without giving treasury a useful forecast. Coverage and width must be read together, and the five-day count alone is too small to establish long-run calibration.
workedArithmetic: Days 1, 3, 4 and 5 are covered; day 2 is not. Original coverage = 4/5 = 80%.
Widths are [30, 20, 20, 30, 10], so mean width = 110/5 = $22 million.
Widened intervals are [80, 130], [90, 130], [75, 115], [120, 170], [90, 120]. All five actuals are covered: 5/5 = 100%.
Adding 10 to both sides increases each width by 20; mean width = 22 + 20 = $42 million.

formulas.readAloud: Coverage is the share of observed outcomes inside their predicted intervals. Mean width is the average distance between upper and lower bounds. Evaluate them together: high coverage can be achieved by making intervals so wide that they provide little guidance.

symbols.meaning: Fraction of outcomes lying between their predicted lower and upper bounds.

Upper forecast bound for case i.

M25.title: Penalize a Cash Shortage More Heavily
M25.scenario: A quantile is a target position in the distribution of future values. A 95th-percentile forecast is intended to be at least as high as about 95% of similar outcomes over many dates, if it is well calibrated. Amounts are in millions of dollars. Pinball loss scores this target by weighting underforecasts by tau and overforecasts by 1 − tau.
M25.task: For each day, use the 0.95 weight when actual liquidity need is above the forecast and the 0.05 weight when the forecast is above actual need. Average those scores. Then compare equal-sized shortfalls and excess forecasts. These are scoring weights, not automatically the bank’s real borrowing and idle-cash costs.
M25.interpretation: The asymmetric weights define the quantile being estimated. They are not automatically the institution’s actual funding-cost ratio, and the score is not realized cash loss.
M25.summary: Mean pinball loss: {average}. Equal-miss penalties: underforecast {under}, overforecast {over}; ratio {ratio}.

labels.equalError: Equal miss size to compare ($ millions)

losses.title: Daily pinball losses
hints: If actual ≥ forecast use tau × (actual − forecast); otherwise use (1 − tau) × (forecast − actual).
losses.explanation: For each day, compare the forecast with actual cash need. If it underestimates, multiply the shortage by the chosen quantile; if it overestimates, multiply the excess by one minus that quantile. This makes shortages and excesses carry different penalties.

average.title: Mean pinball loss
hints: Average the daily losses.
average.explanation: Add the daily pinball penalties and divide by the number of days. Lower average loss means better performance for this chosen asymmetry and quantile on the evaluated data; it does not mean every day’s forecast is safe.

under.title: Penalty for an underforecast
hints: Multiply the equal miss size by tau.
under.explanation: Read the underforecast penalty weight from the quantile: this is the cost assigned per unit of shortage. A high quantile makes shortages more expensive and tends to favor a higher forecast.

over.title: Penalty for an overforecast
hints: Multiply the equal miss size by 1 − tau.
over.explanation: Read the overforecast penalty weight as one minus the quantile. This is the cost per unit of excess cash reserved; a high quantile therefore makes overforecasting relatively less costly.

ratio.title: Underforecast-to-overforecast penalty ratio
hints: Divide the underforecast penalty by the overforecast penalty.
ratio.explanation: Divide the shortage penalty weight by the excess penalty weight. This ratio shows the relative emphasis in the chosen scoring rule; if the overforecast weight is zero, the ratio is undefined.

readAloud: Pinball loss assigns one weight to an underforecast and another to an overforecast. At quantile q, a shortage receives weight q and an excess receives weight 1 minus q. The average scores forecasts for the selected tradeoff; it does not reveal the dollar consequences unless the units and costs are also interpreted.
workedExplanation: This scoring rule strongly discourages underestimating a high liquidity quantile. The 19-to-1 weighting comes from choosing the 95th percentile; it is not automatically the bank’s actual funding-cost ratio. The computed score is not a realized cash loss.

The high quantile intentionally penalizes shortfalls more than excess. The weights describe the scoring target, not observed borrowing fees or a stated regulatory reserve requirement. The average 6.5 is in weighted million-dollar error units, not realized loss.
workedArithmetic: For actual 150: loss = 0.95 × (150 − 130) = 19. For actual 120: loss = 0.05 × (130 − 120) = 0.5. For actual 130: loss = 0.
Mean loss = (19 + 0.5 + 0) / 3 = 6.5 weighted million-dollar error units.
Equal 10-unit misses give underforecast penalty 0.95 × 10 = 9.5 and overforecast penalty 0.05 × 10 = 0.5. Their ratio = 9.5/0.5 = 19.

formulas.readAloud: Pinball loss assigns one weight to an underforecast and another to an overforecast. At quantile q, a shortage receives weight q and an excess receives weight 1 minus q. The average scores forecasts for the selected tradeoff; it does not reveal the dollar consequences unless the units and costs are also interpreted.

symbols.meaning: Pinball loss for target quantile q.
Chosen quantile between 0 and 1; larger q places more penalty weight on underforecasting.
Actual cash need.
Forecast for quantile q.
Select the positive penalty branch so under- and over-forecast cases are handled separately.

M26.title: Does the Customer Belong in This Segment?
M26.scenario: Customers are grouped using measured details that have been scaled so dollar amounts and percentages have a comparable influence on distance. A cluster is one assigned group. For each customer, a is the average distance to others in its own group; b is the smallest average distance to any other group.
M26.task: For each customer, compare the two average distances with (b − a) / max(a, b), then average the scores. A result near 1 means the assigned group is closer; near 0 means both groups are similarly close; below 0 means another group is closer on average.
M26.interpretation: Positive scores mean the assigned cluster is closer on average. Negative scores suggest inspecting another cluster assignment. These geometric relationships do not establish profitability or response to an offer.

labels.b: Smallest average distances to alternative clusters

scores.title: Silhouette score for each customer
hints: Subtract a from b and divide by the larger of a and b.
scores.explanation: For each customer, compare its average distance to customers in its assigned cluster with the average distance to the nearest alternative cluster. The silhouette score balances within-cluster closeness against separation. Values near 1 suggest a clear fit, near 0 suggest a boundary, and below 0 suggest a possible poor assignment.

mean.title: Mean silhouette score
hints: Average the customer scores.
mean.explanation: Add the customer-level silhouette scores and divide by the number of customers. This summarizes the sample’s average cluster fit, but can hide individuals with negative scores and does not prove that the segments are useful for a business decision.

readAloud: For each customer, compare its average distance to its own cluster with the average distance to its nearest alternative cluster. A positive silhouette favors the assigned cluster; a negative one means another cluster is closer on this distance measure.
Average the customer scores to summarize the dataset. The mean can conceal a mix of well-placed and poorly placed customers, so inspect the individual distribution too.
workedExplanation: A is closer to its own segment. B lies near a segment boundary. C is, on average, closer to another segment than to its assigned one, so its assignment needs inspection. The near-zero mean suggests weak separation for these customers. None of these values demonstrates that the segments improve marketing response, retention, or profitability.

Positive, zero, and negative values indicate different geometric relationships. Those signs do not mean profitable, neutral, and unprofitable customers. Geometry is only one part of validating whether a segmentation is useful.
workedArithmetic: B’s silhouette = (4 − 4) / 4 = 0. C’s silhouette = (3 − 6) / 6 = −0.50.

formulas.readAloud: For each customer, compare its average distance to its own cluster with the average distance to its nearest alternative cluster. A positive silhouette favors the assigned cluster; a negative one means another cluster is closer on this distance measure.

symbols.meaning: Silhouette score for customer i, comparing within-cluster distance a(i) with nearest-other-cluster distance b(i).
Average distance from customer i to other customers in its assigned cluster.
Smallest average distance from customer i to another cluster.

formulas.readAloud: Average the customer scores to summarize the dataset. The mean can conceal a mix of well-placed and poorly placed customers, so inspect the individual distribution too.

M27a.title: When Does Another Segment Stop Helping?
M27a.scenario: Four customers’ monthly savings are shown in hundreds of dollars. Compare three supplied groupings (partitions): all customers together; the first two and last two; and the first two together with each remaining customer alone. A centroid is each group’s average value, its center for this calculation.
M27a.task: For each grouping with k = 1, 2, or 3, find the group centers and add the squared distance from each customer to their group’s center. This total is called inertia. Compare how much inertia falls each time; more groups can always make a tighter fit, so the decrease alone does not show that the extra group is useful.
M27a.interpretation: Inertia measures compactness on the chosen scale. More clusters can reduce it even without adding a useful business distinction. Look for a substantial change in improvement and check stability and usefulness separately.

labels.values: Customer savings in ascending order ($ hundreds)

c.title: Centroid with one cluster
hints: Average all four savings values.
c.explanation: With one cluster, assign every customer to the same group and calculate the mean of the supplied feature values. This centroid is the group’s representative location.

c1.title: First centroid with two clusters
hints: Average the first two values.
c1.explanation: For the two-cluster solution, calculate the mean feature value for customers assigned to the first cluster. The centroid is a summary point, not necessarily an actual customer.

c2.title: Second centroid with two clusters
hints: Average the last two values.
c2.explanation: Calculate the mean feature value for the second cluster using only its assigned customers. Its position helps show how the split separates the data.

I1.title: Inertia with one cluster
hints: Sum squared distances from the overall mean.
I1.explanation: For one cluster, add the squared distance from each customer to the single centroid. This within-cluster total, called inertia, measures compactness in the chosen units and features.

I2.title: Inertia with two clusters
hints: Sum squared distances from each customer’s two-cluster centroid.
I2.explanation: Repeat the squared-distance sum using the two centroids and each customer’s assigned centroid. Adding clusters cannot increase the best achievable training inertia, so a decrease alone does not prove the extra segment is valuable.

I3.title: Inertia with three clusters
hints: Only the first pair contributes nonzero distances; singleton clusters contribute zero.
I3.explanation: Calculate inertia with three clusters under the same distance and feature scaling. Use it to compare the marginal reduction from the second to the third cluster.

reduction12.title: Inertia reduction from one to two clusters
hints: Subtract two-cluster inertia from one-cluster inertia.
reduction12.explanation: Subtract two-cluster inertia from one-cluster inertia. The reduction measures how much closer the training points become to their assigned centroids after adding a second cluster.

reduction23.title: Inertia reduction from two to three clusters
hints: Subtract three-cluster inertia from two-cluster inertia.
reduction23.explanation: Subtract three-cluster inertia from two-cluster inertia. Compare this improvement with the first reduction to see whether adding the third group helps less; the elbow is a judgment aid, not an automatic optimal cluster count.

readAloud: A cluster centroid is the average location of the customers assigned to that cluster. Inertia adds each customer’s squared distance to its assigned centroid. Extra clusters usually lower training inertia, so compare the size of the improvement rather than choosing the lowest value automatically.
Inertia reduction is the earlier solution’s inertia minus the later solution’s inertia. It measures improvement in within-cluster fit on this dataset as another cluster is added.
workedExplanation: Two groups explain most of the variation here: lower and higher savings. A third adds little compactness. Inertia uses squared feature units, not dollars of business value; it also cannot establish stability or usefulness. Giving every customer a separate cluster would produce zero inertia but no meaningful segmentation.

The squared distances quantify compactness on the chosen scale. Dividing a group into smaller groups can reduce the total even if no useful business distinction is added, so the minimum inertia alone is not a defensible stopping rule.
workedArithmetic: Two-cluster centers are 1.5 and 8.5. Inertia = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 1.
Three-cluster centers are 1.5, 8 and 9. Inertia = 0.25 + 0.25 + 0 + 0 = 0.5.
Reductions are 50 − 1 = 49, then 1 − 0.5 = 0.5. The apparent elbow is k = 2.

formulas.readAloud: A cluster centroid is the average location of the customers assigned to that cluster. Inertia adds each customer’s squared distance to its assigned centroid. Extra clusters usually lower training inertia, so compare the size of the improvement rather than choosing the lowest value automatically.

M27b.title: Did the Same Segments Reappear?
M27b.scenario: The same customers are grouped twice, and a 2-by-2 table counts how many land in each old/new group combination. Cluster names such as “1” or “2” are arbitrary; what matters is whether the same pairs of customers stay together.
M27b.task: Count customer pairs that stay together in both runs, pairs together in each run, and all possible pairs. The adjusted Rand index (ARI) compares the observed shared pairs with what might happen by chance for group sizes like these. ARI near 1 means the groupings agree; near 0 is chance-level agreement; below 0 is less agreement than that chance reference.
M27b.interpretation: Cluster names are arbitrary. ARI compares membership pairs and adjusts for a reference holding cluster sizes fixed. A negative result is below that reference, not negative classification accuracy.
M27b.summary: Adjusted Rand index: {ARI}. Observed within-cell pair count: {S}; chance-reference count: {chance}.

S.title: Sum of within-cell pair counts
hints: Calculate n(n − 1)/2 for each overlap cell and add.
S.explanation: Within each cell of the two-clustering comparison table, count how many customer pairs appear together in both clusterings, then count pairs using n choose 2. Summing these values captures agreements on shared assignments.

R.title: Sum of row-total pair counts
hints: Find both row totals, calculate their pair counts and add.
R.explanation: For each row total, count pairs placed together in that row’s clustering using n choose 2, then add. This records pair agreement implied by the first partition, regardless of the second.

C.title: Sum of column-total pair counts
hints: Find both column totals, calculate their pair counts and add.
C.explanation: Apply the same pair count to each column total and add. This records agreement implied by the second partition.

T.title: All unordered customer pairs
hints: Add all cells to get N, then calculate N(N − 1)/2.
T.explanation: Count every possible unordered customer pair among N customers as N times N minus 1 divided by 2. This is the total comparison pool for pair-based agreement.

chance.title: Chance-reference pair count
hints: Calculate R × C / T.
chance.explanation: Use the row and column pair totals to calculate the expected agreement from their margins under the index’s chance model. Subtracting this reference prevents raw agreement from looking impressive just because large clusters create many easy pair agreements.

ARI.title: Adjusted Rand index
hints: Subtract chance from S, then divide by (R + C)/2 minus chance.
ARI.explanation: Compare observed pair agreement above the chance reference with the maximum possible agreement above that same reference. The adjusted Rand index is 1 for matching partitions, near 0 at chance expectation, and can be negative when agreement is below that reference.

readAloud: The adjusted Rand index compares pairs of customers: together in both clusterings, apart in both, or split differently. It adjusts the observed agreement for the agreement expected from the cluster sizes, so it is more informative than raw pair agreement when partitions have different sizes.

Convert each cell and each row or column total into the number of unordered customer pairs using n choose 2. The total T counts every possible pair. These pair counts form the observed and chance-expected agreement terms.
workedExplanation: These two runs disagree substantially on who belongs together; agreement is below the chance-adjusted reference for these cluster sizes. The value is not “negative accuracy.” Cluster names are arbitrary: exchanging X and Y would leave ARI unchanged. This small exercise does not establish stability for the bank’s full customer population.

Compute pair counts, not percentages of matching letters. A relabeling can change every displayed group name without moving any customer. ARI therefore ignores names and compares the underlying grouping structure.
workedArithmetic: Overlap rows are [2, 1] and [1, 2]; both row totals and column totals are [3, 3]. Total customers = 6, so T = 6 × 5 / 2 = 15 pairs.
Within-cell pairs: S = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2. Row pairs R = 3 + 3 = 6; column pairs C = 3 + 3 = 6.
Chance-reference count = RC/T = 36/15 = 2.4.

formulas.readAloud: The adjusted Rand index compares pairs of customers: together in both clusterings, apart in both, or split differently. It adjusts the observed agreement for the agreement expected from the cluster sizes, so it is more informative than raw pair agreement when partitions have different sizes.

symbols.meaning: Chance-adjusted agreement between two ways of grouping the same customers.
Number of customers shared by row cluster i and column cluster j.
Size of row cluster i.
Size of column cluster j.
Total customers being compared.

formulas.readAloud: Convert each cell and each row or column total into the number of unordered customer pairs using n choose 2. The total T counts every possible pair. These pair counts form the observed and chance-expected agreement terms.
