M28.title: Find All the Evidence
M28.scenario: A retrieval system finds text passages for each question. Reviewers have already marked which passages contain the needed evidence. The system returns the same number of distinct passages, K, for every question; one question can need more than one passage to be fully answered. Context precision here is a simple relevant share, not a rank-weighted measure.
M28.task: For each question, divide relevant passages found by all relevant passages available to get recall. Divide relevant passages found by K to get context precision, the useful share of returned passages. Then average each rate across questions, giving each question equal weight.
M28.interpretation: Finding one relevant passage is a hit, but may leave required evidence missing. Averaging per-query recall is different from pooling all passage counts. Answer quality needs its own evaluation.
M28.summary: Mean retrieval recall: {meanRecall}; mean context precision: {meanPrecision}.

labels.relevant: All relevant passages available per question

recalls.title: Recall for each question
hints: Divide relevant passages retrieved by all relevant passages available for that question.
recalls.explanation: For each question, divide relevant evidence passages retrieved by all relevant passages known for that question. This checks how much useful evidence retrieval found; a higher value can still come with many irrelevant passages.

precision.title: Context precision for each question
hints: Divide relevant passages retrieved by K.
precision.explanation: For each question, divide relevant retrieved passages by all passages retrieved. This checks how much of the retrieved context is useful. Its denominator is retrieved passages, unlike recall’s denominator of all known relevant passages.

meanRecall.title: Mean retrieval recall
hints: Average the per-question recall fractions.
meanRecall.explanation: Add the question-level recall values and divide by the number of questions. This gives each question equal influence, so the average can hide a difficult question with poor retrieval.

meanPrecision.title: Mean context precision
hints: Average the per-question context-precision fractions.
meanPrecision.explanation: Average the question-level precision values across the same questions. Read it alongside recall because retrieving only one obvious passage can yield high precision but miss important evidence.

readAloud: Retrieval recall divides relevant passages found by all relevant passages available for a query. Context precision divides relevant passages found by all passages retrieved. Recall measures coverage; precision measures relevance of the returned context.
workedExplanation: Both questions have an evidence “hit,” but Q1 is missing half its required source material. A 100% question-level hit rate is not 100% relevant-chunk recall. Two-thirds of the supplied context is irrelevant in both cases. Generation still needs separate evaluation.

The missing B chunk in Q1 matters even though A was retrieved. Counting Q1 as a binary “hit” discards information about completeness. Mean recall across questions also differs from pooling all retrieved chunks into one global numerator and denominator.
workedArithmetic: Q1 retrieves one of its two relevant passages: recall = 1/2 = 50%; context precision = 1/3 ≈ 33.33%.
Q2 retrieves its only relevant passage: recall = 1/1 = 100%; context precision = 1/3 ≈ 33.33%.
Mean recall = (0.5 + 1) / 2 = 75%. Mean context precision = (1/3 + 1/3) / 2 = 1/3 ≈ 33.33%.

formulas.readAloud: Retrieval recall divides relevant passages found by all relevant passages available for a query. Context precision divides relevant passages found by all passages retrieved. Recall measures coverage; precision measures relevance of the returned context.

symbols.meaning: Relevant evidence retrieved for query q divided by all known relevant evidence for q.
Relevant retrieved passages divided by all passages retrieved for q.
Number of relevant passages retrieved for query q.
Total passages retrieved for query q.
Total known relevant passages for query q.

M29a.title: How Soon Does the First Useful Source Appear?
M29a.scenario: For each analyst question, record the position of the first passage containing relevant evidence: rank 1 is first, rank 2 is second, and so on. Use 0 when the search returns no relevant passage in the evaluated list.
M29a.task: Give a found passage a score of 1 divided by its rank, so results near the top earn more and an unsuccessful search earns zero. Average across every question, including misses, then replace the last query’s missing result with the supplied new rank and recalculate.
M29a.interpretation: Include unsuccessful queries in the mean. MRR measures how early the first relevant passage appears; it ignores additional relevant passages and does not measure answer correctness.

labels.ranks: First relevant ranks (0 means not found)
labels.newRank: New relevant rank for the last query

RR.title: Reciprocal rank for each query
hints: Use 1/rank when rank is positive and 0 for a missing result.
RR.explanation: For each query, locate the rank of its first relevant source and take one divided by that rank. A source at rank 1 receives 1; one farther down receives a smaller score. A query with no relevant result follows the stated zero convention.

MRR.title: Mean reciprocal rank
hints: Average all reciprocal ranks, including zero values.
MRR.explanation: Add the reciprocal-rank scores across queries and divide by the number of queries. Mean reciprocal rank emphasizes how quickly the first useful source appears; it ignores additional relevant sources after the first.

newMRR.title: MRR after improving the last query
hints: Replace the last reciprocal rank by 1/newRank, then average.
newMRR.explanation: Replace the last query’s reciprocal-rank score with the score at its improved rank, then average across the same query set. Keeping all other queries fixed isolates the effect of moving that result.

improvement.title: MRR improvement
hints: Subtract original MRR from revised MRR.
improvement.explanation: Subtract the original MRR from the revised MRR. A positive difference means the first relevant source moved earlier on average under this query set; it does not measure whether the sources support a complete answer.

readAloud: Reciprocal rank is one divided by the position of the first relevant result. Mean reciprocal rank averages that score across queries, so early useful results count more and later relevant results are not reflected.
workedExplanation: The first useful passage now appears earlier for more questions, reducing how far an analyst or downstream system must search. MRR is not the percentage of correct answers and ignores the ordering of additional relevant passages after the first.
The unresolved question belongs in the denominator of the original MRR. Dropping it would inflate the reported retrieval quality by evaluating only successful searches.
workedArithmetic: Moving the last query’s first relevant passage to rank 2 changes its contribution to 1/2. New MRR = (1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.5) / 4 = 0.5625.

formulas.readAloud: Reciprocal rank is one divided by the position of the first relevant result. Mean reciprocal rank averages that score across queries, so early useful results count more and later relevant results are not reflected.

symbols.meaning: One divided by the rank of the first relevant result for query q; zero when none is found under the stated convention.
Rank position of the first relevant result for query q.
Average reciprocal rank across the evaluated queries.
Number of queries evaluated.

M29b.title: Put the Best Evidence First
M29b.scenario: Reviewers give each retrieved passage a relevance grade, with a higher grade meaning more useful evidence. This example gives grade r a gain of 2^r − 1 and reduces credit for lower-ranked passages by dividing by log₂(rank + 1), where rank 1 is first.
M29b.task: Add the discounted gain for the list as returned (DCG). Then sort the same grades from highest to lowest to calculate the best possible score (ideal DCG). Divide the returned-list score by that ideal to get nDCG, a share of the ideal score. Use full precision in logarithms.
M29b.interpretation: nDCG is a fraction of the ideal discounted-relevance score under the same gain and cutoff. It is not the fraction of relevant passages or the probability that an answer is correct.

DCG.title: Discounted cumulative gain
hints: For each rank, divide 2^grade − 1 by log2(rank + 1), then add.
DCG.explanation: For each ranked result, multiply its relevance grade by the discount for its position, then add the contributions. Relevant material near the top counts more because users are less likely to inspect deep results.

IDCG.title: Ideal discounted cumulative gain
hints: Sort the grades highest first and repeat the same discounted-gain calculation.
IDCG.explanation: Sort the same relevance grades in the best possible order and calculate DCG. This is the ideal score for this query and provides a scale for normalization.

nDCG.title: Normalized discounted cumulative gain
hints: Divide actual DCG by ideal DCG.
nDCG.explanation: Divide the actual ranked list’s DCG by its ideal DCG. A value near 1 means the ordering is close to ideal for these relevance judgments. If ideal DCG is zero, the ratio is undefined and needs the stated convention.

readAloud: Discounted cumulative gain adds each result’s relevance grade after reducing its influence according to its rank. Normalize by the score from the ideal ordering to compare rankings on a zero-to-one scale when the ideal score is positive.
workedExplanation: The retriever found the strongest passage but put it behind weaker evidence. Its discounted relevance score is about 71% of the ideal ordering’s score. Moving the grade-3 passage first gives nDCG of 1 here. Neither score establishes that the generated answer uses the passage correctly.

The normalized result is a fraction of ideal discounted relevance, not the fraction of sources that are relevant. Ranking the strongest source second loses more credit under exponential gain than a simple relevant-versus-irrelevant count would reveal.
workedArithmetic: Gains for grades [1, 3, 0] are [2¹ − 1, 2³ − 1, 2⁰ − 1] = [1, 7, 0].
Ideal grades [3, 1, 0] give IDCG = 7/log2(2) + 1/log2(3) + 0/log2(4) ≈ 7.6309.
nDCG ≈ 5.4165/7.6309 ≈ 0.7098. These totals use the unrounded logarithms.

formulas.readAloud: Discounted cumulative gain adds each result’s relevance grade after reducing its influence according to its rank. Normalize by the score from the ideal ordering to compare rankings on a zero-to-one scale when the ideal score is positive.

symbols.meaning: Discounted sum of relevance grades in the returned ranking.
Relevance grade of the result at position i.
Rank discount that reduces the contribution of results farther down.
DCG for the ideal ordering of the same relevance grades.
Actual DCG divided by ideal DCG, when the denominator is positive.

M30.title: Three Checks, Three Denominators
M30.scenario: A financial answer is audited for three separate properties: support anywhere in retrieved evidence, correctness of its attached citations, and correctness of numeric figures. Revenue figures use the same units and period basis.
M30.task: Calculate revenue growth and the three audit rates from their separate counts. A true statement can still have the wrong attached citation.
M30.interpretation: Use the denominator belonging to each check: all claims, claim–citation pairs, or financial figures. Averaging these rates into one accuracy number would hide the type of failure.
M30.summary: Revenue growth: {growth}. Faithfulness: {faithfulness}; citation correctness: {citation}; numeric accuracy: {numerical}.

growth.title: Revenue growth
hints: Subtract old revenue from new revenue and divide by old revenue.
growth.explanation: Divide the change in revenue by the starting revenue and convert to a percentage. The result describes relative growth over the stated period; a small starting value can make the percentage look large.

faithfulness.title: Claim faithfulness
hints: Divide supported claims by all claims.
faithfulness.explanation: Count answer claims supported by the retrieved evidence and divide by all checked claims. This estimates support among claims, not whether every important source was retrieved or the answer is factually complete.

citation.title: Citation correctness
hints: Divide correctly supported claim–citation pairs by all cited pairs.
citation.explanation: Divide citations that correctly point to supporting sources by all citations checked. A citation can exist yet fail this test if it points to the wrong passage or does not support the claim.

numerical.title: Numeric accuracy
hints: Divide correct financial figures by all evaluated figures.
numerical.explanation: Compare the answer’s numeric claims with the supplied source values and count those that match under the stated tolerance. This catches arithmetic or transcription errors, but not unsupported nonnumeric claims.

readAloud: These measures use different denominators. Revenue growth compares change with starting revenue; faithfulness checks supported claims among claims made; citation correctness checks citations; numeric accuracy checks numeric statements. Keep their counts separate before interpreting each rate.

A rate is the number of successes divided by the items inspected for that specific question. The denominators differ across revenue records, answer claims, citations, and numeric claims, so these percentages should not be averaged as if they measured one thing.
workedExplanation: A true statement can carry the wrong citation, and a well-cited answer can still contain false statements. Different denominators are intentional. These scores should not be averaged into a single “accuracy” number; one material debt error may be sufficient to reject the answer.

Claim 3 is numerically correct and supported somewhere in the supplied corpus, but its own citation is wrong. A single answer can therefore pass one check and fail another. The exact counting rubric is part of the definition, not a formatting detail.
workedDetails: Evidence A gives 2024 revenue of $100 million and 2025 revenue of $120 million. Evidence B gives 2025 net profit of $12 million. Evidence C gives 2025 debt of $40 million.
The answer claims: revenue was $120 million [A]; revenue grew 20% [A]; net profit was $12 million [C]; debt was $30 million [C]; and debt will fall next year [no citation].
The net-profit claim is true but cites the wrong evidence. The debt amount is false; the future-debt claim is unsupported.
workedArithmetic: Revenue growth = (120 − 100) / 100 = 20%.
Claims 1 and 2 are supported by A, and claim 3 by B: faithfulness = 3/5 = 60%.
Only claims 1 and 2 have correct attached citations: citation correctness = 2/4 = 50%.
Figures 120, 20% and 12 are correct; the debt figure 30 should be 40. Numeric accuracy = 3/4 = 75%.

formulas.readAloud: These measures use different denominators. Revenue growth compares change with starting revenue; faithfulness checks supported claims among claims made; citation correctness checks citations; numeric accuracy checks numeric statements. Keep their counts separate before interpreting each rate.

symbols.meaning: Revenue change divided by starting revenue over the stated period.
Supported answer claims divided by all answer claims checked.
Citations that point to supporting evidence divided by citations checked.
Correct numeric claims divided by numeric claims checked.

formulas.readAloud: A rate is the number of successes divided by the items inspected for that specific question. The denominators differ across revenue records, answer claims, citations, and numeric claims, so these percentages should not be averaged as if they measured one thing.

symbols.meaning: Count meeting the named quality condition.
Count inspected for that same condition.
x divided by n, with the category and denominator stated.

M31.title: Return Relative to Which Risk?
M31.scenario: Two funds have returns and variability measured over the same year. Volatility describes how widely returns move. The supplied 3% reference rate is used both as the comparison return for Sharpe and the minimum acceptable return for Sortino. Annualized values are expressed on a per-year basis.
M31.task: For each fund, first subtract the 3% reference from its return. The Sharpe ratio divides this extra return by all return variability; the Sortino ratio divides it by downside variability below the target. Compare the ratios, remembering they describe this sample rather than promising future results.
M31.interpretation: Sharpe charges for total volatility; Sortino charges for downside deviation from the stated target. Ratios describe the evaluated return and risk estimates, not guaranteed future performance or tail safety.
M31.summary: Sharpe ratios: A {sharpeA}, B {sharpeB}. Sortino ratios: A {sortinoA}, B {sortinoB}.

labels.rf: Risk-free rate and minimum acceptable return

excessA.title: Fund A excess return
hints: Subtract the reference return from A’s mean return.
excessA.explanation: Subtract the risk-free return from fund A’s return over the same period. This is the return above the cash-like reference, expressed in percentage points for the period.

excessB.title: Fund B excess return
hints: Subtract the reference return from B’s mean return.
excessB.explanation: Use the same risk-free reference and period for fund B. Matching time units is essential before comparing risk-adjusted results.

sharpeA.title: Fund A Sharpe ratio
hints: Divide A’s excess return by A’s total volatility.
sharpeA.explanation: Divide fund A’s average excess return by the standard deviation of all its returns. The Sharpe ratio rewards higher excess return and penalizes total volatility, including upward movement.

sharpeB.title: Fund B Sharpe ratio
hints: Divide B’s excess return by B’s total volatility.
sharpeB.explanation: Calculate fund B’s Sharpe ratio using the same return frequency and risk-free rate. A larger value indicates more excess return per unit of total volatility in this sample, not guaranteed future performance.

sortinoA.title: Fund A Sortino ratio
hints: Divide A’s excess return by A’s downside deviation.
sortinoA.explanation: Divide fund A’s average excess return by downside deviation, which measures returns below the stated target. Unlike standard deviation, upside variation does not increase this denominator.

sortinoB.title: Fund B Sortino ratio
hints: Divide B’s excess return by B’s downside deviation.
sortinoB.explanation: Use the same target and downside-deviation convention for fund B. Compare with Sharpe to see whether conclusions change when only downside variation counts.

readAloud: Excess return subtracts the risk-free rate from the fund return. Sharpe divides average excess return by total return volatility; Sortino uses downside deviation relative to a target. Their values depend on the observation period and annualization convention.

Use consistent return periods to compare excess returns and volatility. If annualizing, apply the course’s stated frequency rule to both funds; annualization changes scale but does not add new evidence about future returns.
Standard deviation measures spread around average returns; downside deviation measures shortfalls below a chosen target. The risk measure should match the investor’s question.
workedExplanation: B’s higher return came with more risk. It does not win on either risk-adjusted ratio here. A Sharpe ratio of 0.50 means half a unit of excess return per unit of measured volatility—not a 50% return or a 50% chance of profit. These estimates do not establish future performance or tail safety.

The numerator rewards performance above the specified reference. The denominator identifies the kind of variability being charged against that performance. B’s extra return is not enough to overcome its larger total volatility on Sharpe, while both funds have the same return per unit of supplied downside deviation.
workedArithmetic: Excess returns: A = 9% − 3% = 6%; B = 11% − 3% = 8%.
Sortino ratios: A = 6/6 = 1; B = 8/8 = 1. Use consistent percentage units in both numerator and denominator.

formulas.readAloud: Excess return subtracts the risk-free rate from the fund return. Sharpe divides average excess return by total return volatility; Sortino uses downside deviation relative to a target. Their values depend on the observation period and annualization convention.

symbols.meaning: Fund or portfolio return over the stated period.
Risk-free reference return over the same period.
Standard deviation of portfolio returns, measuring total variability.
Downside deviation below the selected target.
Average excess return per unit of total return variability.
Average excess return per unit of downside deviation.

formulas.readAloud: Use consistent return periods to compare excess returns and volatility. If annualizing, apply the course’s stated frequency rule to both funds; annualization changes scale but does not add new evidence about future returns.

symbols.meaning: Average return over the observations.
Average risk-free return over matching observations.
Number of return observations.

formulas.readAloud: Standard deviation measures spread around average returns; downside deviation measures shortfalls below a chosen target. The risk measure should match the investor’s question.
