Target return below which observations count as downside.
Number of periods in the stated calculation.

M32a.title: The Loss Hidden by a Good Ending
M32a.scenario: An account follows the supplied value path in thousands of dollars, with no deposits or withdrawals. A running peak is the highest value seen up to that date. Drawdown measures the fall from that earlier peak as a share of the peak, reported here as a positive loss size.
M32a.task: At each point, compare the account value with the highest value reached so far. Divide the fall by that earlier peak; the largest such fall is maximum drawdown. Separately compare the final value with the starting value to get final return. These show different parts of the experience.
M32a.interpretation: Only peaks reached by that time belong in a drawdown calculation. A profitable ending can follow a severe decline; final return does not describe the funding or behavioral strain along the path.

peaks.title: Running peaks
hints: At each observation take the largest value seen so far.
peaks.explanation: At each date, keep the highest portfolio value seen so far. These running peaks provide a fair reference for measuring losses from a prior high, even if the portfolio later recovers.

drawdowns.title: Drawdowns from the running peaks
hints: Divide running peak minus current value by running peak.
drawdowns.explanation: For each date, compare current value with its running peak and express the shortfall as a fraction of that peak. This shows the percentage decline an investor experienced from the previous high.

MDD.title: Maximum drawdown
hints: Take the largest drawdown along the path.
MDD.explanation: Choose the largest drawdown over the period. Maximum drawdown describes the deepest observed peak-to-trough loss, but not how long recovery took or how often losses occurred.

finalReturn.title: Final return
hints: Divide final value minus initial value by initial value.
finalReturn.explanation: Compare the final portfolio value with its starting value and express the change as a percentage. A strong ending return can coexist with a deep drawdown along the way.

readAloud: A running peak is the highest value reached up to each date. Drawdown compares current value with that peak; maximum drawdown is the worst such decline. Final return only compares the ending and starting values, so it can hide the path between them.
The ending return is final value minus starting value, divided by starting value. It is a whole-period result and does not describe the sequence of losses and recoveries.
workedExplanation: An investor ended up 25% but first endured a one-third decline from the account’s earlier peak. Final return hides that path. The later value of 125 cannot be used as the peak for the earlier decline to 80.

The denominator is the earlier peak of 120, not the starting value of 100 or the later value of 125. The numerator measures the investor’s decline from that peak. A strong final return cannot remove the funding or behavioral strain experienced during the earlier drawdown.

formulas.readAloud: A running peak is the highest value reached up to each date. Drawdown compares current value with that peak; maximum drawdown is the worst such decline. Final return only compares the ending and starting values, so it can hide the path between them.

symbols.meaning: Highest portfolio value reached through date t.
Portfolio value at date t.
Fractional decline from the running peak at date t.
Largest drawdown observed over the full period.

formulas.readAloud: The ending return is final value minus starting value, divided by starting value. It is a whole-period result and does not describe the sequence of losses and recoveries.

symbols.meaning: Starting portfolio value.
Portfolio value at the final date T.
Total return from start to finish.

M32b.title: Can the Allocation Be Implemented?
M32b.scenario: A fully invested portfolio changes its asset weights, with no market movement or deposits/withdrawals during the rebalance. A weight is an asset’s share of the portfolio. One-way turnover is the share shifted from one set of assets to another; gross trading counts both the dollars sold and dollars bought. Fees apply to every traded dollar.
M32b.task: For the proposed weights, find each change, add the absolute changes and divide by two for one-way turnover. Multiply the full change by portfolio value to count purchases plus sales, then apply the fee rate. Separately check whether any alternative weight exceeds its cap.
M32b.interpretation: Selling and reinvesting the same amount creates two sides of gross trading. A cap violation is a separate feasibility failure and cannot be offset by favorable expected return.
M32b.summary: One-way turnover: {turnover}; gross trading: {gross}; fees: {cost}. Largest alternative-weight excess: {violation}, or {violationDollars}.

labels.alternative: Alternative weights to check against cap
labels.costRate: Fee per dollar bought or sold

changes.title: Changes in asset weights
hints: Subtract current weight from proposed weight for each asset.
changes.explanation: Subtract each current asset weight from its target weight. Positive changes are purchases and negative changes are sales; weights are shares of the portfolio, not dollar amounts yet.

turnover.title: One-way turnover
hints: Add absolute weight changes and divide by 2.
turnover.explanation: Add the absolute weight changes and divide by two. The division avoids counting the same portfolio rebalance once as dollars sold and again as dollars bought.

gross.title: Gross dollars bought and sold
hints: Multiply the full absolute-weight-change sum by portfolio value.
gross.explanation: Multiply one-way turnover by portfolio value to find the dollars on one side, then double it to count both purchases and sales. Equivalently, multiply the full sum of absolute weight changes by portfolio value.

cost.title: Transaction fees
hints: Multiply gross trading dollars by the fee rate.
cost.explanation: Multiply traded dollars by the transaction-fee rate. This estimates implementation cost under the supplied fee assumption and excludes market impact unless separately included.

violation.title: Largest alternative-weight cap excess
hints: Subtract the cap from the largest alternative weight; use zero if none exceeds it.
violation.explanation: For each alternative portfolio, calculate how far any asset weight exceeds its permitted cap, then select the largest positive excess. A zero means no cap was exceeded under these constraints.

violationDollars.title: Dollar value above the cap
hints: Multiply the excess weight by portfolio value.
violationDollars.explanation: Multiply the excess weight by total portfolio value to convert the constraint breach into dollars. This shows the size of the position above the cap, not the trading cost to fix it.

readAloud: Portfolio changes are target weights minus current weights. One-way turnover is half the sum of absolute changes because each rebalance balances buys with sells. Multiply by portfolio value to estimate traded dollars, then apply the fee rate.

A cap violation is the amount by which a weight exceeds its allowed maximum. Multiplying the excess fraction by portfolio value expresses the oversize position in dollars; feasibility is separate from expected return.
The absolute change counts both buys and sells. Halve the total to report one-way turnover under a fully funded rebalance.
workedExplanation: Turnover estimates the trading burden; the fee calculation depends on the stated convention. A mandatory allocation cap is a separate pass/fail condition. Better expected performance does not make a noncompliant proposed allocation feasible.

Selling 20% of portfolio value and reinvesting it creates 20% one-way turnover but 40% gross trading. The stated fee charges both sides. Likewise, an asset at 55% breaches a 50% cap by five percentage points, not by 5% of its current holding.
workedArithmetic: Fees = $400,000 × 0.001 = $400, charging both purchases and sales.
Alternative cap violation = 0.55 − 0.50 = 0.05, or 5 percentage points; dollar excess = 0.05 × $1,000,000 = $50,000.

formulas.readAloud: Portfolio changes are target weights minus current weights. One-way turnover is half the sum of absolute changes because each rebalance balances buys with sells. Multiply by portfolio value to estimate traded dollars, then apply the fee rate.

symbols.meaning: Target portfolio weight for asset i.
Current portfolio weight for asset i.
Change in asset i’s weight.
One-way fraction of portfolio value traded.
Total portfolio value.
Fee rate applied to traded dollars.

formulas.readAloud: For each asset, subtract its current weight from its target weight to find the change. Absolute changes count both sales and purchases; multiplying their total by portfolio value gives gross dollars traded. The same total equals twice one-way turnover.

symbols.meaning: Target weight for asset i after rebalancing.
Current weight for asset i before rebalancing.
Change in asset i’s share of the portfolio.
Total portfolio value in dollars.
One-way share of the portfolio shifted, counting purchases or sales once.

formulas.readAloud: A weight above its permitted cap is a constraint violation. Subtract the cap from the proposed weight and keep only positive results; multiplying that fraction by portfolio value expresses the excess position in dollars. A zero means the cap is met.

symbols.meaning: Proposed weight for asset i.
Maximum permitted weight for that asset.
The amount by which the proposed weight exceeds its cap, or zero when it does not.
Total portfolio value in dollars.

M32c.title: How Far Does the Fund Wander from Its Benchmark?
M32c.scenario: A fund and its benchmark have returns for the same periods. Active return means fund return minus benchmark return in one period; it can be positive or negative. Tracking error describes how much these differences vary around their average. Use the sample standard deviation, dividing by n − 1.
M32c.task: Calculate the fund-minus-benchmark difference for each period, average those differences, and measure how widely they vary around that average. Annualize the result by multiplying by the square root of periods per year, under the supplied assumption that periods are stable and uncorrelated. This variability is not average underperformance.
M32c.interpretation: Tracking error measures variability around mean active return. It does not tell whether the fund outperformed. A short sample and the annualization assumptions limit its use as a risk estimate.
M32c.summary: Periodic tracking error: {monthly}; annualized tracking error: {annual}. Mean active return: {mean}.

active.title: Active returns
hints: Subtract benchmark return from fund return in each period.
active.explanation: Subtract the benchmark return from the fund return for each period. These active returns measure how much the fund led or lagged its benchmark, not its absolute gain or loss.

mean.title: Mean active return
hints: Average the active returns.
mean.explanation: Add the active returns and divide by the number of periods. A positive mean indicates average outperformance in this sample; it does not tell how consistently that occurred.

squares.title: Sum of squared active-return deviations
hints: Subtract mean active return from each active return, square and add.
squares.explanation: Subtract the mean active return from each period’s active return, square the deviations, and add. This measures variability of the fund’s benchmark-relative performance.

monthly.title: Periodic tracking error
hints: Divide squared deviations by n − 1, then take the square root.
monthly.explanation: Divide the squared-deviation total by one fewer than the number of periods, then take the square root. Using n − 1 estimates variability from a sample. The result is tracking error for one period, in the same units as returns.

annual.title: Annualized tracking error
hints: Multiply periodic tracking error by the square root of periods per year.
annual.explanation: Multiply periodic tracking error by the square root of the number of periods per year. This annualizes variability under an assumption that period-to-period returns are independent; it does not annualize the mean return.

readAloud: Tracking error is the standard deviation of active returns, the fund’s returns minus its benchmark’s. Annualization multiplies periodic tracking error by the square root of periods per year under the usual independence assumption.
workedExplanation: Tracking error describes the variability of benchmark-relative returns—not a 4% loss or 4% underperformance. Mean monthly active return is zero here, yet active risk is positive. Annualization and this four-observation estimate should not be treated as reliable without more data.

Active returns of +1 and −1 percentage point average to zero but still fluctuate. Tracking error measures that fluctuation. Computing the standard deviation of the fund’s returns alone would answer a different question about total risk rather than benchmark-relative risk.
workedArithmetic: Annualized tracking error = 0.011547 × √12 ≈ 0.04 = 4%, under the stated uncorrelated-period assumption.

formulas.readAloud: Tracking error is the standard deviation of active returns, the fund’s returns minus its benchmark’s. Annualization multiplies periodic tracking error by the square root of periods per year under the usual independence assumption.

symbols.meaning: Active return in period t: fund return minus benchmark return.
Mean active return over the evaluated periods.
Standard deviation of active returns, or tracking error.
Number of periods per year used for annualization.

M33.title: Threshold versus Tail Average
M33.scenario: Equally weighted one-day loss scenarios are listed in $ thousands. Use the nearest-rank empirical VaR convention. Expected Shortfall is the mean of the worst (1 − confidence) fraction of scenarios.
M33.task: Sort losses, select VaR at rank ceiling(confidence × count), average the worst tail and count losses strictly above VaR.
M33.interpretation: VaR marks a threshold, not the maximum loss. Expected Shortfall describes average loss in the chosen tail. Both results depend on the scenario distribution and stated small-sample conventions.
M33.summary: One-day VaR: {VaR}; Expected Shortfall: {ES}. Observed fraction strictly exceeding VaR: {exceed}.

sorted.title: Losses in ascending order
hints: Sort every scenario from smallest to largest.
sorted.explanation: Sort the simulated or historical losses from smallest to largest. Ordering first lets the chosen percentile be located by rank under the stated nearest-rank convention.

VaR.title: Nearest-rank Value at Risk
hints: Select rank ceiling(confidence × scenario count), with ranks starting at 1.
VaR.explanation: Find the loss at the nearest-rank position for the selected confidence level. VaR is a threshold: under the modeled distribution, the stated fraction of losses should be at or below it. It does not describe how severe losses beyond it may be.

ES.title: Expected Shortfall
hints: Average the largest (1 − confidence) fraction of losses, rounding the tail count upward.
ES.explanation: Average losses in the specified tail at or beyond the VaR cutoff, following the exercise’s inclusion convention. Expected Shortfall describes tail severity more directly, but remains dependent on the sample and model.

exceed.title: Fraction strictly above VaR
hints: Count losses greater than VaR, excluding equal values, then divide by scenario count.
exceed.explanation: Count losses strictly greater than VaR and divide by all losses. This empirical tail fraction can differ from the nominal tail probability because of finite samples and tied values.

readAloud: Value at Risk is a selected loss quantile: a threshold expected not to be exceeded at the stated confidence level under the model. Expected Shortfall averages losses in the tail beyond that threshold. A threshold alone does not reveal tail severity.

The nearest-rank convention selects the observation at the ceiling of confidence level times sample size. State this convention because alternative quantile interpolation rules can produce a different cutoff.
workedExplanation: Under this empirical scenario distribution, 80% of one-day losses are no more than $7,000; the worst fifth averages $15,000. VaR is not a maximum loss: even this tiny sample includes a $20,000 loss. The 80% level is a teaching choice, not a recommended risk policy.

VaR identifies where the tail begins under the chosen convention. Expected Shortfall describes the size of losses within that tail. They can differ considerably because the threshold does not reveal how far the worst observations extend beyond it. Both are conditional on the supplied scenario distribution.
workedArithmetic: Sorted losses are [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 20] thousand dollars.
VaR rank = ceiling(0.80 × 10) = 8. The eighth loss is $7 thousand.
The worst 20% contains two losses; Expected Shortfall = (10 + 20) / 2 = $15 thousand.
Two losses strictly exceed 7, so the exceedance fraction = 2/10 = 20%.

formulas.readAloud: Value at Risk is a selected loss quantile: a threshold expected not to be exceeded at the stated confidence level under the model. Expected Shortfall averages losses in the tail beyond that threshold. A threshold alone does not reveal tail severity.

symbols.meaning: Loss quantile at confidence level α under the stated convention.
Average loss in the tail beyond the VaR threshold under the stated inclusion rule.
Loss at sorted rank i.
Confidence level, such as 0.95.
Number of loss observations or simulations.

formulas.readAloud: The nearest-rank convention selects the observation at the ceiling of confidence level times sample size. State this convention because alternative quantile interpolation rules can produce a different cutoff.

symbols.meaning: Selected rank, rounded up under the nearest-rank rule.
Round up to the next whole rank.
Chosen confidence level.
Number of observations.

M34.title: How Much of the Estimate Is Simulation Noise?
M34.scenario: Independent, equally weighted simulation runs estimate the probability of losses exceeding a reserve under one fixed model.
M34.task: Divide breaches by runs, calculate SE = sqrt(p × (1 − p) / N), and form the approximate 95% interval p ± 1.96 × SE. Recalculate SE for the new run count with p held fixed.
M34.interpretation: More independent runs reduce Monte Carlo error. The interval is conditional on the simulation model; it does not include uncertainty about default probabilities, recoveries or correlations. The normal approximation is unsuitable for some small or extreme-probability samples.
M34.summary: Breach estimate: {p}. Approximate interval: {lower} to {upper}. Standard error changes from {SE} to {newSE}.

p.title: Estimated reserve-breach probability
hints: Divide the number of breach runs by the total number of runs.
p.explanation: Divide reserve-breach simulations by all simulation runs. This estimates the breach probability for the simulated assumptions; it is not a guarantee about the next period.

SE.title: Monte Carlo standard error
hints: Calculate the square root of p × (1 − p) / N.
SE.explanation: Calculate the standard error for an estimated proportion using p and the number of independent runs. It approximates simulation sampling noise; it does not include errors in the model assumptions.

lower.title: Approximate 95% lower bound
hints: Subtract 1.96 × standard error from the estimated probability.
lower.explanation: Subtract approximately 1.96 standard errors from the estimated proportion to form a rough lower endpoint for a 95% interval. If the result falls below zero, use a suitable proportion interval method rather than interpreting a negative probability.

upper.title: Approximate 95% upper bound
hints: Add 1.96 × standard error to the estimated probability.
upper.explanation: Add approximately 1.96 standard errors to the estimate for a rough upper endpoint. The interval describes Monte Carlo uncertainty under the simulation setup, not total real-world uncertainty.

newSE.title: Standard error with the new run count
hints: Keep p unchanged and replace N by the new run count in the standard-error formula.
newSE.explanation: Recalculate the standard error using the proposed run count. More independent runs reduce Monte Carlo noise roughly with the square root of the count, while leaving model bias or wrong assumptions unresolved.

readAloud: The estimated breach probability is the fraction of simulation runs that breach the reserve. Its standard error approximates the variation from using a finite random sample of runs. Increasing the run count narrows that sampling uncertainty, but does not fix unrealistic inputs.
workedExplanation: Quadrupling independent runs halves simulation noise. It does not validate assumed default probabilities, recoveries, or correlations. This interval describes uncertainty in the estimated probability conditional on the specified simulation model, not uncertainty about whether that model is realistic.

A single run says breach or no breach. More runs make the average of those binary outcomes more stable. With the probability held fixed, multiplying run count by four divides its standard error by two because the denominator enters under a square root. It does not halve uncertainty about whether the financial assumptions are correct.
workedArithmetic: Estimated breach probability = 250/2,500 = 0.10 = 10%.
At 10,000 runs, SE = √(0.09/10,000) = 0.003, or 0.3 percentage points.

formulas.readAloud: The estimated breach probability is the fraction of simulation runs that breach the reserve. Its standard error approximates the variation from using a finite random sample of runs. Increasing the run count narrows that sampling uncertainty, but does not fix unrealistic inputs.

symbols.meaning: Estimated breach probability: breach runs divided by all runs.
Number of independent simulation runs.
Approximate Monte Carlo standard error of the estimated probability.
Multiplier chosen for the approximate confidence interval, about 1.96 for 95%.

M35.title: Does the Tail Forecast Hold Up?
M35.scenario: A bank compares each day’s actual loss with the VaR forecast made for that day. A strict exceedance is an exception.
M35.task: Calculate the observed exception rate, nominal exceedance rate, expected exception count and observed-to-nominal rate ratio.
M35.interpretation: The nominal count is an expectation, not an automatic acceptance range. Inspect exception clustering, sizes and changing market or data conditions; a count alone cannot identify the cause of a forecasting problem.
M35.summary: Observed exception rate: {observed}; nominal rate: {nominal}. Expected count: {expected}; rate ratio: {ratio}.

labels.exceptions: Days with loss strictly above that day’s VaR

observed.title: Observed exception rate
hints: Divide exception days by evaluated days.
observed.explanation: Divide the number of actual exceptions by the number of forecasts evaluated. This observed rate can be compared with the forecast’s nominal exception rate over the same period.

nominal.title: Nominal exception rate
hints: Subtract the VaR confidence target from 1.
nominal.explanation: Use the stated tail probability implied by the risk forecast. For example, a 99% confidence threshold has a nominal 1% exceedance rate; the two percentages are complements.

expected.title: Nominal expected exceptions
hints: Multiply evaluated days by the nominal exception rate.
expected.explanation: Multiply the nominal exception probability by the number of evaluated periods. This is the average number of exceptions expected under the forecast, not an exact count that every sample must match.

ratio.title: Observed-to-nominal exception-rate ratio
hints: Divide observed rate by nominal rate.
ratio.explanation: Divide the observed exception rate by the nominal rate. A ratio above 1 means exceptions were more frequent than the forecast target; it is a diagnostic signal, not proof of the cause.

readAloud: Compare actual exceptions with the forecast’s nominal tail probability. Expected exception count is nominal rate times the number of periods; the observed-to-nominal ratio shows how often exceptions occurred relative to that target.
A forecast for a 99% confidence threshold implies a 1% tail rate. Put observed and nominal rates on the same proportion scale before comparing.
workedExplanation: The model’s tail forecast deserves investigation: exceptions are more frequent than its nominal target, and many are clustered. Frequency tests, dependence checks, breach sizes, and market or data changes are needed to assess the problem. The count alone does not prove a particular cause or quantify losses beyond VaR.

Using the daily matching forecast matters: comparing every day against one convenient annual-average VaR would change the test. The nominal 1% rate follows from the 99% target; it does not explain why this sample’s observed rate is 4% or why six exceptions appeared close together.
workedDetails: In this worked example, six of the ten exceptions occur within one ten-day period. The annual exception count alone hides that clustering.
workedArithmetic: Observed exception rate = 10/250 = 4%. Nominal rate = 1 − 0.99 = 1%.
Expected exceptions = 250 × 0.01 = 2.5; this is an expectation, not an acceptance range.
Observed-to-nominal rate ratio = 0.04/0.01 = 4. Six exceptions in ten days also reveal clustering that the annual rate does not show.

formulas.readAloud: Compare actual exceptions with the forecast’s nominal tail probability. Expected exception count is nominal rate times the number of periods; the observed-to-nominal ratio shows how often exceptions occurred relative to that target.

symbols.meaning: Observed exceptions divided by evaluated periods.
Nominal exception probability specified by the forecast.
Number of periods evaluated.
Expected exception count under the nominal rate.

formulas.readAloud: A forecast for a 99% confidence threshold implies a 1% tail rate. Put observed and nominal rates on the same proportion scale before comparing.

symbols.meaning: Confidence level.
Nominal probability of an exception beyond the threshold.

M36.title: Better Than the Baseline, Short of Hindsight
M36.scenario: A learned execution policy, TWAP baseline and best feasible hindsight schedule complete the same order. Each comparison includes the same cost components. Reward is negative cost and is undiscounted.
M36.task: Add policy costs, calculate cumulative reward, savings versus TWAP and regret versus hindsight. Convert savings and regret to basis points of order notional.
M36.interpretation: Beating a feasible baseline and matching hindsight are different comparisons. Hindsight has information unavailable to the live policy. Omitted costs or incomplete-order penalties can make a reward misleading.
M36.summary: Cumulative reward: {reward}. Saving versus TWAP: {saving} ({savingBps}); hindsight regret: {regret} ({regretBps}).

cost.title: Policy total execution cost
hints: Add interval costs.
cost.explanation: Add the policy’s execution costs over all trades or periods under the specified cost definition. The total should use the same principal and time window as the comparison policies.

reward.title: Cumulative reward
hints: Negate total cost, since rewards equal negative costs.
reward.explanation: Add the per-period rewards. Here reward is defined as negative execution cost, so higher cumulative reward means lower cost under this setup; it is not investment profit.

saving.title: Saving versus TWAP
hints: Subtract policy cost from TWAP cost.
saving.explanation: Subtract the policy cost from TWAP cost. A positive difference means the policy spent less than the time-weighted average price benchmark in this sample.

regret.title: Regret versus hindsight
hints: Subtract hindsight cost from policy cost.
regret.explanation: Subtract the policy cost from the hindsight cost benchmark using the stated sign convention. Regret measures distance from a best choice that would have required knowing future prices; it is not a feasible strategy available in advance.

savingBps.title: Saving in basis points
hints: Divide dollar saving by order value and multiply by 10,000.
savingBps.explanation: Divide the cost saving by the traded notional and multiply by 10,000 to express it in basis points. One basis point is one hundredth of one percent.

regretBps.title: Regret in basis points
hints: Divide dollar regret by order value and multiply by 10,000.
regretBps.explanation: Divide regret by the same traded notional and convert to basis points. Normalizing permits comparison across order sizes; it does not remove differences in market conditions.

readAloud: In this exercise, reward is negative execution cost, so summing rewards reverses the cost direction. Compare total costs with TWAP for realized savings and with hindsight for regret; hindsight is an unattainable benchmark that knows future prices.
Convert a dollar difference into basis points by dividing by traded notional and multiplying by 10,000. This expresses the amount relative to order size.
Cumulative reward is the sum of period rewards. Since reward is negative cost here, a larger reward means a smaller accumulated cost.
workedExplanation: The policy saves 3 basis points versus TWAP but costs 2 basis points more than the hindsight schedule. Hindsight has information the live policy did not possess. A less negative reward is better here; reward becomes economically misleading if material costs or incomplete-order penalties are omitted.

The policy can beat a realistic baseline while still falling short of hindsight. Those are different comparisons and should not be combined. The order-value denominator turns dollar differences into comparable cost fractions, while the reward sign convention determines which numerical direction is better.
workedArithmetic: Policy cost = $300 + $200 + $400 = $900; cumulative reward = −$900.
Saving versus TWAP = $1,200 − $900 = $300. Hindsight regret = $900 − $700 = $200.
One basis point = $1,000,000 × 0.0001 = $100. Saving = 300/100 = 3 bps; regret = 200/100 = 2 bps.

formulas.readAloud: In this exercise, reward is negative execution cost, so summing rewards reverses the cost direction. Compare total costs with TWAP for realized savings and with hindsight for regret; hindsight is an unattainable benchmark that knows future prices.

symbols.meaning: Execution cost in period t under the exercise definition.
Reward in period t, defined here as negative cost.
Time-weighted average price benchmark cost.
Cost of the hindsight benchmark with future information.
Traded notional used for normalization.

formulas.readAloud: Convert a dollar difference into basis points by dividing by traded notional and multiplying by 10,000. This expresses the amount relative to order size.

symbols.meaning: Basis points; 10,000 basis points equal 100 percent.
Cost saving or regret in dollars, using the stated sign convention.
Traded notional in dollars.

formulas.readAloud: Cumulative reward is the sum of period rewards. Since reward is negative cost here, a larger reward means a smaller accumulated cost.

symbols.meaning: Sum of per-period rewards.
Reward in period t.

M37.title: Completed, Checked, and Within Authority?
M37.scenario: An invoice agent is audited at task and tool-call levels. Success means correct completion plus all required checks. Unsafe-attempt count is the number of tasks with at least one unauthorized attempt.
M37.task: Calculate task success, verification pass rate, unsafe-attempt rate, unsafe-execution rate and tool-call error rate.
M37.interpretation: A task may recover from a tool error and still succeed. A blocked unauthorized attempt remains worth inspecting even when no unauthorized action occurred. These categories overlap and need not sum to 100%.
M37.summary: Task success: {success}; verification: {verification}. Unsafe attempts: {unsafeAttempt}; unsafe executions: {unsafeExecution}; tool errors: {toolError}.

labels.executed: Tasks with an executed unauthorized action

success.title: Task success rate
hints: Divide correctly completed and verified tasks by assigned tasks.
success.explanation: Divide tasks completed successfully by all tasks evaluated. This measures end-to-end task completion, which can differ from whether each field was accurate or each action was authorized.

verification.title: Field-verification pass rate
hints: Divide tasks passing field checks by assigned tasks.
verification.explanation: Divide tasks that passed the required field checks by tasks evaluated. This checks whether outputs matched the verification rules; it should be interpreted beside task success and safety rates.

unsafeAttempt.title: Task-level unauthorized-attempt rate
hints: Divide tasks with an unauthorized attempt by assigned tasks.
unsafeAttempt.explanation: Divide tasks containing an unauthorized attempt by all tasks. This measures attempted policy violations even if the system blocked them before they caused an action.

unsafeExecution.title: Task-level unauthorized-execution rate
hints: Divide tasks with an executed unauthorized action by assigned tasks.
unsafeExecution.explanation: Divide tasks where an unauthorized action actually occurred by all tasks. This is a separate, more severe outcome than an attempted action.

toolError.title: Tool-call error rate
hints: Divide errored tool calls by all tool calls, not by task count.
toolError.explanation: Divide tool calls that returned errors by all tool calls. This rate measures tool reliability; it does not by itself show whether errors harmed a user or were safely recovered.

readAloud: Each operational rate has its own denominator. Task success and unsafe events are counted per task; tool errors are counted per tool call. Keep attempts distinct from actions that actually executed.
A percentage is interpretable only with its numerator, denominator, and observation window. For example, task-level rates use tasks as the denominator while a tool error rate uses calls.
workedExplanation: Passing field checks does not guarantee that an invoice workflow finished. Zero executed unauthorized actions shows that the blocking control worked in this sample—not that the agent never tried to exceed its authority. Tool errors use a different denominator from task outcomes and may be recoverable. Inspect the four unsafe-attempt traces even when final task results look acceptable.

A recovered tool error can occur during a task that ultimately succeeds. An unsafe attempt can also be blocked before causing an unauthorized action. These counts therefore need not be mutually exclusive or add to 100%; each rate measures a distinct failure or control outcome.
workedArithmetic: Task success = 90/100 = 90%; field-verification pass rate = 95/100 = 95%.
Unauthorized-attempt rate = 4/100 = 4%; unauthorized-execution rate = 0/100 = 0%.
Tool-call error rate = 10/200 = 5%. Its denominator is tool calls, not assigned tasks.

formulas.readAloud: Each operational rate has its own denominator. Task success and unsafe events are counted per task; tool errors are counted per tool call. Keep attempts distinct from actions that actually executed.

symbols.meaning: Successfully completed tasks divided by tasks evaluated.
Tasks passing the required checks divided by tasks evaluated.
Tasks with an unauthorized attempt divided by tasks evaluated.
Tasks with an unauthorized action executed divided by tasks evaluated.
Failed tool calls divided by tool calls made.

formulas.readAloud: A percentage is interpretable only with its numerator, denominator, and observation window. For example, task-level rates use tasks as the denominator while a tool error rate uses calls.

symbols.meaning: Count of cases with the named outcome.
Number of tasks or calls observed, as appropriate.
x divided by the matching denominator n.

M38.title: Has the Applicant Mix Changed?
M38.scenario: Credit scores use two identical bands in both periods: lower risk, then higher risk. Current and reference shares are positive and sum to one.
M38.task: For each band calculate (current − reference) × ln(current/reference). Add the contributions for PSI and calculate the higher-risk share change.
M38.interpretation: PSI measures distribution change without using realized outcome labels. It cannot establish accuracy deterioration or its cause. Investigate population, policy and data changes before drawing conclusions.

labels.current: Current band shares (lower risk, higher risk)
labels.reference: Reference band shares (lower risk, higher risk)

terms.title: PSI contribution from each band
hints: Multiply each share difference by the natural log of the current-to-reference ratio.
terms.explanation: For each applicant band, compute that band’s contribution from the difference between the new and reference shares, using the logarithm of their ratio. A zero share needs a stated smoothing convention because its logarithm is undefined.

PSI.title: Population stability index
hints: Add the band contributions.
PSI.explanation: Add the band contributions to get Population Stability Index. A larger value signals a bigger distribution shift under this measure, but cutoffs are rules of thumb and the index does not tell whether model performance worsened.

shift.title: Change in the higher-risk share
hints: Subtract reference higher-risk share from current higher-risk share.
shift.explanation: Compare the share of applicants in the higher-risk bands between the reference and current populations. This makes the direction of one meaningful mix change visible; overall PSI alone does not say which group changed.

readAloud: Population Stability Index adds band-by-band differences between current and reference shares, weighted by the log of their ratio. It flags changes in the input mix; it does not prove performance drift or explain why the population changed.
workedExplanation: The score distribution has changed. Investigate applicant channels, product mix, policy changes, and the data pipeline. PSI is not an accuracy score or a default-rate estimate; outcome labels are needed to assess prediction quality. Identical band shares would give PSI of zero, but zero PSI would not guarantee a sound model.

For the lower band, both the share change and the log ratio are negative, producing a positive contribution. For the higher band, both are positive. The sum records the distribution change without establishing that predictions became wrong or that default rates actually rose.
workedArithmetic: PSI ≈ 0.27489 + 0.14100 = 0.41589. Higher-risk share increased by 80% − 50% = 30 percentage points.

formulas.readAloud: Population Stability Index adds band-by-band differences between current and reference shares, weighted by the log of their ratio. It flags changes in the input mix; it does not prove performance drift or explain why the population changed.

symbols.meaning: Sum of distribution-shift contributions across the supplied bands.
Current population share in band i.
Reference population share in band i.
Natural logarithm of the current-to-reference share ratio.

M39a.title: The Average Can Pass While the Service Fails
M39a.scenario: Requests are grouped by eventual response time. A response after the caller’s deadline is a failure even if it eventually arrives; a response at the deadline is on time.
M39a.task: Calculate total response-time sum, mean, nearest-rank p95 and p99, late fraction and on-time fraction. The service objective is 99% on time.
M39a.interpretation: Weight each duration by its request count. The mean and one percentile can look good while the deadline objective fails. Use the stated percentile and timeout conventions when comparing services.
M39a.summary: Mean latency: {mean}; p95: {p95}; p99: {p99}. On-time share: {onTime}.

total.title: Sum of request response times
hints: Multiply each group’s count by its duration, then add.
total.explanation: Add response times for all requests in the observation window. The total is useful for computing the mean but can be dominated by system volume and says little about the slowest individual requests.

mean.title: Mean request latency
hints: Divide total response-time sum by total requests.
mean.explanation: Divide total response time by request count. This average gives a broad typical value, but a small number of very slow requests can be hidden by many fast ones.

p95.title: 95th-percentile latency
hints: Select rank ceiling(0.95 × request count) in the expanded sorted request list.
p95.explanation: Sort the response times and locate the 95th percentile using the stated convention. About 95% of requests are at or below this time; the remaining tail can still affect users severely.

p99.title: 99th-percentile latency
hints: Select rank ceiling(0.99 × request count) in the expanded sorted request list.
p99.explanation: Locate the 99th percentile the same way. This focuses on the slowest one percent of requests and can reveal a tail problem that mean latency misses.

late.title: Deadline-failure rate
hints: Count requests with duration strictly above the deadline and divide by all requests.
late.explanation: Divide requests that exceeded the service deadline by all requests. This directly measures deadline failures during this window; it does not explain whether the cause was service capacity, network delay, or another bottleneck.

onTime.title: On-time rate
hints: Subtract the deadline-failure rate from 1.
onTime.explanation: Subtract the late share from 1, or divide on-time requests by all requests. This is the proportion meeting the deadline and should be reported with the threshold and time window.

readAloud: Mean latency averages all request times, while the 95th and 99th percentiles describe slower parts of the distribution. Deadline-failure rate counts requests above a specified limit. Report the window and percentile convention because averages can hide tail delays.
The mean is total response time divided by requests. The late rate is requests above deadline divided by all requests, and on-time rate is its complement when each request is classified once.
workedExplanation: The mean and p95 look fast, but the 99%-within-100-ms objective is missed. Five payment decisions arrive too late for the caller. The percentile convention and treatment of late responses are stated explicitly so the result can be reproduced.

The 95 fast requests dominate the average and determine p95. The next four requests determine p99 and create deadline failures along with the slowest request. Averaging the three latency values without their request counts would give each group the wrong weight.
workedArithmetic: p95 is request rank 95, at 40 ms. p99 is rank 99, among the 180 ms requests.
Late requests = 4 + 1 = 5. Deadline-failure rate = 5/100 = 5%; on-time rate = 95%, below the 99% objective.

formulas.readAloud: Mean latency averages all request times, while the 95th and 99th percentiles describe slower parts of the distribution. Deadline-failure rate counts requests above a specified limit. Report the window and percentile convention because averages can hide tail delays.

symbols.meaning: Response time for request i, in the stated time unit.
Number of requests observed.
Latency at or below which 95% of requests fall.
Latency at or below which 99% of requests fall.
Deadline threshold used to classify late requests.

formulas.readAloud: The mean is total response time divided by requests. The late rate is requests above deadline divided by all requests, and on-time rate is its complement when each request is classified once.

symbols.meaning: Sum of observed response times.
Number of observed requests.
Requests exceeding the deadline.
Maximum response time considered on time.

M39b.title: Calculate Both Bottlenecks
M39b.scenario: A scoring API and a human investigation team have separate queues. Both start empty, arrivals and completion rates stay constant, and no items are dropped.
M39b.task: Convert API capacity to requests per second and calculate its backlog after the supplied minutes. Separately calculate human daily capacity, daily excess, multi-day backlog and per-analyst pace needed to keep up.
M39b.interpretation: Increasing API speed does not increase human review capacity. Multiply a rate gap by matching elapsed time to obtain a backlog count; do not confuse that count with latency.
M39b.summary: API backlog: {requestBacklog} requests. Human backlog: {alertBacklog} alerts. Required analyst pace: {requiredPace}.

labels.pace: Cases completed per analyst per day

capacity.title: API capacity per second
hints: Divide requests-per-minute capacity by 60.
capacity.explanation: Multiply the number of API workers or servers by the request rate each can safely handle per second. This is estimated service capacity under the stated conditions, not necessarily sustained real-world throughput.

requestBacklog.title: API request backlog
hints: Multiply positive arrival-minus-capacity gap by elapsed seconds.
requestBacklog.explanation: Compare incoming request rate with service capacity over the stated seconds. If arrivals exceed processing, the difference accumulates as waiting requests; if capacity is higher, this simplified queue does not grow.

human.title: Daily human review capacity
hints: Multiply analyst count by cases per analyst per day.
human.explanation: Multiply the number of reviewers by cases each can complete in a day. This is daily human capacity and depends on the same working-day assumptions as the incoming alert count.

dailyBacklog.title: Daily added alert backlog
hints: Subtract daily human capacity from new daily alerts; use zero if capacity is sufficient.
dailyBacklog.explanation: Subtract daily reviewer capacity from alerts arriving each day, keeping positive excess. This is the daily increase in unfinished work when demand exceeds review capacity.

alertBacklog.title: Alert backlog after the supplied days
hints: Multiply daily added backlog by elapsed days.
alertBacklog.explanation: Multiply the daily excess by the number of days, then add any starting backlog. This simplified estimate assumes arrivals and capacity stay constant; real queues can vary day to day.

requiredPace.title: Required cases per analyst per day
hints: Divide incoming daily alerts by analyst count.
requiredPace.explanation: Divide the alert workload that must be cleared by available analysts and days. This is the cases-per-person-per-day pace required; compare it with realistic capacity before accepting the plan.

readAloud: A backlog grows when arrivals exceed processing capacity. Calculate API requests per second and human reviews per day separately because their units and bottlenecks differ; do not add them into one queue.
For human review, daily excess alerts equal arrivals minus cases reviewed when that difference is positive. Over several days, backlog grows by the daily excess if rates remain constant.
Required pace divides the workload by the available person-days. The result must be compared with a realistic per-person capacity and must use matching time units.
workedExplanation: There are two separate capacity failures: scoring cannot keep up with incoming payments, and investigators cannot work the generated queue. Increasing API capacity would not fix the review backlog. A threshold or staffing change must account for the fraud that would remain unreviewed.

A rate difference has units of requests per second or alerts per day. Multiplying by matching elapsed time produces a count. Keeping the units explicit prevents confusing 12,000 requests per minute with 12,000 per second, or interpreting a queue count as a response time.
workedArithmetic: API capacity = 12,000/60 = 200 requests/second. Arrival excess = 250 − 200 = 50 requests/second.
Ten-minute API backlog = 50 × 10 × 60 = 30,000 requests.
Human capacity = 15 × 20 = 300 cases/day. Daily backlog growth = 500 − 300 = 200 alerts; three-day backlog = 200 × 3 = 600.
Required analyst pace = 500/15 ≈ 33.33 cases/day, compared with the supplied capacity of 20.

formulas.readAloud: A backlog grows when arrivals exceed processing capacity. Calculate API requests per second and human reviews per day separately because their units and bottlenecks differ; do not add them into one queue.

symbols.meaning: Incoming request or alert rate, in its stated time unit.
Processing capacity in the same unit.
Unfinished work accumulated as backlog.
Duration over which excess arrivals accumulate.

formulas.readAloud: For human review, daily excess alerts equal arrivals minus cases reviewed when that difference is positive. Over several days, backlog grows by the daily excess if rates remain constant.

symbols.meaning: Alerts arriving per day.
Cases reviewers can complete per day.
Number of days in the estimate.
Starting backlog, if any.

formulas.readAloud: Required pace divides the workload by the available person-days. The result must be compared with a realistic per-person capacity and must use matching time units.

symbols.meaning: Total cases that must be completed.
Number of analysts.
Available working days.

M39c.title: Price the Entire Workflow
M39c.scenario: A financial assistant either answers automatically or abstains and routes to human review. Every reviewed request is resolved correctly. Model-and-retrieval spending includes all requests, including abstentions.
M39c.task: Calculate routing rates, review spending, all-in operating cost and costs per incoming request and per correct resolution. Also calculate accuracy among automatic answers. Exclude downstream financial harm.
M39c.interpretation: Use all operating spending in both cost numerators. Automatic-answer accuracy uses automatic answers as its denominator; cost per correct resolution includes correct human resolutions. Operating cost alone omits harm from wrong answers.
M39c.summary: Operating cost: {totalCost}; per incoming request: {perRequest}; per correct resolution: {perCorrect}. Automatic-answer accuracy: {autoAccuracy}.

abstention.title: Abstention rate
hints: Divide reviewed requests by incoming requests.
abstention.explanation: Divide requests sent for human review or left unanswered by all incoming requests. Abstention can improve the quality of automatic answers, but it moves work and cost to the review path.

coverage.title: Automatic-answer coverage
hints: Divide incoming minus reviewed requests by incoming requests.
coverage.explanation: Subtract the abstention share from 1 when every non-abstained request receives an automatic answer. Coverage measures how much work automation handles; it is not the same as correctness.

reviewSpend.title: Human review spending
hints: Multiply reviewed requests by cost per review.
reviewSpend.explanation: Multiply abstained requests by the cost of one human review. This is review spending for the stated volume and unit cost; it excludes automation costs unless specified.

totalCost.title: Total operating cost
hints: Add model/retrieval spending and human review spending.
totalCost.explanation: Add human review spending and the other supplied operating costs. Include only cost categories defined by the exercise and keep them on the same time and request basis.

perRequest.title: Cost per incoming request
hints: Divide total operating cost by incoming requests.
perRequest.explanation: Divide total operating cost by all incoming requests, including those sent to review. This measures average cost per request handled by the whole workflow.

correct.title: Correctly resolved requests
hints: Add correct automatic answers and all reviewed requests.
correct.explanation: Multiply automatically answered requests by their accuracy rate and add correctly resolved reviewed cases if the definition includes them. Follow the stated correctness definition so numerator and denominator align.

perCorrect.title: Cost per correct resolution
hints: Divide total operating cost by correctly resolved requests.
perCorrect.explanation: Divide total workflow cost by correctly resolved requests. This is cost per successful resolution; if no request is correctly resolved, the value is undefined.

autoAccuracy.title: Accuracy among automatic answers
hints: Divide correct automatic answers by incoming minus reviewed requests.
autoAccuracy.explanation: Divide correct answers among automatically handled requests by all automatic answers. This checks the quality of the automated subset; it says nothing about coverage or the reviewed cases.

readAloud: Automation coverage and accuracy answer different questions. Coverage is the share handled automatically; accuracy is the share of those automatic answers that are correct. Abstentions shift requests to review, which adds cost but may protect answer quality.
Human review spending is reviewed volume times cost per review. Add other stated operating expenses to obtain total cost, then divide by all requests or correct resolutions depending on the question.
Cost per successful resolution uses correct outcomes in the denominator; cost per incoming request uses all incoming cases. These are different service measures and can move in opposite directions.
workedExplanation: Abstention adds review expense and routes those cases to correct manual resolution under the exercise’s assumptions. Model spend alone understates operating cost. Even the all-in $0.80 per request excludes the consequences of the 100 wrong answers; it is not a complete economic loss measure.

The same numerical fraction can represent different concepts: 800/900 is automatic-answer accuracy, while $800 divided by 900 correct resolutions is a cost in dollars. The numerator’s units and the denominator’s population determine the meaning. The scenario does not establish what automatic answers would have been produced on the abstained cases.
workedArithmetic: Abstention = 100/1,000 = 10%; automatic coverage = (1,000 − 100) / 1,000 = 90%.
Review spending = 100 × $3 = $300; total operating cost = $500 + $300 = $800.
Cost per incoming request = $800/1,000 = $0.80. Correct resolutions = 800 + 100 = 900; cost per correct resolution = $800/900 ≈ $0.89.
Automatic-answer accuracy = 800/900 ≈ 88.89%. This shares the numerical fraction with cost per correct resolution but has different units and meaning.

formulas.readAloud: Automation coverage and accuracy answer different questions. Coverage is the share handled automatically; accuracy is the share of those automatic answers that are correct. Abstentions shift requests to review, which adds cost but may protect answer quality.

symbols.meaning: Automatically handled requests divided by all incoming requests.
Requests diverted from automatic handling divided by all requests.
Correct automatic answers divided by automatic answers.
Total incoming requests.
Requests answered automatically.

formulas.readAloud: Human review spending is reviewed volume times cost per review. Add other stated operating expenses to obtain total cost, then divide by all requests or correct resolutions depending on the question.

symbols.meaning: Cost of human review.
Number of requests sent to human review.
Cost per reviewed request.
All included workflow costs.

formulas.readAloud: Cost per successful resolution uses correct outcomes in the denominator; cost per incoming request uses all incoming cases. These are different service measures and can move in opposite directions.

symbols.meaning: Total workflow cost for the observed period.
Number of requests resolved correctly under the stated definition.
All incoming requests.

M39d.title: Translate the Percentage into Minutes
M39d.scenario: A service is scheduled continuously for the supplied number of days. Use time-based availability, not request-weighted success.
M39d.task: Convert the scheduled period to minutes, calculate available minutes and availability, then compute downtime allowed by the objective and downtime beyond that allowance.
M39d.interpretation: An availability percentage must be compared with its exact target. Time-based availability also does not reveal how many requests were affected or whether downtime coincided with peak demand.
M39d.summary: Achieved availability: {availability}. Allowed downtime: {allowed}; downtime beyond allowance: {excess}.

scheduled.title: Scheduled service minutes
hints: Multiply scheduled days by 24 × 60.
scheduled.explanation: Multiply the number of minutes in the reporting period by the scheduled operating share. This is the time during which the service was expected to be available.

available.title: Available service minutes
hints: Subtract unavailable minutes from scheduled minutes.
available.explanation: Subtract downtime from scheduled service minutes. Planned exclusions should follow the stated availability definition; changing that definition changes the result.

availability.title: Time-based availability
hints: Divide available minutes by scheduled minutes.
availability.explanation: Divide available service minutes by scheduled service minutes and convert to a percentage. This measures time-based availability over this window, not whether every request was fast or successful.

allowed.title: Downtime allowed by the objective
hints: Multiply scheduled minutes by 1 − objective.
allowed.explanation: Multiply scheduled service minutes by the downtime fraction permitted by the availability objective. This gives the time budget for downtime during the period.

excess.title: Downtime beyond the allowance
hints: Subtract allowed downtime from actual downtime; use zero when the objective is met.
excess.explanation: Subtract allowed downtime from actual downtime and keep a positive result. This is how far the service exceeded its objective’s downtime allowance, not necessarily the cause of the outage.

readAloud: Availability is available service time divided by scheduled service time. Convert the target percentage into its complementary allowed downtime fraction, then compare actual downtime with that allowance. State the reporting window and planned-maintenance rule.
The downtime budget is scheduled time times one minus the availability target. Comparing actual downtime with this budget shows whether the objective was met during this particular window.
workedExplanation: “Over 99% available” is not enough for the specified 99.9% objective. The service was unavailable for more than twice its allotted downtime. Time-based availability also does not reveal how many payment requests were affected or whether the outage coincided with peak demand.

A target of 99.9% leaves 0.1% of scheduled time for unavailability, not 0.9%. Multiplying that small fraction by the full month’s minutes makes the allowance concrete. The same outage length can affect very different payment volumes depending on when it occurs.
